66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary:
Visitors stand under the national framework in every state: federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker was eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor's documents can mismatch; airport screening and visa decisions follow national rules, including visa discretion over transgender athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events.

Idaho carries the country's strictest criminalised restroom regime. Its 2026 facility-use law, effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching their birth sex — in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants and hospitals — with a misdemeanour of up to one year and a felony of up to five years on a repeat within five years. Four successive legislative rounds ran from 2023 to 2026, alongside a ban on official recognition of Pride flags.

A federal lawsuit followed the law's passage; contemporaneous reporting states the law was partially blocked, leaving it in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Since then a March 2026 bill extending felony restroom penalties to all public accommodations has passed the House, a March 2026 forced-outting statute has been signed, a birth-marker freeze has been in effect since January 2026, and the federation's Supreme Court declined in 2024 to review the state's bar on gender-affirming care.

First offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to a year in jail. The ACLU filed suit on 30 April 2026 arguing due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations, noting the law targets no actual criminal conduct.
National wire reporting covers the legislature passing the transgender bathroom ban and jail threats, and the lawsuit that partially blocked it.

Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

The consequence axis reaches custody on two fronts: the Women's Privacy Act expressly applies to prisons and other state government buildings — but on restroom use matching the sex on one's birth certificate, not on cell or facility assignment — while in Gibson v. Collier (2019) the Texas prison system denied a transgender inmate gender-confirmation surgery under its official policy, and the courts affirmed no deliberate indifference, treating the refusal as a permissible medical choice, leaving a trans person in Texas custody without a proven judicial remedy for denial of gender-affirming care.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and voids state-issued IDs with corrected markers — licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified. The law also creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.

sources.summary: ACLU of Kansas SB 244 FAQ: the law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities and creates new civil and criminal penalties. The reclassification follows the new bathroom-bounty law, which lets private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities. The assessment addresses interstate-travel exposure.

sources.title: Trans Teen Cannot Change Name, Mississippi Supreme Court Rules - Mississippi Free Press
sources.summary: Mississippi Free Press/AP (23 Apr 2025): on 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the trans boy as a 'minor female' and cited the 2023 REAP Act - which bans both surgical and non-surgical treatments for transgender minors - as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest. 66186276B98021244841737.name: Alabama
66186276B98021244841737.summary:
Alabama stands under the United States national framework, which applies in every state. Travel documents are the sharpest exposure: since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Identity documents are the fastest-moving area of restriction at state level. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a visitor encounters depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Alabama's own facility bans, enacted in 2022 and 2024, are in force. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update records that Alabama's 'Don't Say Gay' bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, placing the state in the assessment's worst-law grouping of legislatively-eroding jurisdictions. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates these state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. Following the federal document and data rules, multiple countries issued advisories warning their trans citizens about travelling to the United States. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Internal risk assessments are equally stark. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Recorded killings of trans women in Alabama stand at 3.8 per 100,000 per year, an undercount floor, on the 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025, according to The Needle's July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams data. That analysis grades Alabama in the worst-law group.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data) records Alabama's killing rate of trans women at 3.8 per 100k per year, an undercount floor, on the 428-victim 2008–2025 base. The state is graded in the worst-law group.

sources.title: Indiana bans driver's license gender changes despite public pushback
sources.summary: Indiana residents lost the option to change their gender marker on driver's licenses or other identification cards when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles' new ban took effect on Feb. 1, 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court-ordered gender change or physician statement. The ban culminates an administrative rule change the BMV initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents. Pending Indiana Senate Bill 182 would create legal definitions for sex and gender, ban amendments to birth certificates, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons.

sources.title: Indiana Senate backs bill restricting transgender school restroom use
sources.summary: On Jan. 27, 2026, Indiana Senate Republicans approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House; the bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on their reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. Author Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women 'continue to have their private spaces'; opponents including GenderNexus argued that letting anyone 'directly or indirectly injured' sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

sources.title: Indiana Supreme Court denies birth certificate gender change in split ruling
sources.summary: In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases of transgender girls seeking to change the gender on their birth certificates; the denials left appeals-court rulings standing that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One case involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access. This is the court outcome that kept Indiana's birth-certificate gender-marker change off limits ahead of the 2026 identity-document law.

sources.title: Utah joins 10 other states in regulating bathroom access for transgender people

66186276B86295910312663.name: Arkansas
66186276B86295910312663.summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Arkansas restricts trans students' use of school facilities. Act 619 became law on 11 April 2023, making Arkansas the fourth state to confine trans students to bathrooms matching their birth sex in K-12 schools, and the provision was amended and extended in 2025. It remains in force. Because the statute is directed at schools, a visitor's direct exposure to it is narrower than in states whose bans reach adult facilities in government buildings and other public places.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 and published on 27 August 2026 places Arkansas in its 'Worst States' tier, one of sixteen states graded at that level, below the four states designated Do Not Travel. The same assessment records a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect' for the 2026 legislative season.

sources.summary: The Movement Advancement Project (MAP) equality-map page catalogues state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity. Its Feb 2026 citations PDF is cited for HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. Both the page URL and the citations PDF return 404; MAP has moved the page.

Erin In The Morning, 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map: July 2026' (Stonewall News, published 27 Aug 2026): a per-state legal-risk grading of anti-trans law. The adult map lists 'Do Not Travel (FL, ID, KS, TX)' and 'The Worst States (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY)' - this state is in the worst group. The update records Idaho's promotion to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years; partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists), Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, and a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'.

The page also notes Arkansas was the first state (2021) to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, a law a federal judge enjoined for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation continued, and that state law has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981. sources.title: Iowa enacts transgender bathroom bill and ban on gender-affirming care for minors
sources.summary: Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds signed two bills on March 22, 2023: Senate File 538 bars doctors from administering gender-affirming care to anyone under 18 (covering puberty blockers, hormone therapy and transition-related surgeries), and Senate File 482 prevents transgender students from entering school bathrooms or changing rooms that correspond with their gender identities. The restroom restriction applies to multiperson restrooms and locker rooms at public and private elementary and secondary schools and took effect immediately, with single-person facilities available to trans students who obtain written consent from legal guardians. Names both statutes behind this record's Iowa summary.

Iowa Dept. of Human Services that the state discriminated against two transgender women by denying their Medicaid claims for transition-related surgery, holding that excluding Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming surgery violates the Iowa Civil Rights Act. Documents the Iowa court carve-back of the state's surgery-coverage ban for adults that this record references.

66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Visitors stand under the national framework in every state: federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker was eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor's documents can mismatch; airport screening and visa decisions follow national rules, including visa discretion over transgender athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events.

Florida's 2023 facilities law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes remaining in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — once a government employee orders departure. It applies in every building owned or leased by the state or local government — offices, courthouses, legislative buildings, prisons/jails, parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private, with only private businesses outside it. For every trans visitor whose document marker differs from presentation, this is universal, continuous exposure: every bathroom or changing-facility use inside a covered venue is a possible trigger, and the exposure holds regardless of how often the law is enforced.

The exposure is invoked, not hypothetical: in March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested for using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban — and a Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 only on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. That dismissal is a procedural outcome, not evidence of limited force: among at least 14 states with facility restrictions, only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning trans travellers and movers of the risks.

Legal exposure and street-level violence are independent visitor risks, and both are documented here: a July 2026 analysis over 2008–2025 data scores Florida 8.0 on an anti-trans law scale and labels the state 'Do Not Travel', while recording 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year — itself an undercount floor and below the average of the worst-law states.

Private businesses are outside its scope; the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

NBC News (2025): Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after declaring 'I am here to break the law' and entering a women's restroom — believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. She faces a misdemeanor trespass charge punishable by up to 60 days in jail; at least 14 states have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Metro Weekly (July 6, 2025): On June 20, 2025, Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw out the trespass case against Marcy Rheintgen. As a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. She had been charged March 19, 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Statehouse.

Equality Florida travel advisory (April 12, 2023): the organization took the 'unprecedented step' of warning about risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people, reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks, and book bans/curriculum censorship. The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; EQFL reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

National law-vs-violence analysis (2008-2025 data): Florida scores 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year, labelled 'Do Not Travel'; the article's core finding is that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates (trendline nearly flat across the 26 states with data) — legal climate and street-level violence are independent visitor risks.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States — Wikipedia (federal prison-placement rule + August 2022 Nebraska ruling)
sources.summary: In August 2022 a federal judge in Nebraska ruled against a transgender woman who had been denied gender-affirming care in prison and placed in a cell with a male sex offender who sexually assaulted her, holding there was insufficient evidence of deliberate indifference to her gender dysphoria and that she had not proven more than minimal injuries from the assault, and finding no support that a substantial risk could be inferred from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction 'coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison.' Nebraska housed her by assigned sex at birth in a men's prison, and the placement followed her there. Federal Bureau of Prisons policy permitted transfer to facilities of the gender prisoners identify with under January 2017 Obama-era guidelines until May 11 2018, when the BOP rescinded them so that assigned sex at birth determines where trans prisoners are jailed.

sources.title: Transgender inmate loses lawsuit over prison's treatment for her gender dysphoria — Lori Pilger, Lincoln Journal Star (via Norfolk Daily News, archived)
sources.summary: The Lincoln Journal Star reported that on Aug. 10, 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for Nebraska prison officials and workers sued by a transgender inmate identified only as 'Jane Doe', who was diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning to be a woman while held in Nebraska's men's prison. The judge dismissed her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her: he had previously dismissed the claim that guards failed to protect her after she was placed in a cell with a convicted sex offender who victimized her, wrote that 'without medical evidence, no reasonable jury could conclude that the providers were deliberately indifferent to Doe's serious medical need', and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. Nebraska housed her by assigned birth sex among male prisoners and celled her with a male sex offender.

66186276B62688952876525.name: Alaska
66186276B62688952876525.summary:
Alaska stands within the United States national framework, so the federal document rules bind every traveller arriving in Juneau, Anchorage or anywhere else in the state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid only until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the Department to proceed with its changed treatment. A visitor's passport can therefore mismatch their presentation and be lawfully refused a matching marker.

Entry screening carries two further national exposures. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose trans status to TSA officers and other passengers.

Alaska's own record is graded Moderate in Erin In The Morning's national legal-risk assessment of July 2026, grouped with Kentucky and North Carolina: states that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. That places Alaska above the worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below the protective groupings, slightly below the national score of 0.36. Idaho was flagged do-not-travel on 13 July 2026, bringing the total of so-designated states to four; Alaska is not among them.

Restriction in Alaska has arrived through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. The Alaska State Medical Board, whose members are appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation classifying gender-transition care for anyone under 18 as 'unprofessional conduct' subject to disciplinary action. That draft must still be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then pass through a 30-day public comment period, so it is not yet in force. No adult-care ban accompanies it.

Facility rules in Alaska are local rather than statewide. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to permanently require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex at birth or a private option such as the nurse's office, overturning guidelines that had stood for more than seven years; AP described the policy as an apparent first for Alaska. It binds a school district, not adult access to public facilities, and no adult facility ban is recorded for the state. Nine states and one territory do have school and government-building bathroom bans, and in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Gov. Dunleavy's earlier bid to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while a board he appointed limited transgender girls' participation in girls' sports teams. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no facility ban at all, and the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates, so the document rules a visitor encounters after entry depend on the state involved. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

66186276B89395128410123.name: Arizona
66186276B89395128410123.summary:
Arizona lies within the United States federal framework, and that framework governs the documents a trans visitor carries. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire.

Documentation failures are documented rather than hypothetical. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 places Arizona in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. Arizona and Virginia are named as having enacted policies affecting trans youth which the assessment's author judges unlikely to be extended to adults. The classification records restraint rather than protection: no extraordinary protective measures for trans visitors are recorded for Arizona.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules with public warnings. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

sources.title: Transgender legal history in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners has shifted repeatedly. A January 2015 ICE memo directed housing transgender immigration detainees according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual in the opposite direction, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and making placement 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination', with gender identity used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware-specific placement policy is documented.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ rights in Michigan - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQIA+ rights in Michigan page records that on 8 March 2023 Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed the first major expansion of the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, codifying sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections into state law, with such discrimination already unlawful since a July 2022 Michigan Supreme Court ruling. The legislature also banned conversion therapy (2023) and the gay/trans panic defense (2024), and a March 2025 House resolution urged the state high-school athletic association to exclude transgender athletes from girls' sports. Directly supports the record's 'fairly robust non-discrimination policies' characterization.

sources.title: Michigan House advises MHSAA to ban transgender athletes from girls' sports - Upper Michigan's Source
sources.summary: Upper Michigan's Source (13 March 2025, by Stephen DeLadurantaye) reported from Lansing that the Michigan House passed a non-binding resolution urging the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) to ban transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. The measure is advisory only and does not change state law or the state's non-discrimination protections.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nevada - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's state page for Nevada records that the state's anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, and that since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required and similar changes available for driver's licenses and state IDs; a May 2017 law (signed June 22, 2017) abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents. In March 2018 the state's Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex-reassignment surgery costs, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and Nevada offers an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licenses, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required (2019). In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, while the legislature-passed 2023 omnibus bill SB 302 shielding gender-affirming care and abortion was vetoed by the governor; a separate June 2023 bill requiring health insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments became law effective January 1, 2024. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Federal policy applying within Nevada: on January 20, 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14168 ('Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government'), recognising only two sexes based on gametes, revoking federal recognition of a third gender, and directing agencies to implement the binary definition. On January 22, 2025 the State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes, ending the 'X' passport option available on a self-identification basis from 2022 to 2025; passports issued before January 2025 with markers not matching assigned sex remain valid. On June 18, 2025 the US Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Skrmetti that state bans on gender-affirming care for minors are constitutional.

sources.title: Transgender legal history in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018. A January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and replacing it with placement on 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination' and gender identity is used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware- or Maryland-specific placement policy is covered.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Accounts of trans women held in men's facilities describe the V-coding practice of assigning trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterized as 'a central part of a trans woman's sentence'. Trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often criminally charged with assault and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge then used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found that 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported being made to perform unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault, and 88% reported a 'marriage-like relationship'. No Maryland-specific placement rule, special unit, or named case is recorded.

sources.title: Colorado Supreme Court sides with transgender youth in fight against Children's Hospital Colorado
sources.summary: The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on May 18, 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated the state's anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume the care, covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity.' Two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.

sources.title: Colorado voters will decide whether to ban trans kids from gendered sports, outlaw gender-affirming surgery for children
sources.summary: Colorado voters will decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender kids from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after state elections officials certified voter signatures on the three measures, including Initiative 108 on child sex trafficking (The Colorado Sun, Mar. 17, 2026). The initiatives were pushed by conservative activists and would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into state law.

sources.title: Colorado to suspend Medicaid coverage for some gender-affirming care for youth due to new federal rule
sources.summary: Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning Oct. 13, 2026, because a new federal rule finalized in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care for people under 18 (and under 19 under the CHP+ child program); the state's Medicaid agency said resuming coverage 'will require legislative action' (The Colorado Sun, Aug. 21, 2026). About 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, and patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period while behavioural healthcare is unaffected. The suspension shows Colorado's protections operating under direct federal-funding pressure, relevant to a trans visitor's assessment of the state.

Polis) required CDOC to expand health care and create voluntary specialized housing — a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison — and to pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. Placement axis: no identity-based-housing statute; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief achieved through litigation and consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

sources.title: CeCe McDonald (Wikipedia; Minnesota prisoner-placement case)
sources.summary: Documented Minnesota DOC placement practice, birth-sex determined: CeCe McDonald, a transgender woman, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was 'no way' she would be sent to a women's prison and 'really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity'. The Minnesota Department of Corrections placed her in an adult male facility, Minnesota Correctional Facility - St. Cloud, after a state gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility; despite a later transfer to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment (a petition during her imprisonment led DOC to administer the correct hormone regimen). She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial, and in May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound requiring eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation.

Federal 2025 document and passport restrictions still apply here as across the federation.

Washington is listed in mapresearch.org's nationwide tracker of states with shield laws or executive orders (2023 and 2024 batches) enforceable against out-of-state action, and appears in the full all-states directory.

sources.published: 2026-09-19 (revision 1375707468; section reports events of Oct 2023 and Jul 2024)
sources.summary: Prison section: in October 2023, Washington state prisons (under court order and rulings) were legally required to provide gender-affirming healthcare and/or sexual-reassignment surgery to inmates; in July 2024, a trans woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison. Placement outcome documented: birth-sex (men's) housing used as sanction in 2024.

64170238B96397749018979.name: Monaco
64170238B96397749018979.summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. A visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever: no bathroom laws, no border friction (a tiny tourist enclave embedded in the neighbouring country of France, entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans incidents, and street violence of any kind is rare in this heavily-policed, very low-crime destination.

The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness: no functioning legal gender recognition process and limited explicit trans protections.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

An autonomous constituent country within a Western European kingdom, Aruba legislates positively rather than merely tolerating: its parliament voted 11-5 in 2016 to open registered unions carrying married-couple benefits (pension succession, emergency medical decisions) — the first island in the Caribbean to act, by its own government's account — and the official tourism authority runs a dedicated LGBT programme marketing the island as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly a hundred nationalities resident.

Travel-culture reporting through the kingdom's networks characterises Aruba, with its two sister islands, as quiet, tolerant and mostly open — a small, stable, tourism-dependent society. The parliamentary vote's own record notes religious and cultural opposition to full equal marriage, which remains unlegislated, and no local gender-recognition or specialist-care pathway is evidenced. No enforcement against trans or same-sex visitors is documented anywhere in the record: protection by registered partnership and tourism economics rather than full equality.

sources.summary: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

SYN-ABW.tangentialFactors: By the government's own account, the 2016 vote made Aruba the first in the region to act on registered unions. Religious and cultural opposition, recorded in the very account of the parliamentary vote, confined the outcome to partnerships rather than full equal marriage — a regional-comparison context rather than anything enforceable against visitors.
SYN-ABW.localsOnly: No purely resident-facing datum is documented for Aruba beyond the general record: no local discrimination survey or resident testimony appears in the dossier, and the registered-union framework governs residents as it governs visitors.
SYN-ABW.outOfScopeNotes: Part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. Whether the registered-union pathway is ever exercised by visitors, and whether the absence of documented enforcement reflects absence or non-reporting, is unresolved: the record rests on official tourism self-description and kingdom-network travel reporting, with no independent local enforcement data.

Safety rests on statutory partnership and tourism norms rather than complete equality.

SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Anguilla; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz country report on Anguilla (2012): profile of a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands, framing gay life against dependent-territory law — Britain holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by British order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change; Anguilla never had the exact prohibition law itself in the same form.

Commercial destination-wedding page for Anguilla: states plainly that 'Same-sex marriage is not currently recognized under the law in Anguilla', while marketing the island's venues for ceremonies — useful as a practical marker that only symbolic ceremonies are possible for same-sex couples there.

Associated Press via SodomyLaws (Jan 5, 2001): Britain's Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos — acting unilaterally after local legislatures refused to repeal, drawing protests from religious leaders.

AFAR first-person travel piece (Jun 2023): a queer family's visit finds gay sex legal in Anguilla through the British decriminalisation order (article says 2000) but a muted, not 'out and proud' scene rooted in that imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice; notes roughly 15,000 residents as one reason the gay scene stays small.

SYN-AIA.tangentialFactors:
Parent-nation context: the United Kingdom's law-making council ordered the January 2001 reform across five of its territories after their local legislatures refused to repeal the laws themselves, and religious leaders protested the change; the sources describe the order as unilateral imposition.

The 2023 first-person travel account traces the muted public scene to the imposed historic legacy of that order rather than to local choice, and the wire coverage dates the reform to January 2001 against that account's 2000.
SYN-AIA.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: this territory has almost no public LGBT life — no community organisations, no venues, no Pride event — and local wedding-marketing pitches the destination to same-sex couples on a 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere'; the resident population, roughly 15,000, keeps any scene small, and a 2012 country report records that this territory never had the exact prohibition law in the same form that its neighbours did.
SYN-AIA.outOfScopeNotes:
A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted.

No source in this record verifies the current marriage-recognition status: the only statement comes from a commercial wedding page and says same-sex marriage 'is not currently recognized under the law', and whether that has changed since is unverified. The dating difference between 2000 and 2001 is unresolved between the travel account and the wire coverage. No source addresses border-screening or document practice for trans travelers at entry, and no trans-specific incident data exists for this territory.

SYN-BES.name: Bonaire Sint Eustatius and Saba
SYN-BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

These are not autonomous countries but special municipalities of the kingdom itself, so metropolitan equality law applies directly: same-sex marriage has been performed on the islands since 2012 — one small island hosted the region's first such wedding after the 2010 status change and markets civil ceremonies openly — with the state's penal-code discrimination grounds and partnership frameworks in force, and a current-status review confirming no later change.

The caveats are the kingdom's own, and they are real: legal gender change still requires a medical expert's statement (the self-declaration act was withdrawn at kingdom level in July 2025), non-binary markers demand months-long court procedure, and three tiny church-dense communities leave service depth thin — the same rights overview that documents these gaps rates them with the metropolitan standard attached. Travel-side evidence is warm and wedding-positive; no adverse enforcement is documented.

sources.summary: GayCities (14 Dec 2022, updated 1 Sep 2023): 'Top 10 destinations that celebrate marriage equality in the Caribbean and Latin America' ranks Bonaire at #5 — as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are protected by strict anti-discrimination laws, same-sex couples are warmly welcomed; notes Bonaire uses the US dollar. For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (5 Dec 2012): the Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union — Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27) on 4 Dec 2012, two visiting residents. For this record: same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012, and the territory has a track record of performing them for visitors.

Saba Tourism official weddings page: the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony is the Court Room in the Administrative Building; registrar Julieta Woods is documented as flexible with couples' wishes; full destination-wedding infrastructure (caterers, flowers, accommodations). For this record: practical logistics for a couple — civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry.

SYN-BES.tangentialFactors: Assessment context: a current-status review confirms no later change to the applied position, and the rights overview rates the destination with the metropolitan standard attached. The self-declaration act's withdrawal at kingdom level (July 2025) is a parent-state statutory shift, not a local decision — regional-comparison context rather than local statutes.
SYN-BES.localsOnly: Three tiny church-dense communities limit service depth for residents as for visitors, and no resident-specific discrimination data or local surveys appear in the dossier.
SYN-BES.outOfScopeNotes: Special municipalities of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; local deviations noted in the summary. The dossier records same-sex marriage performed since 2012 while the freshness confirmation cites 2018 — the earliest-performed date is unresolved; how the medical-expert gender-change statement is applied in practice is unverified.

SYN-BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
SYN-BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

Under the metropolitan civil law that governs this collectivity: same-sex marriage since 2013, gender-identity anti-discrimination protections, surgery-free legal gender change, gender-affirming care available for decades, and the state's 2023 conversion-practice ban — no legal restriction touches trans or same-sex visitors, and a rights-rating page scores the territory among the region's strongest frameworks with the caveat that non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the island attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. The only documented adverse mechanism remains the framework-wide prison findings. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.

sources.summary: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on ~40 referrals since 2010, it finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

Dossier on BLM trans rights: the French framework applies — legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Travel guide: 'full equality' under French law on ~8 square miles and ~10,000 residents; luxury-yacht economy long welcoming to gay couples with zero visible scene — discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10 (9 positive rights, 1 red flag): legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access; no government LGBT+ travel advice (FCDO shows no warnings); no trans-specific visitor tips yet submitted.

Luxury-operator guide: low crime, open and accepting culture with no Pride-specific events, staff trained for diverse guests; visitors are high-end and discreet — no LGBTQ venues or scene, but no hostility noted.

SYN-BMU.name: Bermuda
SYN-BMU.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the more telling fact is the protection gap: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all. Church influence is significant in local politics — when a prominent entertainer's gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007 the premier's colourful defence was needed against religious objections — and the tourism economy that the island depends on has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Social climate: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre' — organised religious hostility to visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections — a debate that split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

SYN-BMU.tangentialFactors: Statutory and litigation flux frames this visitor-relevant status: marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act applying to both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making this the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality, and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld the restored traditional-marriage definition. The record carries no claims about parent-country policy turbulence or neighbouring-jurisdiction comparisons on these questions, so the reversal's uniqueness is the only comparative frame the sources support.
SYN-BMU.localsOnly: For residents the 1994 decriminalisation itself divided the community: the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, and the debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and religious groups led by the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change. The 2013 human-rights amendment outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and the 2018 Domestic Partnership Act governing family status for same-sex and heterosexual couples alike are the resident-facing legal landmarks.

No source covers border screening or identity-document practice for transgender visitors, so that element of the visitor picture is unverifiable; nothing in the record documents how the 2013 discrimination ban is enforced in practice.

SYN-COK.name: Cook Islands
SYN-COK.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islands; local criminal law governs conduct.

A self-governing island state in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands criminalised male same-sex acts under a 1969 colonial-era Crimes Act (terms to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until parliament repealed the provisions in April 2023, effective 1 June 2023 — after a decade of stalled bills, NZ-assisted drafting, and sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the laws 'draconian' colonial relics. Enforcement in living memory was essentially absent; the repeal removed a held-over risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonisation. Post-decriminalisation there is still no marriage equality and no general non-discrimination statute; public life is strongly church-inflected; the islands are some 15,000 people where everyone is known — decriminalised, unequal, and small.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

SYN-COK.tangentialFactors: Legislative flux: a decade of stalled bills, drafting assisted by its partner New Zealand, preceded the April 2023 repeal — a contested path rather than a quick legislative turn.
SYN-COK.localsOnly: Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonial administration. The repeal followed sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the old laws 'draconian' colonial relics.

SYN-CUW.name: Curaçao
SYN-CUW.summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

Also an autonomous constituent country of the same kingdom, the island's audited record is one of official intent colliding with friction: representatives of all kingdom governments agreed in 2015 on an equal-rights package for Caribbean-country LGBT residents — yet the same reporting documents Pride permit difficulties as recently as 2013 and organised parliamentary opposition that the island's own government publicly opposed while supporting the community.

Travel-culture surveys place the island inside the region's quiet tolerant mainstream. For a visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin infrastructure: no documented state hostility, an active but negotiating community in the capital, and no evidenced local gender-recognition pathway or care capacity. The record is brief; what exists shows institutions contested rather than hostile.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

SYN-CUW.localsOnly: No resident-facing fact specific to Curaçao is documented in the dossier beyond the community-organising record; the equal-rights package and permitting practice govern residents as they govern visitors, with no resident discrimination data recorded.

SYN-CYM.name: Cayman Islands
SYN-CYM.summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. In 2020 the Court of Appeal held that a same-sex couple's overseas marriage must be recognised, and in July 2021 roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the islands' first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts a community there has seen.

The sharp turn came in 2022: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect and, in March of that year, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it. Same-sex couples therefore have no marriage or civil-partnership status, the country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself.

sources.summary: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder (wed in Ireland), the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds; recaps that Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019 (later overturned on appeal, Aug 2019 — the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived). Core source for the 'recognition without status' travel posture.

SYN-CYM.tangentialFactors: Parent-authority policy turbulence frames the later recognition rulings: in 2009 legislators of the parent country criticised the draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave local courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Article 14 requires, while the United Kingdom countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended.
SYN-CYM.localsOnly: For residents, family status is the contested terrain: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect in 2022, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself. The Grand Court's March 2019 strike-down of the same-sex marriage ban was overturned on appeal in August 2019, leaving only the recognition-for-immigration-effects line standing for the resident couples it protected.
SYN-CYM.outOfScopeNotes: A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted. No source documents border-screening practice, documents handling, arrest patterns, or the operational enforcement of the unequal age of consent, and nothing on the record distinguishes protections or risks specific to trans travelers as opposed to same-sex couples. The practical working of the recognition-for-immigration-effects line at ports of entry is unverified.

SYN-ESH.name: Western Sahara
SYN-ESH.summary:
A disputed North African territory under military administration by a neighbouring state, whose penal code governs any visitor: same-sex intimacy is criminalised (six months to three years) with wide police discretion, and morality articles are the tool turned on visibly trans people — rights reviews document involuntary outing, expression discrepancies at checkpoints and registries, no gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition (a 2021 path covers intersex people only); the administering state's religious establishment has condemned transition.

Occupation stacks the risk: 170 charged in the administering state in one year, a 2020 organised outing campaign, rights defenders tried at the territory's own court (a 2005 case of eight Sahrawis remains a landmark), and a 2018 legal study recording LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike. For an outed visitor: criminalisation, morality enforcement and occupation policing, with no civil space and negligible accountability.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch (9 Dec 2005): trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; HRW called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. Documents Moroccan state authority exercised over the territory (security services, courts) and detention of Sahrawi activists - the legal framework a visitor to the territory stands under.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and states that it has been illegal there for decades. The partially-recognised state, an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. The status recorded for July 2017 is criminalised.

SYN-ESH.tangentialFactors: Governance context: the disputed North African territory sits under military administration by a neighbouring state; a 2017 legality roundup records the partially recognised claimant administration as likewise criminalising same-sex conduct.

SYN-FLK.name: Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
SYN-FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, legislate locally: same-sex activity has been legal since 1989, the age of consent has been equal since 2005, and same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017 — approved 7-1 after a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships, with adoption following the same year and the first Pride held in Stanley that April. The Constitution Order 2008 bans sexual-orientation discrimination (Article 16).

UK law does not automatically apply here. The Equality Act 2010, the UK's 2025 single-sex-services code and the April 2025 Supreme Court 'For Women Scotland' ruling govern Great Britain, not the Islands, and no Order in Council extends them; the Islands' own ordinances govern instead. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 criminalises stirring up hatred on grounds of sexual orientation, and the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014 treats sexual orientation as an aggravating factor.

Trans-specific law is narrow. The UK Gender Recognition Act 2004 does not itself extend to the Islands, but the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014 treats the holder of a UK gender recognition certificate as their acquired gender at law; there is no local self-identification process and no non-binary recognition, so a trans visitor without a UK certificate is treated at law as their birth-registered sex. No gender-identity anti-discrimination protection exists — the constitutional ban names sexual orientation only.

Social picture: a tiny, remote island community. The 'open, tolerant and respectful' characterisation rests on a single local official's statement; no attitude-survey data and no trans-specific incidents are recorded. The remote dependency administered from Stanley (South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands) did not follow on marriage equality.

sources.summary: PinkNews (12 Apr 2017): the Legislative Assembly passed same-sex marriage (7-1) plus civil partnerships open to same-sex AND opposite-sex couples, after a public consultation showing 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in the ~3,000-resident territory — the operative equality reform.

[1] Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

Mirror summary of the Wikipedia LGBTQ rights page (wiki-derived): legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005; same-sex marriage and civil partnerships since 29 April 2017; stepchild and joint adoption since 2017; constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination; UK responsible for defence; attitudes largely positive (90% consultation support).

SYN-FLK.tangentialFactors: The United Kingdom is responsible for defence and foreign affairs; the Islands run their own immigration and policing, so UK entry rules do not set the border regime here. UK passport policy affects UK passport holders wherever they travel and does not change local law. UK measures could in principle be extended by Order in Council, but none of the single-sex-services or prison-placement changes has been so extended.
SYN-FLK.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the public consultation before the 2017 vote showed 90 per cent support for same-sex marriage and 94 per cent for civil partnerships among residents; the registrar confirmed the reform had become law in June 2017; adoption law followed the same year; and a community official described the territory as 'open, tolerant and respectful'.

SYN-GIB.name: Gibraltar
SYN-GIB.summary:
