Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

Governance of the territory is subject to regular scrutiny by the UK parliament's overseas-territories committee, which has pressed accountability standards across the portfolio.

For visitors: legal protection complete, community present but small, discretion still the norm.

SYN-MSR.name: Montserrat
SYN-MSR.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north. Gay life barely exists locally: 'gays are everywhere but hardly here,' and the social scene is decimated.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

SYN-MSR.tangentialFactors: Parent-nation context: the January 2001 decriminalisation order came from the same reform the United Kingdom imposed across five of its territories after the local legislatures refused to repeal the laws, and the wire reporting frames the episode as a cultural rift with the United Kingdom.
SYN-MSR.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable', and the territory appeared resigned to following the United Kingdom's order; the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions buried half of the territory, displaced more than half the population, and left a scatter of survivors, and a 2012 country report records that public gay life barely exists locally and has only partially recovered.
SYN-MSR.outOfScopeNotes:
A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted.

The description of the social scene rests on a dated 2012 country report, and no newer survey data is recorded. Whether the scene has recovered since the disasters is not measurable from the available sources. No source in this record addresses border-screening or document practice for trans travelers at entry, no trans-specific incident data is recorded, and no source addresses marriage or partner recognition for same-sex couples.

SYN-MTQ.name: Martinique
SYN-MTQ.summary:
Martinique stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

As a full overseas department, the island carries the entire metropolitan framework: same-sex marriage and full anti-discrimination protection (constitutional provisions extending state law here are explicit in the rights record), decriminalised for two centuries, with simplified judicial gender-marker change available under the state's 2016-17 reforms. Nothing criminalises being trans, and case law and state protection capacity track the metropolitan norm.

Community infrastructure is real but modest: the island's lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans network organises private parties and garden socials and provides information and meeting services, supported by gay-friendly allies — there is no large commercial scene in the capital. The trans-relevant state mechanism documented across the framework is custodial: the national detention-places watchdog's findings of serious persistent violations against transgender prisoners apply to the island's prisons as to the metropole.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): trans women in France are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code) — most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'), placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). Covers placement, isolation, safety and staff-training recommendations. Binds the department's prisons as French establishments.

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique resource page: same-sex acts decriminalised in 1815; Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department; 2013 marriage-equality law applies; discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited in goods/services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code arts. 225-1/225-2) and in employment since Labour Code art. L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters. Its active, dated operation evidences local community infrastructure on the island.

SYN-MTQ.tangentialFactors:
Parent-nation context: the applicable policy is the national framework in full — relations decriminalised for two centuries, the 2013 same-sex marriage statute, and the 2016-17 gender-marker reforms — with no national policy turbulence documented in the dossier that would alter local application. The framework-wide custodial findings are the only litigation-adjacent flux in evidence.

Comparisons with neighbouring territories are not documented in this dossier, so no relative regional assessment is possible.

SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

On paper the fullest of regional frameworks: French civil and criminal law applies — same-sex marriage (a genuine rarity in this part of the world), gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and legal gender change by simplified procedure following the national reforms. No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship.

The gap between book and life is the documented story. A 2023 report on a binational couple describes a 'long and complicated' path even to marry on this predominantly Muslim island; a legal-access directory shows no openly LGBT-friendly lawyer resident in the department (metropolitan counsel take cases); and the framework's prison findings — the state detention watchdog's report of serious violations against transgender prisoners — apply to the local jails. Social environment is conservative in a way the audited sources show through practice, not statute. For visitors, legal protection exists and enforcement of rights is slow; visibility invites social pressure more than police action.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework binds this department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

LINFO.re (French-language report): the French National Assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people). French law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 May 2023, Moïse Manoël-Florisse): Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner (pseudonym Abdallah) married at Sada Town Hall after a 'long and complicated' path — showing the gap between formal French rights and lived reality on this predominantly Muslim island. Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Avocat Gay-Friendly directory (French): no LGBT-friendly lawyer is yet referenced in Mayotte — the town list (Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and others) returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' — while Paris-based Maître Isabelle Zribi (lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law) is listed as available. Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

Parent-nation context: the applicable policy is the national framework in full — the national assembly's reform simplifying legal gender change, and the 2013 same-sex marriage statute extended automatically — with no national policy turbulence documented in the dossier. The 2023 binational couple's 'long and complicated' marriage path is the nearest thing to litigation flux in the record.

The automatic extension of the framework follows from the territory's continuing status within France — a fact of local status rather than a visitor-specific variable. Comparisons with neighbouring territories are not documented in this dossier.

SYN-NCL.name: New Caledonia
SYN-NCL.summary:
Full France metropolitan law does not extend to New Caledonia unchanged; the territory legislates locally on many matters, with France responsible for documents and justice.

The metropolitan civil-law framework applies to this Pacific collectivity: same-sex marriage under the 2013 statute extended here, penal-code discrimination grounds covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and judicial gender-marker change under the state's reforms. Nothing criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and the protections read as fully national in scope.

The practical picture is therefore one of complete formal protection in a small, close-knit society where community discretion is the reasonable assumption; this record is explicitly evidence-thin rather than affirmatively warm or hostile.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their legal gender marker (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities facing detainant assault threats, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to this collectivity's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — referrals since 2010 on some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse; eight trans women and one trans man interviewed). Extends to establishments here as French law applies.

Same-sex marriage has been available in this collectivity since France's 2013 marriage-equality law, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on France's first same-sex wedding under that law.

French law extends marriage equality to this collectivity. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Yagg (July 2012, French): 'identité sexuelle' (sexual identity) became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code via the sexual-harassment law — enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination. French law applies to the collectivity, and the same provision was updated to read 'gender identity' in 2016.

SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Pitcairn Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Pitcairn's roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves, and on paper they have adopted the most complete equality package in this group of territories: activity legal since 2001, a 2010 constitution that bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and a 2015 Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance — marriage defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity, foreign civil partnerships recognised, and adoption open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

No islander is known to be in a same-sex relationship — on an island this size, invisibility is arithmetic rather than atmosphere. Defence and external affairs are the United Kingdom's responsibility; family law is set locally as above.

sources.summary: Same-sex activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001. The 2010 Constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation, with protections in place since 2010. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015 and adoption since 2015. None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship. Military service falls under UK responsibility.

The 2010 Pitcairn Constitution Order bans discrimination on sexual orientation. Marriage is defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. Adoption is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Full Wikipedia republication: same-sex sexual activity legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001; anti-discrimination constitutional protection from the 2010 Constitution Order; same-sex marriage legal 14 May 2015 — ordinance unanimously approved by the Island Council 1 Apr 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair 5 May, published 13 May 2015; adoption legal since 2015; page also indexes the territory within UK LGBT-rights timelines.

SYN-PCN.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context: the equality package rests on locally-enacted law beneath the United Kingdom's framework — the 2010 constitutional order supplies the discrimination ban, and the 2015 ordinance was unanimously approved by the local council on 1 April 2015, signed by the governor on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015, entering into force on 14 May 2015; the United Kingdom is responsible for defence and military service.
SYN-PCN.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves through the local council, and no resident is known to be in a same-sex relationship; the 2015 ordinance was unanimously approved by the council and recognises civil partnerships performed outside the territory; adoption is open to married, unmarried and single people alike.
SYN-PCN.outOfScopeNotes:
A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted.

The practicality of the on-paper equality package is unverified: no source records any same-sex couple or trans resident, no venues or organisations exist, and practical visitation is negligible. No source in this record addresses border-screening or document practice for trans travelers at entry, and the everyday enforcement of the legal protections is not documented here.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
Full France metropolitan law does not extend to French Polynesia unchanged; the territory legislates locally on many matters, with France responsible for documents and justice.

French equality law applies in full — gender-identity anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions since 2017, a conversion-practice ban since 2022, and legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites — and it lands on genuinely entrenched indigenous ground: the mahuu third-gender role predates colonisation, rae-rae identities are visible in daily life across the archipelago, the territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023 with government and church participation, and travel literature calls the openness cultural rather than legal.

The undertow is real but social, not statutory: the rights overview records varying stigma, employment discrimination, and episodic transphobic violence that has pushed some rae-rae into sex work, while healthcare depth thins sharply outside the main island. For a visitor the combination is among the region's strongest — law, culture, and visibility aligned — with the standard framework caveat that the state's prison-system findings apply here too, and small-island anonymity cuts both ways.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): in France, detention follows the gender marked on an ID, and Article D248 requires separate men's and women's establishments, so trans women holding male markers are held with men. The article treats this as a legal grey area. France's framework governs French Polynesia as an overseas collectivity subject to French law.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

Grokipedia trans rights in Tahiti: gender-diverse care limited by local expertise; some trans people (raerae) face family rejection and migrate to mainland France for specialised services; mahu social role - traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity where mahu embody both male and female qualities and hold cultural standing. Care access + cultural role.

OutTraveler (4 Jul 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags' - openness described as ingrained in the culture; mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands; first-hand account of visiting gay couple gauging safety (Googling 'is it safe' first) finding mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and pride-free acceptance. Visitor-experience picture.

RNZ Pacific: French Polynesia LGBTQIA reflection - churches round table with University of French Polynesia; Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment (progesterone/testosterone) like mainland France, but after heated Territorial Assembly debate the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Concrete care-access reform failed.

Out Adventures gay travel guide presents Tahiti and Bora Bora across the 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture. The assessment is travel-oriented and reports no trans-specific finding.

SYN-PYF.tangentialFactors:
Parent-nation context: the national 2016-17 reforms underpin the local gender recognition regime, with no further national policy turbulence documented in the dossier beyond the framework's custodial findings (the national detention watchdog's opinion).

Local policy flux: a government proposal to fully reimburse hormonal treatment was debated in the elected local legislature and failed to gain sufficient support after a heated debate; a rights round table drew church participation alongside the university; and no comparison with neighbouring territories is documented in this dossier.
SYN-PYF.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the traditional mahuu third-gender role holds cultural standing as a long-recognised expression of gender diversity; some rae-rae residents face family rejection and migrate to the metropole for specialised services. Residents also bear varying stigma, employment discrimination, and episodic transphobic violence that has pushed some into sex work, and specialised healthcare is limited outside the main island's urban centre.

SYN-REU.name: Réunion
SYN-REU.summary:
Réunion stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

French equality law applies in full as an overseas department: same-sex marriage reached the island with the metropolitan statute (2013), 'sexual identity' has been a prosecutable discrimination ground in the penal code since 2012, and the national amendments that produced simplified legal gender change apply here as state law. No offence attaches to being trans, and the protection framework is actionable rather than nominal.

No local violence series, enforcement pattern, or institutional hostility programme appears in the sources, and equally no documented local support infrastructure; a small, discreet community should be assumed but is not evidenced.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): in France, where prisoners are placed by the sex on their ID under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, transgender women held in male prisons fall into a legal grey area and are 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes' — the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities, based on referrals since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site/document inspections, with recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. National framework covering Réunion.

PinkNews (26 Aug 2012): PM Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the same-sex marriage and adoption bill would go to the National Assembly and Senate in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge; both houses had to approve, and the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption. The marriage statute that subsequently applied to Réunion with the 2013 metropolitan law.

Yagg (25 Jul 2012, French): the harassment bill adopted by the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 to add 'identité sexuelle' as a discrimination ground, making transphobia prosecutable; deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervened in the debate. the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

A scattered South Atlantic territory of three island groups that legislated equality island by island: the 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation across all three, and equal age of consent sits at 16. Marriage equality arrived in staggered fashion — the first dependency's council approved the ordinance 5-0 in May 2016 and it commenced January 2017, the most remote island followed in August 2017, and the principal island itself completed the set on 20 December 2017 — with adoption law following the same year.

SYN-TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
SYN-TCA.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Turks and Caicos Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

the United Kingdom's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz resident account by 'Eddi' (May 2009) reports that there is virtually nothing on the Internet about gay life in TCI. About two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority compared with foreigners, so there is no visible scene and privacy is the norm.

UK HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile (Crown copyright 2025): official operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents for the territory — states adoption is legal and that 'transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands', i.e. the administering state's passport office handles gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction.

TC Weekly News: Court of Appeal landmark ruling ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar — refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened constitutional guarantees; 'spouse' in the Immigration Ordinance read to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, with equality/non-discrimination/private-life guarantees invoked (marriage definition left untouched). Directly relevant: same-sex partners of visitors/residents get residence recognition.
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001, and discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is constitutionally prohibited.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

The custody axis completes the picture: the state operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the state serve their time in Italian prisons with costs covered by the state, so there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case in this jurisdiction; any custodial consequence for a visitor would be served in another nation's prison system, outside this record's scope.

SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to British Virgin Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the United Kingdom's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.

sources.summary: An AP report of January 2001, republished by GLAPN, states that Britain scrapped the homosexuality laws in its five remaining Caribbean territories, including the British Virgin Islands, by Privy Council order after local legislatures refused to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded, 'there is nothing we can do.'
GlobalGayz (Aug 2012/2017) rates the BVI among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean, while describing native homophobia as 'silent and invisible' and gay life there as lived in secret.

BVI News (29 Jul 2022): the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack in the case testing whether the UK same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under BVI law.

SYN-VGB.tangentialFactors: The decriminalisation was imposed from the parent country — Britain scrapped the homosexuality laws in its five remaining Caribbean territories by order of the Privy Council after local legislatures refused to act; parent-country policy acting above the local record. SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary:
The French civil and criminal framework applies: gender-identity anti-discrimination protection since 2012 and judicial gender-marker change under the 2016-17 reforms without surgery or diagnosis requirements; same-sex relations are lawful; non-binary recognition does not exist. No law criminalises trans presence.

Exposure here is shaped by scale and mores rather than statutes. The rights overview describes an isolated community of roughly eleven thousand where Catholic and Polynesian social norms create practical barriers to visibility, a traditional third-gender presence (fakafafine) coexists with stigma, there are no local gender specialists — residents travel out for any care — and anonymity in village life is close to zero. No hostile state action is documented; the only state-level adverse mechanism in evidence is the framework's own prison findings (the national detention watchdog's report). Visitors should expect personal identifiability, warm discretion, and effectively absent local institutional support.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

sources.title: Italy 'to open first prison for transgender inmates' | BBC News
sources.summary: BBC News (12 Jan 2010): Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence - converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners (mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences); gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. The report states that until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons 'where they are often segregated for their own safety' - the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice in Italy. sources.title: La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere | La Repubblica (Inchieste)
sources.summary: La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere' (28 Aug 2013): at that date the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities, with placement tracking legal sex - female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men,' trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections.' Segregation practice: in some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking - described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety - and protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia (Rome) and the protected section at Poggioreale (Naples) imposed limitations, including on partner visits. Documented ruling: the 2011 Terni case in which the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision. The dedicated Pozzale transgender prison project (2008-2010), which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano (Florence), was shelved.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta is a province within Canada and stands under the national framework: gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16 in 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, no Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Entry carries no trans-specific friction, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker.

Alberta's own statutes run against that framework. In December 2024 the legislature passed a package of three measures affecting transgender people as a class: the Education Amendment Act 2024, which requires parental opt-in for classroom instruction and sets rules on student pronouns and school sports; a health-statutes act barring puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation at the time, calling the package discriminatory.

The care prohibition is the element with direct bearing on a visitor. It is a statutory bar in Alberta's health statutes on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for anyone under 18, so gender-affirming medical care for a trans minor cannot be obtained in the province while it stands.

Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the same sitting and invoked the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families state that their court challenge to the underlying statutes continues regardless. The laws are in force and constitutional litigation is pending.

Trans people held in federal custody inside Alberta fall under Correctional Service of Canada policy in force since 2018, which accommodates offenders on the basis of gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth. Gender-diverse offenders may request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents, and a request is refused only where the Correctional Service finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the service reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's.

The Office of the Correctional Investigator called the 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged two gaps: no clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern, and no dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

Alberta's statutory package deliberately stops short of custody and shared facilities. Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement covered the care ban, parental-consent rules for school pronouns and sexuality instruction, and a ban on trans women in women's sports, and stated that the measures would not include women's shelters, women's prisons or changing rooms. No provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented.

sources.summary: CBC (4 Dec 2024): Alberta's trio of trans-youth bills passed final legislative stage — the Education Amendment Act 2024 (parental opt-in for classroom instruction, student pronoun and sport rules), a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors, plus sports policy. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory.

CBC (Dec 2024): Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting, invoking the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years; Egale Canada, Skipping Stone Foundation and five families said their court challenge to Bill 26 continues regardless. Result: laws in force, constitutional litigation pending.

As of 2025 CSC reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. 82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.

sources.summary: Government of Saskatchewan education-ministry news release (22 Aug 2023) announcing the parental inclusion and consent policies: schools must seek parent/guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. The release that started the court challenge.

Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (11 Aug 2025): the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision — courts lack jurisdiction to test s.1/s.15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where s.33 was invoked — so the policy stands. Supersedes the injunction-era chambers ruling.

sources.title: Saskatchewan Appeal Court says challenge of province's pronoun law can continue
sources.summary: The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years.

sources.title: Amnesty International Canada welcomes ruling in court challenge to Saskatchewan pronoun law
sources.summary: Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

sources.title: Supreme Court to weigh in on Saskatchewan's school pronoun case
sources.summary: On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause, a five-year override. Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Canada (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal placement policy applicable to trans prisoners in federal custody inside Saskatchewan: since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada accommodates offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement in a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression regardless of anatomy or identity-document sex/gender marker, refusing requests individually only where 'overriding health or safety concerns' cannot be resolved. As of 2025, of 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody, 73 were housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. 82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for the informal use of chosen names and pronouns by students of any age (it remains required for formal use in official records for students under 16), with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its application to the whole school environment, including "visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors", so current school rules technically reach non-residents present in classrooms.

Deviation: 0.02 below the national score of 0.86. The reversal is a strong positive institutional response — a government that legislated against trans students repealed the provision after one term. The residual signal is the demonstrated capacity for hostile policy within an election cycle and the 2023 protest period, which create a slightly higher baseline of political volatility than provinces that never legislated against trans people. No street-level disruption of public expression events was documented.

Compared to Alberta (0.76) and Saskatchewan (0.79), New Brunswick is materially higher: it did not use the notwithstanding clause, and its hostile policy was reversed rather than immunised from judicial review. Compared to the national score, the gap is small and time-sensitive — the current effective policy is protective, and further reversal would bring New Brunswick to or above the national level.

sources.title: Policy 713: LGBT school policy change causes political turmoil in Canada
sources.summary: Changes to New Brunswick's Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity policy (Policy 713) took effect on 1 July 2023, barring teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropping explicit wording that let students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government updated the policy without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers quit in protest and two others were pushed out. Party dissidents called for a leadership review, and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick 'need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians'.

sources.title: New Brunswick's proposed education policy change sparks backlash in Ottawa
sources.summary: Canadian Press via Global News (9 June 2023): the Higgs government's proposed Policy 713 changes would force children under 16 to get parental consent to change their names or pronouns at school, with the changes set to take effect 1 July 2023, reversing a three-year-old policy that required teachers to get the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. Eight Progressive Conservative members, including six cabinet ministers, sat out question period to protest the lack of process and transparency. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick 'need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians'.

sources.title: 'We know it saves lives:' hundreds go to N.B. rally against review of LGBTQ policy
sources.summary: About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the government's review of Policy 713, the 2020 policy that requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said 'we know it saves lives' and warned that 'with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids'. Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review.

31927357B79016588373767.summary:
The capital recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide was made a distinct crime in July 2024 (“Ley Paola Buenrostro”, the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created in December 2024 covers all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requires feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines; and a new Gender Police launched in August 2025 with 30 patrol units. For a visitor assaulted in the capital there is trained machinery to investigate, where other jurisdictions have none. Modestly above the national score (0.55): the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force (Aug 2025); Nayarit was first in the country to typify the crime (March 2024). Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.

Verificado (2024): Nuevo Leon recorded 7 attacks on LGBT people, 3 forced disappearances and 4 transfeminicides during the year, and transfeminicidio is not typified in the state penal code. 31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
The state has not typified hate crime at all, per its own LGBT+ welfare sub-director (June 2026), who also located most attacks on the community in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence. Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including 'Daniela,' a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026 — a suspect was arrested, a positive institutional response. Two additional deaths in Morelia in April 2026, one of them a gay man, were linked by the attorney general's office to organised crime. An NGO observatory report counted 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024, led by Morelia (11), then Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5) and Zamora (4), with 2015 the deadliest year (10 victims).

Colectivo PRIDE Michoacán reports rising attacks in the municipalities bordering Jalisco, that victims are no longer attended to, and that the state does not acknowledge the violence. No transfeminicide offence, no hate-crime typification, no investigative protocol — the only counterweights are individual arrests.

Context for comparison: Veracruz, similarly hostile, at least passed a gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025; Mexico City pairs comparable lethality with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocols. Michoacán has no legal machinery whatsoever, plus an armed-group amplifier that makes the violence harder to escape or report.

The record's core practical-safety signal is the worst in the national data: this state led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, with 19 of 32 jurisdictions recording victims — and closed 2025 with at least 15 recorded hate crimes; the killing of a 27-year-old trans woman, stabbed to death in a motel on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted nine hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women, and the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as this state's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform.

Legal protections and enforcement are absent in practice: before the 2025 civil-code gender-identity reform — among the last to be legislated — a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct gender documents, and there is no functioning investigation or prosecution machinery, distinct from other jurisdictions where laws exist but enforcement is weak. Activists cite deliberate filing-away of cases, the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely, and in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the homicide file had simply disappeared; the impunity here is total.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body, and the events are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.

Newer reporting profiles the region as a fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, with possible municipal-police participation, and the official answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. A trans visitor therefore stands under a formally protective framework alongside customary exclusion and violent-incident reports at exactly the events tourists attend.

31927357B1137737933275.name: Puebla
31927357B1137737933275.summary: Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people, and trans women were 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year across at least 17 states reporting victims - a top-of-table lethality record a visitor must weigh against any formal protections. Its legal gender recognition law (2021) still carries an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, and the state congress has still not corrected the text: for a visitor whose documents must match their presentation, the unmet duty to conform the law to the binding ruling is itself a live hostility signal, and no state-level enforcement data exists to temper it.

1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 people crossing the long, porous international border - including seven transgender people - in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to the financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power.

Tripura shares an 856-km porous border with Bangladesh.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal replicates the checkpoint script documented in its neighbour: police arrested a transgender person arriving from across the long, porous international border for allegedly "infiltrating", treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity. It is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating that some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime occurs at a detectable rate.

The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than a repeated-sweep pattern elsewhere: the documented record here is a single arrest plus the broader infiltration framing. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism - trans presentation treated as evidence of illegal entry.

Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), West Bengal row: of the 7 Transgender Persons Act cases nationally in 2021, 3 were registered in West Bengal (highest that year alongside Assam/Kerala) — detectable-rate crime plus the report's caveat that national counts are tiny (20 cases 2019-23) from police-registration bias, and 2025 survey prevalence of 27.2% physical / 22.3% sexual violence.

sources.summary: The Quint (5 November 2024) publishes an RTI investigation into transgender welfare boards: West Bengal is one of the 12 states/UTs that notified a board, but the majority of boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since their creation, and the 17 existing boards 'are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism, or any power', with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people. West Bengal's constituted welfare board operates without a functioning policy framework.

1811400B91946361694107.name: Punjab
1811400B91946361694107.summary:
In Amritsar - the spiritual centre of the region's dominant faith - the annual Pride assembly cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade after "mounting resistance" from the faith's religious organisations, including a prominent faction and the faith's highest temporal authority; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason. No other law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears in the audited sources for this record.

For a trans visitor the documented signal is institutional, not criminal: no statute here targets trans people, but an organised religious authority compelled the cancellation of the region's annual public trans assembly, and the event simply did not happen. Public trans visibility therefore carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition, and the absence of any recorded state intervention to preserve the event is part of that record.

sources.title: LGBT rights in India - Wikipedia
sources.summary: On September 6, 2018 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. No Punjab-specific law or institution targeting trans people appears in this material, consistent with the finding that the documented signal in Punjab is institutional rather than criminal.

sources.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019) is the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people; criticism holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. No statute in Punjab targets trans people, and this is the framework a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under.

1811400B78322693766699.name: Assam
1811400B78322693766699.summary:
Assam stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel, including in Assam: transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. Elsewhere in the country, a trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender; at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification; and passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Assam appears in national crime records as one data point within a countrywide pattern. Assam accounted for 2 of the 7 cases registered under the Transgender Persons Act nationally in 2021 and none in the 2023 tally. The source cautions that national counts are tiny — 20 cases across 2019–23 — because of police-registration bias, and reports 2025 survey prevalence of 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence against trans people nationally. Registered cases therefore prove the complaint system is reachable, not that violence is uncommon.

State protective machinery was thin. In the December 2021 national government reply listing the 12 states and union territories that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules, Assam is not among them, so no state welfare body stood in place as of that date. No Assam-specific protective or restrictive statute, ordinance or checkpoint operation is documented in the audited sources.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: national recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026 — including custody treatment of trans people by the Railway Protection Force in Assam — set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

PIB reply to parliament (Dec 2021): the 12 states and union territories listed as having constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules do not include Assam, so no state welfare machinery existed there as of Dec 2021.

1811400B11231190780494.name: Uttar Pradesh
1811400B11231190780494.summary:
For a trans visitor, the visitor-facing fact is a seasonally concentrated institutional recognition in Uttar Pradesh, at the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj (Jan-Feb 2025), the world's largest religious gathering: a trans monastic order's highest-ranking monk headed 15 trans spiritual leaders in ceremonial bathing, placing a trans visitor inside an institutionally recognised religious hierarchy rather than a marginalised underground. The inclusion is contested: a rival leadership instalment drew protests, gurus threatened to boycott the 2037 gathering, and a top-ranking trans monk who objected was physically attacked on 12 February 2025 — festival-week exposure therefore carries a real but episodic risk of confrontation. The jurisdiction also has a constituted welfare board, though the sources show no visitor-facing enforcement mechanism.

The only recorded violence is a lone incident — a transgender woman strangled during a robbery in August 2025 — with no patterned state-actor response and no regional finding under the single-incident rule. Against the national 0.43 the record sits +0.03; the net positive is narrow and temporally concentrated at the festival period.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
For a trans visitor the operative risk in Ceará is sustained lethal exposure: the jurisdiction recorded 11 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — the region's highest toll and third nationally — and 8 in 2025, tied for the highest state total of that year's 80 nationwide; two consecutive years at the top of the ranking indicate an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip. There is no state-level legal distinction: the national constitution and penal code apply uniformly.

The national victim profile sharpens the exposure for a visibly trans traveller: 97% of victims are travestis and trans women, over half aged 18–29, 70% of those with recorded race are Black, 97% killed in public spaces with most incidents outside capitals.

sources.summary: G1/Globo report (28 Jan 2025), citing the ANTRA dossier: Ceará was the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024, with 11 killings, third highest nationally.

Igbá Agência (26 Jan 2026): per the 9th ANTRA dossier, Ceará was among the states with most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases; Brazil totalled 80 (18th year as world's highest). Among 57 victims with race data, 70% were Black (avg 77% over 2017-2025).

SBT News (26 Jan 2026): ANTRA 9th dossier — Ceará and Minas Gerais topped the 2025 state ranking with 8 killings each; Brazil's 80 total down 34% vs 2024, still 1st worldwide; 1,261 killings 2017-2025 (avg 140/yr).

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison
sources.summary: Wikipedia's general overview article (28 Sep 2026) sets out international placement norms for trans prisoners: Scotland's 2022 inspection standards admit trans and intersex prisoners to facilities matching their lived or experienced gender, and Canada places prisoners by gender identity. Its Brazil paragraph states only that traumatic social vulnerability and stigma facing travestis and transgender people shape rehabilitation. The article reports no codified Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Brazil
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' article (28 Sep 2026), in its Politics section, states that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transgender people ('transsexuals') have the right to be called by their social name and not their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing. The statement is footnoted (ref. 253) to a Mix Brasil (UOL) article, 'Vivemos uma inercia no congresso...', archived 18 Jan 2012, supporting placement-follows-identity in Brazil as of c.2012. Treat as dated evidence; recency not re-verified.

14911670B19428866735507.name: Bahia
14911670B19428866735507.summary:
Bahia, in Brazil's north-east, records trans and travesti killings at a rate that places it among the country's highest-burden states. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only a handful of states; on the same reckoning Bahia ranks third nationally across 2017 to 2025 with 97 killings, after São Paulo (151) and Ceará (107). Valor Internacional reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, and the figure appears in consecutive annual dossiers rather than in a single outlier year: the ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year.

The victim profile is consistent. The overwhelming majority of those killed are travestis and trans women, most aged 18 to 29, around 70% Black among cases in which race was identified, and most killings take place outside the state capital. The burden falls on Black trans women and on young people in interior municipalities, not on visitors to Salvador's tourist districts as a matter of statistical fact.

A specific case in December 2025 illustrates both the killing pattern and the response. G1 Bahia reported on 9 December 2025 that police were investigating the death of Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, as a feminicide: she was strangled in Luís Eduardo Magalhães in the interior of Bahia on the weekend of 6–7 December. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove her body to the police station himself and was released after confessing and claiming self-defence; the Civil Police confirmed the feminicide classification notwithstanding the suspect's initial release.

Bahia-specific statutory restriction was not identified in the sources reviewed. The national framework governs: Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal ruled in 2019 that discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are criminal, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism, and same-sex couples' marriage and spousal-visa rights have operated nationwide since 2013. Nothing in the audited sources indicates a Bahia ordinance narrowing or widening those national rules.

14911670B85657526756793.name: Rio de Jeneiro
14911670B85657526756793.summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — roughly 0.18 per million against a population near 17 million — well below the national average, so lethal violence is the weakest part of the risk picture here. The visitor-facing signals are about enforcement: a documented extortion racket in Niterói ran for about two years under the appearance of backing from public agents, and in Copacabana the tourist police arrested two trans women for extorting a visiting tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos.

Institutional response was mixed. The state court decreed preventive detention in February 2026 for the alleged extorter, an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, so the judiciary can act, and the tourist-police arrests likewise show police presence in tourist areas. Yet the Niterói scheme operated openly for roughly two years, forcing trans sex workers to pay weekly exactions, which signals weak protection for the most exposed trans residents and a tourist-area climate in which visibly trans people may be treated as scam suspects.

14911670B9724590061217.name: Alagoas
14911670B9724590061217.summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. The annual dossiers of the national trans movement put numbers on that gap: CNN Brasil reported on 27 January 2025 that 122 trans and travesti people were killed in Brazil in 2024, a figure 16% below 2023, and SBT News reported on 26 January 2026 that ANTRA's 9th annual dossier counted 80 killings in 2025, a fall of roughly 34% year-on-year. Alagoas accounted for 6 of the 122 killings in 2024 and 2 of the 80 in 2025.

Brazil ranked first in the world for the killing of trans people for a 16th consecutive year in the 2024 dossier and remained at the top of world rankings in the 2025 count. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence; in 2024 they were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, the region Alagoas belongs to.

Alagoas's own totals are small in absolute terms, so a few cases move the state's position sharply between consecutive annual counts, and the national totals themselves fell by about a third across the same two dossiers while Brazil kept the leading world ranking. For a visibly trans visitor, the hazard documented here is lethal violence directed at travestis and trans women, most of them young and Black, carried out with extreme force.
