Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — about 0.83 per million per year, more than double the national rate — after the 2024 dossier counted 8 killings in the state, its highest year. The dossier's finding that most killings happen outside the capitals makes small-town exposure relevant for visitors travelling beyond the capital, so the elevated per-capita reading is the core of the assessment even though three cases on a small population are statistically fragile.

On documents and institutional response, two local positives exist: a 2021 decree guarantees the social-name right, accepted by state public offices and usable on badges, cards and identification documents, and a 2026 jury conviction of 13 years and 6 months for the gender-motivated killing of a trans woman shows the courts can deliver. No trans-specific ordinance or protection beyond these was found; the national framework applies uniformly.

14911670B84195346134564.name: Distrito Federal
14911670B84195346134564.summary:
The Distrito Federal recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area. Brasília is the seat of the STF, the national protective apparatus, and the offices of human-rights bodies; ANTRA's own Dossiê is compiled and reported from DF desks. The capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence.

These factors justify a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71. Compared with São Paulo (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, the DF's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor. The 2 killings against ~3 million population give a rate of ~0.67/million—above the national average in per-capita terms—so the positive deviation is qualitative (institutional visibility, international presence) rather than purely numerical.

10402087B89016843004490.name: Sachsen
10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Visitors in every Land stand under the national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove the federal floor.

Two documented 2025 features raise Sachsen above the German norm for visitor risk around queer visibility: neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest intended to disrupt Dresden's pride march on 31 May 2025 (the march proceeded); and the state government, with two neighbouring states, co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after an abuse-of-self-ID court case ('Fall Liebich'), alleging misuse of the self-ID right — an organised, multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law.

Germany's national protections and functioning rule of law apply unchanged here; the documented counter-action was policed without event cancellation or reported injuries. Earlier assertions of a wider multi-city attack pattern (Bautzen mob sizes, Döbeln prosecutions) lack support in the retained sources and are removed from the record.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
Visitors in every autonomous community stand under the national framework: the 2023 trans-equality law grants self-declared gender marker change and national anti-discrimination protections, and the penal-code reform protects against hate crimes.

The Comunitat Valenciana holds both a dedicated integral law on the right to gender identity and expression and a general LGTBI-equality statute — one of only three communities to legislate in both the trans-specific and general-LGTBI categories — and, unlike the peer community that shares the dual structure, it has not amended or narrowed its provisions. The statutory framework supports institutional response channels for a visitor encountering discrimination.

Enforcement evidence is thin but positive: a documented conviction in the community's court system — six months' prison, suspended, plus fines and a moral-damages payment — for chasing, insulting and recording a trans woman solely because of her gender identity shows the institutional response channel for discrimination operates.

sources.summary: Spanish trans-rights platform's inventory of autonomous-community gender-identity laws lists Comunitat Valenciana with two statutes: Ley 8/2017 of 7 April (integral recognition of the right to gender identity and expression) and Ley 23/2018 of 29 November (LGTBI equality). Other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña (Ley 11/2014) and Aragón (Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spain's autonomous communities, covering gender-identity protocols and education legislation in each, places the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation.

sources.title: BOE-A-2017-5118 Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género en la Comunitat Valenciana. - BOE
sources.summary: Official gazette text of the Comunitat Valenciana's Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresion de genero, published as BOE-A-2017-5118. Article 1 makes the law's purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana must treat people according to their felt gender identity; Title III provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Primary legal text confirming the 'dedicated integral law on the right to identity and gender expression' this record cites, enacted 7 April 2017.

sources.title: BOE-A-2019-281 Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI. - BOE
sources.summary: Official gazette text of Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI (BOE-A-2019-281), the Comunitat Valenciana's general equality statute for LGTBI people. Its provisions cover non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, access and admission rights (art. 56), reversal of the burden of proof (art. 57), and a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions (arts. 58-66) for discrimination against LGTBI people. Primary legal text confirming the community's general-LGTBI-statute category alongside its 2017 trans-specific law, the dual-category statutory framework on which this record's assessment rests.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country: the provincial human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or by third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people during operations in three cities (La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría), under 'preventive policing' frameworks. Academic legal analysis confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution — devolved to provincial justice in 2005 — and street-offence law as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity: a patterned, state-implicated escalation.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is arbitrary detention during any police stop. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework that measurably increased police persecution of trans women, and the protective institutions that coexist — the provincial ombudsman's 2024 registry-rectification guide and its discrimination-caseload machinery — are resident-facing and do not offset that exposure. No provincial law criminalises gender identity; enforcement practice, not statute, does the work.

sources.summary: Buenos Aires provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office (created by Resolución Nº 100/10) submitted to the UN Human Rights Committee for its review of June and July 2016. The submission documents violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police, or third parties acting under police cover, against trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province, in a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents. The 2012 federal Gender Identity Law remains in force. A national DNU of December 2024 added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care, and is under litigation.

UNLP thesis documenting the criminalisation of trans and travesti women in Buenos Aires province through drug-offence prosecutions under microtrafficking enforcement, focused on La Plata's Zona Roja. After the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation in the province. Regional academic evidence of that practice.

Pensamiento Penal legal analysis: rising criminalisation of trans and travesti women in Buenos Aires province, particularly La Plata's Zona Roja. It records that in 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences, the devolution that enabled provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation.

Provincial Ombudsman's September 2024 guide to gender-marker rectification for people born in Buenos Aires province: registry rectification steps, including provisions for people born in the province now living elsewhere. The guide sets out provincial implementation of the recognition regime established by the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Argentina (Wikipedia) — Prisons section: 2025 women's-prison housing restriction
sources.summary: Wikipedia article 'Transgender rights in Argentina', Prisons section: in February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei implemented a ban on housing trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman in a women's prison. 17162690B23777949290372.name: Podlaskie Voivodeship
17162690B23777949290372.summary:
Podlaskie saw Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event: at the 20 July 2019 Białystok Equality March, roughly 1,000 marchers were attacked by thousands of far-right and football-hooligan groups who attempted to block the route. Police detained 25 people; 32 counter-demonstrations had been registered that day, including a prayer vigil at the Cathedral Basilica. In the run-up, Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda had a proclamation read in every church across the region. The surrounding Białystok County had been declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, though the city itself did not adopt one, and its mayor questioned whether the march was "needed" while the PiS city council filed a motion to stop it.

The state's protective response improved materially: at the fourth Equality March (28 September 2024), ~300 participants were escorted by 500 police officers and the Podlaskie police reported zero incidents. This is positive evidence under the single-incident rule (institutional learning, proportionate deployment), but it does not erase the 2019 pattern—organised mass violence met with a partial 25-person detention response, embedded in a documented church-and-county mobilisation infrastructure.

Score of 0.44 sits 0.08 below the national 0.52. Slightly above Subcarpathian (0.42), which lacked Podlaskie's demonstrable five-year improvement in state protection, but below Masovian (0.56), where the institutional machinery runs the other way.

No march violence or ban is documented at the voivodeship scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

17162690B84565288021286.summary:
Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. 27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists; additional Sharia criminal law applies in the northern states.

For a trans traveler Bauchi means exposure to a religious criminal code with a capital ceiling: the religious penal code of this state remains in force (a June 2025 government note confirms it), and its courts are on record as the place where the ultimate penalty was actually pronounced - in June 2022 a religious court in the town of Ningi sentenced three men, including a 70-year-old, to death by stoning for same-sex acts after a religious-police arrest, the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in the country. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out: no execution is on record, the accused were released on bail pending appeal, and the June 2025 note records the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the governor of this state.

Practical safety: the moral code is actively enforced - the same government note places a further death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a religious court in this state in May 2024, and advisory material in 2025-26 continues to cite corporal enforcement of religious morality law in this state. The appellate counterweight exists but is fragile: an upper court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003, and a monitoring organisation recorded further successful appeals.

sources.summary: Reuters report, 2 July 2022: the Ningi Sharia court sentenced three men, a 70-year-old among them, to death by stoning for homosexuality after a 14 June 2022 Hisbah arrest, the first time the death penalty has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria.

Amnesty International press release (2004): the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning 'sodomy' sentence (convicted 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001) for denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003 - 'a number of cases where convictions and sentences to death have been quashed on appeal'. Also records a then-pending stoning appeal (Usman/Ibrahim) before a Sharia Court of Appeal in Niger State.

sources.title: Proceedings and Judgments in the Safiyatu Hussaini Case (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. V)
sources.summary: On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa in Sokoto State convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. The case shows that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the capital-punishment framework the code carries for married men's same-sex acts; the sentence here concerned zina, not same-sex conduct.

sources.title: On the Adoption and Implementation of Sharia Legal System in Zamfara State (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. II)
sources.summary: Alh. The account documents the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists; additional Sharia criminal law applies in the northern states.

In Imo, enforcement under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law is active: in February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the law with its 14-year term, expressly framing the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'. The parallel risk is community violence: in April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them, and a follow-up inquiry records that police took the two men into custody.

For a discovered visitor the risk comes from neighbours and police alike: mob justice drew no recorded accountability in 2018, while named command-level enforcement invoked the criminal law in 2025. 27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists; additional Sharia criminal law applies in the northern states.

In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the two layers compound each other. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions.

Aceh is the only province in the country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own, the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014). It criminalises same-sex conduct under the headings liwath and musahaqah and criminalises close proximity as khalwat. Sentences are imposed by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside secular Satpol PP units, and the punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

The penalty scale runs to 100 strokes for morality offences, and public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. In August 2025 a Sharia court convicted two men of hugging and kissing and sentenced each to 80 strokes; they were caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, and eight more people were caned the same day. CBS News and AP reported the caning on 26 August 2025. In February 2025 two men were publicly caned in Aceh for a same-sex relationship.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them. A February 2025 round-up at a boarding house detained a waria and a gay student who faced up to 100 strokes under the province's provisions.

A trans visitor has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Venue enforcement is documented as well. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens.

The report concerns a gay couple, and no trans person is identified in it.

This supplies Indonesia-wide context for Aceh on trans violence, including the Jan-2018 detention of twelve transwomen, for which no Aceh-specific source is available.

65028918B28198720309323.name: Central Kalimantan
65028918B28198720309323.summary:
Central Kalimantan shows no sub-national divergence for a visitor: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is not one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations. Visitor risk therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction.

Ordinary local moral policing seen in some neighbouring provinces is absent here, but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction; any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence, and a transgender visitor should assume the national criminal baseline applies in full.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
sources.summary: Indonesia's 2023 Penal Code (RUU KUHP) was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline applying to a visitor in Central Kalimantan, whose risk follows the country's national framework rather than any local divergence.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
North Sumatra is one of the eight provinces whose regional regulations the national study (OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation) examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, including rules touching sexual orientation and gender expression. No specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted local bylaw targeting transgender people is documented in the dossier, so the signal for a visitor is legal divergence without operational evidence.

Practical reading: the discriminatory-regulations finding is a real but small risk factor absent any enforcement documentation, and the one documented legal-process data point — a local court handling a transgender man's name-change application neutrally over a six-week process, with no enforcement action against the applicant recorded — points to routine if conservative administration rather than active persecution.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International's 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy) maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations across eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. It finds much overlap but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: The first but not the last: Indonesian transgender man fights for recognition | UNAIDS
sources.summary: Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, North Sumatra's capital, told UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity. After a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application; the judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. This is the only documented legal-process case for North Sumatra: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally, and the article records no enforcement action against the couple.

sources.title: LGBT Manado Aksi Tolak Kekerasan Seksual - SuaraKita
sources.summary: On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined Manado's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, Manado, from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA; SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation whose director Coco Jericho was quoted, took part. The article records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people - a butch lesbian groped during a raid, per SALUT - and that victims often do not report because of fear their families will not accept their orientation. It documents a public LGBT+ presence in Manado and a local account of raid-era conduct, with no arrests or prosecutions reported in the piece.

sources.title: Ketika Waria Berkontes Ratu Pantai - SuaraKita
sources.summary: On Saturday 10 November (2012) a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach, Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi (BNN) as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS. The report quotes Sinjal saying waria are among local people and deserve attention. It documents official-level engagement with North Sulawesi's waria community through a public pageant - evidence of a visible, organised trans community in Manado - with no adverse official action recorded.

The article confirms a visible trans-women community culture in North Sulawesi - an elected province-level waria queen in Manado - while documenting the media-stoked stigma that follows public visibility. No legal or police action appears anywhere in the account.

65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
Yogyakarta is among the eight provinces whose regional regulations a national study (OutRight's 'Creeping Criminalisation') examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, yet the dossier documents no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people here: the visitor-facing signal is legal divergence without operational evidence.

The one enforcement-adjacent event documented - the February 2016 closure of the trans-Muslim religious school in this special region after a hardline religious group threatened to seal it - proceeded on administrative and religious grounds rather than under any enacted regional anti-trans regulation, and drew public restraint from the regional government. For a traveller, the practical exposure is a discriminatory regulatory layer whose actual operation against visitors is not documented; no trans-specific incident involving travellers, and no visitor documents or border-screening practice, is recorded in the dossier. The national framework therefore carries the assessment, with this region contributing a legal-divergence signal that lacks demonstrated enforcement.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: Pesantren Waria Yogyakarta: Kami hanya belajar agama (BBC Indonesia)
sources.summary: BBC Indonesia (26 February 2016) reports that on the night of Wednesday 24 February 2016 Yogyakarta's Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women ('waria') study Islam, was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam (FJI) threatened to seal it, amid what the BBC describes as rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta'. Banguntapan district head (camat) Jati Bayubroto justified the closure on the grounds the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; founder Shinta Ratri said about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. The report documents an enforcement-adjacent event in Yogyakarta against a trans institution, and shows the shutdown proceeded on administrative and religious grounds rather than an enacted regional anti-trans regulation.

sources.title: Pesantren waria di Yogyakarta ditutup sementara (Rappler Indonesia)
sources.summary: Rappler Indonesia's 25 February 2016 report details the closure meeting: on 24 February 2016 at about 20:00 WIB a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta, attended by ward and residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in the earlier 19 February session, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief (Kapolsek), ended with an agreement to shut the Al-Fatah waria pesantren after the Front Jihad Islam demanded it. A waria witness said an FJI leader delivered 'fiery' anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, calling LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' (fellow children of the nation) and saying the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds without any provincial anti-trans statute being cited.

sources.title: Wajah Solidaritas Waria Yogyakarta di Tengah Pandemi (DW Indonesia)
sources.summary: DW Indonesia (21 June 2021) reports that Yogyakarta's trans women ('transpuan'/'waria') — most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic and were, in DW's words, 'ignored by the government', struggling to pay rent and buy food. The article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren in Yogyakarta run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances. It shows the Yogyakarta waria community and pesantren operating again years after the 2016 closure, while documenting persistent economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.

sources.summary: University of KwaZulu-Natal (Durban) Masters criminology thesis, 2024 (Buthelezi, Ayanda Nomfundo): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minority in KwaMashu Township' — 15 queer participants purposively sampled from the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, in-depth interviews; findings report significant victimisation of queer individuals in township settings and examine adequacy of support/interventions and safety strategies.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.

sources.title: Transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp news feature (6 Aug 2025, Elna Schutz) documenting where transgender prisoners are held in South Africa: Jade September, a transgender woman, was imprisoned in the male section of Pollsmoor and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which ruled that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. Reports that the resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure (SOP) for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. Also notes Lawyers for Human Rights representation of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against DCS over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations' concern about implementation of the SOP.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights
sources.summary: Lawyers for Human Rights case page (14 Nov 2025): the South African High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), finding unfair discrimination and harassment because DCS refused to allow her to express her gender identity (feminizing attire, she/her pronouns) and failed to provide appropriate accommodation. The court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, rejected DCS's contrary argument, and ordered DCS to immediately implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs relating to transgender inmates, and provide the prescribed medical care. Subject-verified: documents that trans inmates are accommodated inside the standard national corrections system (here Johannesburg Correctional Centre) and that placement/accommodation obligations rest on DCS SOPs enforced through litigation.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities (SAHRC)
sources.summary: South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT (designated 4 Dec 2024), media statement (14 Nov 2025) welcoming the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, judgment (delivered 10 Nov 2025) in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). Describes Mokoena, assigned male at birth and identifying as female from early childhood, being restricted from wearing feminine clothing and makeup and misgendered while in a correctional facility. Subject-verified: an official state human-rights body confirming that transgender persons are held in the ordinary correctional system and that the 2025 ruling affirms their rights in correctional facilities, including accommodation.

76434192B51294388644125.name: Nothern Cape
76434192B51294388644125.summary:
Three LGBTIQ+ killings were recorded in this province in 2024, two of them suspected hate-crime murders of transgender people: on 14 May 2024 in Upington a 27-year-old transgender woman was stabbed multiple times and her body set on fire in her own room, discovered by a family member who noticed the house burning; on 1 June 2024 an 18-year-old transgender high-school student was stabbed more than 20 times in Kimberley after a man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her on realising she was transgender. A third LGBTIQ+ person - a gay man - was killed in September 2024.

For a traveller, the exposure is severity-weighted: the methods are extreme and the province-level community shock is real, but the incidents are not clearly patterned or state-implicated, and no provincial legislative or enforcement finding against trans visitors is documented. Police opened murder cases in the first two killings - no arrests were reported at the first entry, and a suspect was reportedly arrested in the second (a claim the reporting could not verify with authorities). The register records that police 'identified' the first decedent by a deadname, an institutional practice a visibly trans traveller should anticipate. No visitor documents or border-screening practice is recorded in the dossier.

sources.summary: TGEU Trans Day of Remembrance register entry (14 May 2024): Jo-Ann Isaks, 27, a transgender woman, was found dead in a burning room in the Paballelo location of Upington after multiple stab wounds; a family member noticed the fire at about 23:00. Police (ZF Mgcawu District) confirmed a murder case, with no arrests at the time of the entry, and referred to the decedent by a deadname; the entry quotes district LGBTIQ+ leader Jenny Sambok and reports the province's LGBTIQ+ community 'shaken'.

sources.title: Upington Transgender Woman Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (24 May 2024) reports that on the night of Wednesday 14 May 2024, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was found dead in her burning room in Paballelo township, Upington, after a family member saw flames at about 23:00 and discovered her body, already alight, with multiple stab wounds to the upper body. ZF Mgcawu District Municipality police spokesperson Sgt Omphile Masegela confirmed a murder case had been opened, called the investigation at a critical stage, reported no arrests at that date, and police publicly identified the victim as Jonathan Isaks. Northern Cape LGBTIQ+ district leader Jenny Sambok said the community in the ZF Mgcawu region had been shaken.

sources.title: Transgender Kimberley High School Teen Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (13 June 2024) reports that on 1 June 2024, 18-year-old transgender learner Karabelo Pudumo, a Grade 10 student at Pescodia High School who lived with her grandparents, was stabbed to death in Kimberley, capital of the Northern Cape. A man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender, stabbing her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, though MambaOnline could not verify this with authorities, and more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. The killing is the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the Northern Cape within a month, after Jo-Ann Isaks' 14 May death in Upington.

sources.title: Kimberley to Host First-Ever Northern Cape Pride (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (2 November 2024) reports the inaugural Northern Cape Pride, set for 30 November 2024 at Kimberley's Galeshewe Open Air Arena under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', featuring a morning parade, speakers and community activities, with Pride Committee member Tebogo Makwati calling it a historic moment for the province. The article also records that the province saw at least three LGBTIQ+ community members murdered in 2024: Jo-Ann Isaks (27, transgender woman, May), Karabelo Pudumo (18, transgender high school student, June) and a 50-year-old gay man, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas (September). It documents both organised community presence and the year's third and latest killing of an LGBTIQ+ person in the Northern Cape.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.

sources.summary: Published letter (June 2010) from the NHTL and its Provincial Houses after meeting at Hazyview, Mpumalanga: while 'respecting' the Constitutional Court same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'; states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it.
The underlying 2016 report documents the NHTL asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

sources.title: Murder of lesbian prompts Mpumalanga march against violence (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp (6 January 2020) reports that Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, Mpumalanga, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, half naked with stab wounds. On 2 January about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. The report documents a deadly anti-LGBTIQ incident and community mobilisation inside Mpumalanga.

sources.title: 1ST MPUMALANGA GAY PRIDE A SUCCESS (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (11 September 2014) reports that Mpumalanga's first LGBTI Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital Nelspruit (Mbombela) under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United', with around 1,000 participants marching from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza and a post-parade picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. Organiser Joy Kunene said police were 'visible and supportive' and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers to assist, and the march launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations. The event is direct evidence of a public, police-supported LGBTIQ+ presence in the province's capital.

sources.title: LGBTIQ+ community speak about discrimination at police in eMbalenhle (Ridge Times)
sources.summary: Ridge Times (29 August 2026) reports that at the Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after being sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. The report, from the Secunda-area local press, documents province-specific LGBTIQ+ grievances about police treatment in Mpumalanga.

76434192B37104984973577.name: Limpopo
76434192B37104984973577.summary:
For a trans traveller in the rural parts of this province, the practical risk is the parallel customary-authority system rather than ordinary criminal law: no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded, but chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. An analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system' for people in the former Bantustans and threatens to undermine security 'for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights'. For an outed visitor in a rural area, the moral authority a complaint lands before is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court, and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual.

The legal baseline behind that system is in flux: the legislation was enacted in 2019 and declared unconstitutional in 2023 by the national court, with the declaration suspended while a replacement is prepared - reducing but not eliminating the parallel-system concern a visitor faces in rural areas. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.

sources.summary: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

Mamba Online (18 Apr 2012, Melanie Judge): the Traditional Courts Bill debated in provincial public hearings would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system; lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out, so those who can are expected to leave rural areas; traditional leaders also opposed the 2006 Civil Union Act.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
North West sits squarely in the former-Bantustan geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the Bantustan-era map: HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in South Africa. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

North West is also the only province outside Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010; the GALA-hosted Love Not Hate review records only three quantitative studies ever attempted nationally), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the "dark figure" of unreported crime that characterises most provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65), the two share the former-Bantustan customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; North West's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above Limpopo because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), North West sits higher because KZN adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA official alignment against queer people; North West has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. vs. Western Cape (0.72) and Gauteng (0.71), the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat applies equally: a province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting than more danger.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and this national campaign study, which measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

sources.title: North West trans community desperate for hormone replacement services
sources.summary: The trans community in North West province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to get it, MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the SA Human Rights Commission. Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

sources.title: Lesbian pupil banned from school in North West
sources.summary: MambaOnline (23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News) reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village, North West, was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl', and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a North West institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

sources.title: New Report on LGBT Community in North West
sources.summary: A report entitled 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010, presented the results of a survey conducted under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology during 2009 and 2010, with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella collaborating; it surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination. Provides the province-level 2010 survey behind this record's data-presence signal for North West.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others, Case No. 2024/070075 - High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg (Fisher J), judgment of 10 November 2025
sources.summary: National placement standard governing trans prisoners in every province including Eastern Cape: the judgment records that DCS agrees that, under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act relating to accommodation of vulnerable inmates and the DCS Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), inmates should be accommodated in cells appropriate to their gender identity where feasible and safe; DCS further conceded its own SOPs prescribe single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. The Equality Court, applying these instruments, ordered the DCS to accommodate the complainant in a single cell or in the same cell with inmates of the same gender identity. This is the operative rule for where trans prisoners are housed in Eastern Cape correctional centres (e.g., St Albans, Mthatha, East London), no province-specific trans-placement case being on record.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.

sources.summary: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

sources.title: Transgender Woman in Brutal Hate Crime Attack in Tshwane Tavern
sources.summary: Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane, Gauteng), was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline (6 January 2025) reported had shown no progress. The province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities
sources.summary: The SA Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism (14 November 2025) welcomed the judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), delivered on 10 November 2025. The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. Demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others, Case No. 2024/070075 - High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg (Fisher J), judgment of 10 November 2025
sources.summary: The only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving life, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: initially housed in Medium A section where she could express her gender identity (long hair, makeup, women's clothing); later transferred to Medium C section; at the time of the judgment she was housed in C Single Section, a segregated/solitary-confinement unit of Medium C, and - despite requesting a single cell - was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates (first two cisgender gay men, then one cisgender male), which DCS justified by overcrowding. The court found the DCS's SOPs prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe and that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, ordering DCS to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate SOPs.

The dossier identifies this province as its 'usually scored as safest' unit, with the strongest civil-society infrastructure and the highest public visibility, centred on the metro of Cape Town; no province-specific trans threat, ban, statute, enforcement action, or violent incident was found. For a foreign visitor, the practical implication is that the institutional response to a discovered trans person runs through a metro court, a trained magistrate, and a visible civil-society network - the tier of protection the national constitution's enumeration of gender identity reaches in practice, with the hate-crime framework and the equality clause operating through functioning and accessible metro institutions.

The February 2025 stadium incident qualifies that picture: a trans woman was threatened with removal from a public stadium after using the women's bathroom, a security guard ordered her to the men's bathroom, and police called four times never arrived in nearly three hours - an enforcement-and-response gap a visibly trans visitor can meet in the province's best-resourced metro, recorded without any provincial rule restricting bathroom use by trans people. No visitor documents or border-screening practice is recorded in the dossier, and no chief's court currently operates against a visitor here.

19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Visitors in every region stand under the national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions.

Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and national 7). The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk; Paris alone records 22 per 100,000 but the official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). Île-de-France has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere in metropolitan France.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The dossier's own caveat is explicit: "high recorded rates in Paris should not be read as Paris being dangerous." Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the state actively banned assembly; Île-de-France's state response to Pride was protective if tense. Compare with PACA (0.65), which shares the metro-rate exposure but adds the Fréjus dress-code incident as a specific negative on public appearance.

sources.summary: Interior-ministry statistics service (SSMSI) Infraction rapide n°53, May 2025: 4,800 recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in France in 2024 (+5% on 2023; crimes/délicts up 14%/year since 2016); only about 4% of victims file complaints; acts concentrate in urban units over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris — whose rate, 22 per 100,000 against the national 7, the note attributes partly to non-resident victims and commuters; recorded victims are >70% men.

franceinfo (June 2025): Paris Pride (Marche des fierte, 28 June 2025) was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry; CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march, with police framed as separating opposing groups and extremists as the enemy. Visitor-relevant: big LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response.

sources.title: LGBTQ culture in Paris - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia (LGBTQ culture in Paris): Paris concentrates France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure - as of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, it hosts France's only officially organised gaybourhoods, and it stages the annual Paris Pride parade (La Marche des Fiertés). The article also records that Bertrand Delanoë became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002 and was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals - dated evidence that even the country's most LGBTQ-visible city carries a targeted-violence history a visitor should weigh.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in France - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia (LGBTQ rights in France), the national framework a traveller in Île-de-France stands under: France introduced same-sex civil partnerships (PACS) in 1999 and became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage in 2013, with anti-discrimination protections on grounds of sexual orientation (1985) and gender identity (2012). Since 2017 transgender people may change their legal gender without surgery or any medical diagnosis, and in 2010 France was the first country in the world to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness. This supplies the legal baseline behind the record's national score (0.67) for travel-with-partner and documentation purposes.

Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.

The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documenting systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's director states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year.

Canada's travel advisory tells travellers to avoid all travel to Russia, names Dagestan among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent, and warns that special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas — an access regime that also hampers independent monitoring of how state and customary authority operate on the ground.

For a visitor the risk here is the regional pattern: the federal ‘extremist’ designation of 2023, which extended violence in detention beyond the region, combined with local security structures and family-honour norms that produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process. No separate Dagestan-specific written law targeting trans people exists, and no Chechnya-scale documented purge infrastructure is attributed to this republic.

28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Visitors in every region stand under the national framework: since 2023 legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are banned nationwide, and the propaganda and 'extremist movement' laws apply in every region.

Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Visitors in every region stand under the national framework: since 2023 legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are banned nationwide, and the propaganda and 'extremist movement' laws apply in every region.

Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in Russia (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a Siberian court in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
For a trans visitor, the capital region offers the strongest local protections in the country, but they are city-scoped: in July 2025 a city of the region became the first local government unit to enact a gender-inclusive health ordinance, creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care, mental-health support and specialist services through the city's public-health system - the only enforceable institutional recourse a discovered visitor can find in the country, invoked through the city's complaint machinery. The national picture otherwise is violence against trans women, documented in a 2024-2025 series of killings without dependable local machinery; the memorial record lists a 29-year-old trans woman strangled during a drinking session in a capital-region city on 1 March 2024.

Protection is real but partial for a traveller: a functioning framework on paper in the country's largest city, with an enforcement-and-services reality that does not yet extend past city limits; no national anti-discrimination statute covers gender identity, and no visitor documents or border-screening practice is recorded for the region.

36201628B76469343449086.name: Soccsksargen
36201628B76469343449086.summary:
In June 2025 a transgender-rights activist was shot dead in General Santos City. Human Rights Watch, an international human-rights organisation, called the killing an "apparent targeted killing" and said police were examining her activism as a possible motive; the national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as "marked by cruelty and impunity" and named her. The killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources, and no protective ordinance or institutional counterweight is documented in this region.

For a trans visitor the finding is targeted lethal violence against activists in a province with an official acknowledgement of impunity and no local machinery to answer it.

36201628B47630810559445.name: Central Luzon
36201628B47630810559445.summary:
The region's principal traveler-facing risk sits in Angeles City and the surrounding Clark-Subic corridor: in June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation's Bataan District Office — the national investigative agency — dismantled a trafficking operation at a bar in Angeles City, arresting four people and rescuing 45 victims including 13 minors; in March 2025 the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices in Angeles City under the expanded anti-trafficking in persons act, rescuing 12 victims including 5 minors.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the venues where trans women are concentrated in commercial sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. No protective ordinance cluster comparable to the capital region or Central Visayas is documented here.

sources.title: NBI dismantles human trafficking operation in Angeles City; rescues 45 victims, including 13 minors (NBI press release, 17 June 2025)
sources.summary: National Bureau of Investigation press release, 17 June 2025: the NBI Bataan District Office arrested Alvin Baguio, registered owner of Field Sensation's Bar, together with four others (Reden Roa, John Parro, Shirly Calilong, Marilyn Ferrer) for human trafficking in Barangay Balibago, Angeles City, following a 19 May 2025 referral from Destiny Rescue Pilipinas Incorporated. Agents ran an entrapment and rescue operation on 1 June 2025 in which 'barfine' transactions ranged from P5,000 to P10,000, and 45 victims including 13 minors were rescued and turned over to the social welfare agency.

sources.title: NBI arrests a foreign national for human trafficking; rescues 12 trafficked victims including 5 minors (NBI press release, 10 March 2025)
sources.summary: National Bureau of Investigation press release, 10 March 2025: the NBI Bataan District Office arrested foreign national Shin Ki Jung and accomplices in Angeles City, Pampanga for violations of R.A. No. 11862 (Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022) and R.A. No. 7610. A complaint from the husband of a trafficked victim alleged women were recruited as Korea-bound performers as cover for work at a club in Angeles City, and a subsequent rescue operation freed 12 victims including 5 minors. The arrested subjects were presented for inquest before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Angeles City.

sources.title: In Philippine red-light district, an uphill struggle to battle trafficking and abuses (Preda Foundation / The Fuller Project, 21 November 2019)
sources.summary: Preda Foundation article, published 21 November 2019, originally The Fuller Project's reporting: hundreds of girls are supplied each year in Angeles City to meet demand from foreign men paying for sex, many of them American, in the city that hosted a former US military base. More than 150 women and girls interviewed by The Fuller Project in Angeles City said they wanted to leave prostitution but did not know how. City-regulated 'entertainers' must take weekly STD tests, which activists criticised as marketing the sex industry as clean. Advocates warned that a new airport terminal on the city's outskirts could triple visitor numbers and expand sex trafficking.
