36201628B63748016552864.name: Cagayan Valley
36201628B63748016552864.summary:
Two killings of trans women are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national series. On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, a 40-year-old trans woman was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects were identified, and the monitored trans-murder count records the cause as stabbing. On 23 June 2025 the body of an 18-year-old trans woman student was found in a river in Cagayan province days after she was reported missing, with signs of physical assault noted; a young male student surrendered to police and denied involvement.

No protective ordinance, institutional-hostility finding or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors is documented in this region beyond these incidents, so the visitor picture is violence without operative local protections.

sources.title: Recent killings of trans women prompt groups to push for LGBTQIA protection (Bulatlat)
sources.summary: Bulatlat, 26 June 2025, reports that 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol (formerly Gian Molina), a business management student at Cagayan State University resident in Zone 7, Centro, Peñablanca, Cagayan, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025, days after being reported missing. Her mother told local media (95.7 XFM Tuguegarao) she saw visible signs of physical assault when the body was found. A criminology student of the University of Cagayan Valley, named online as 'Menco de Guzman'/'Sherwin Kyqle', voluntarily surrendered to the Peñablanca police station, admitting he picked Kierra up on Saturday night but denying involvement. Bahaghari chairperson Reyna Valmores Salinas called the killing proof that LGBTQ+ persons remain unsafe and renewed the call for the SOGIESC Equality Bill (House Bill No. 5551; Senate Bill No. 1600), noting no national anti-discrimination law has passed in 25 years. Second trans-woman killing documented in Cagayan Valley (Cagayan province) within the 2024-2025 national series, with an identified suspect who surrendered to police.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ groups, umalma sa ikalawang tala ng pamamaslang sa estudyanteng trans woman (Manila Today)
sources.summary: Manila Today, 25 June 2025 (Filipino), reports that two days after Kierra Apostol was reported missing, the trans woman student, an incoming first-year Business Management student at Cagayan State University-Caritan Campus and a hair-and-makeup artist active in local gay pageants, was found floating in the river between Amulung and Iguig in Cagayan on the morning of 23 June 2025, her mother citing marks of violence. LGBTQIA+ groups including CSU Crystal (Cagayan State University-Andrew campus), LGBT Pilipinas Taguig City Inc. and Bahaghari chair Reyna Valmores Salinas demanded a full and thorough investigation, justice, and immediate passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Corroborates the second documented trans-woman killing in this region, adding the Amulung-Iguig river location and the suspect-surrender detail beyond the Bulatlat account.

sources.title: Trans woman makes history as she graduates summa cum laude from Capiz State U (Inquirer.net)
sources.summary: Inquirer.net, 7 August 2025, reports that at its 21st commencement exercises Capiz State University produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude: Khaz-JP Padilla, batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honor, an outcome attributed to the Capiz State advocacy campaign that followed the October 2022 hair-and-uniform directive. Padilla describes the school's binary haircut rules she faced in earlier years ('Why is it that whenever I cut my hair... it feels like I'm losing my self-confidence?') and her transition once pandemic-era online classes freed her from the haircut rule. Confirms the milestone of the first openly trans woman graduating as valedictorian with highest honours.

36201628B64564033926366.name: Ilocos Region
36201628B64564033926366.summary:
A visitor in the Pangasinan corridor has a local complaint route absent in most other regions: Bayambang municipality's ordinance protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons on SOGIESC grounds — certified and affirmed at the provincial level in August 2024 — with complaints filed through the barangay mechanism under the local-government code, carrying a penalty ladder from fines to imprisonment.

The route is limited: the protection is municipal, and in the rural parts of two other provinces of the region a customary-justice system recognised by the national courts keeps its own dispute-resolution authority over defined offences, so the applicable institution in a dispute may not be a national court.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision criminalising a person for being transgender. No instrument reviewed for this record creates such an offence at regional level either; the visitor-facing risk in the region is structural, arising from which forum hears a dispute rather than from any statute aimed at gender non-conformity.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, whose drafting began on 29 March 2019, prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause commits the region to adjudication "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws", placing civil and religious law side by side inside the region's own governing statute.

The jurisdiction a visitor's dispute reaches is therefore not settled by default. Since Presidential Decree 1083 of 1977, Shari'ah jurisdiction has been confined to personal-status law; a proposal tabled in the Bangsamoro Parliament on 14 July 2026 would recast that limit through a Shari'ah Justice Code of 10 books extending jurisdiction into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the authority of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. It is not a power in force, and no source reviewed establishes that Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, nor that any such law has passed.

The legal-pluralist marriage regime applies directly to a visitor married to a Muslim spouse. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written-opt-in clauses allowing civil entities to take the same questions. In practice, spouse-status and inheritance questions for such a visitor would run through religious personal-status forums rather than through the civil courts alone.

The reach of those forums is widening. In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law, passed unanimously by the Bangsamoro Parliament, creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, extending the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian provinces of northern Mindanao and the Davao region, parts of the Visayas and Luzon, and Metro Manila. The measure carries the Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing.

No protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure is documented inside the region. The SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances recorded nationally cover eight provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo) and 32 cities and municipalities, none of them within the Bangsamoro, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed and stalled in Congress for 25 years, leaving no national statute as a backstop. National sectoral protections such as the Safe Spaces Act, the Magna Carta of Women and the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers apply by force of national law, but the region has no locally enacted SOGIE protection of its own on the record reviewed.

Violence and detention findings for the Philippines at large cannot be assumed to describe conditions inside the Bangsamoro. The documented cases of killings of trans women in June 2025, the arrest in May 2025 of a foreign national accused of raping a trans woman, and the classification practices recorded at Manila City Jail and Davao City Jail all fall outside this region, and no equivalent documentation for Bangsamoro facilities was located.

36201628B49646111072560.tangentialFactors:
The region is the clearest instance of legal pluralism in the national territory: the same conduct could in theory be assessed by civil, Shari'ah or traditional tribal forums depending on the parties and the question, and the July 2026 proposal would widen the religious forum's subject-matter reach well beyond the personal-status boundaries in force since 1977. A visitor's exposure therefore turns on forum allocation, not on a single criminal code.

The trajectory runs toward expansion rather than contraction. The August 2024 law creating three Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, and the 10-book justice code tabled in July 2026, both push religious jurisdiction outward; the region's own Administrative Code already names Shari'ah and tribal law alongside the Constitution as sources of justice.

Comparatively, the protections a trans traveller expects elsewhere in the Philippines are attenuated here. The eight provinces and 32 cities with SOGIE ordinances sit outside the region, the SOGIE Equality Bill has produced no national statute in 25 years, and campaigners have cited that blockage as the direct reason two killings in June 2025 produced no legislative remedy.

Travel-risk scoring for the country is capital-weighted. A 2026 assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers at 69 of 100 while scoring trans travellers at 62 in the 'Exercise Caution' band; that figure describes Manila and does not extend to the Bangsamoro or to its Shari'ah forums.

Documentation of harm is concentrated elsewhere in the country. The trans-specific killings, the drag-artist assault in Bayambang, Pangasinan in April 2024, the jail head-shaving and informal 'wedding' arrangements recorded at Manila City Jail, and the batch transfer of LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail all come from outside this region, so their absence from the record here reflects sourcing rather than a demonstrated absence of risk.

36201628B92932511992503.name: CAR
36201628B92932511992503.summary:
For a trans traveler in the Cordillera administrative region, the finding is structural uncertainty over which forum decides a dispute — inter-tribal customary justice or the formal court system — rather than any documented trans-specific adverse outcome. The inter-tribal customary justice system runs alongside the formal system: the Kalinga peace-pact system, with its own holders, sanctions and authority over crimes and tribal-related offences, was codified in February 2026 by the provincial government into a 137-page written Pagta, a step its sponsors present as recognition by the national courts.

No trans-specific customary ruling, exclusion or punishment relating to gender expression appears in this record, and no trans-specific adverse outcome is documented. The customary system here is a civil and restorative-justice institution with no criminal-law expansion over morality documented, which keeps it a marginal concern, not a threat finding. No visitor documents, border-screening practice, or marriage/partner-travel provision is recorded in the dossier for this region.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.

Police again restricted the march to a single bus-only lane, and organizers framed the event as resistance to 'hate and discriminatory politics'. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. State-adjacent opposition recurs annually and is judicially contained each time.

It faces standing opposition from religious groups, with an estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups forming a 'gay issue countermeasure committee' in Daegu to block LGBT events. The page records that such opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street, and it carries survey context on national attitudes: Pew Research Center found 18% of South Koreans felt homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013.

sources.summary: No Cut News (English, 8 June 2026): the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea (NHRCK) demanding a change of venue for the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, claiming the event is likely to infringe on public welfare. The group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single NHRCK petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Daegu's Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It responds to the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Court and petition filings show that venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation over the festival continued into the 2026 edition.

For a trans visitor to Daejeon the documented evidence is institutional, not visitor-facing: in October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the military's forced discharge of a transgender soldier, holding the military should have considered her a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — a ruling widely described as a landmark in the case brought to repeal the discharge decision, and the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier.

The practical reading for a traveler is a judicial climate in which a local court delivered a pro-recognition ruling on trans status, with no visitor-facing enforcement action, arrest, or incident documented for this unit, and no visitor documents, border-screening practice, or marriage/partner-travel provision recorded in the dossier.

Byun Hee-soo — the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier — holding the military should have treated her as female after her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that fitness review should weigh basic rights. Decision vindicated the posthumous appeal. For the record: dated, court-level proof that a Daejeon court delivered a pro-recognition ruling on trans military status.

Aju Press (2024-06-25): Korea's first transgender soldier, Byun Hee-soo, was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024. Some 60 activists protested, arguing that the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment. She died by suicide in 2021 after the forced 2020 discharge, gender dysphoria classified as a mental disorder, a post-surgery physical-disability finding, and court appeals. Her state burial in Daejeon stands as official honouring while institutional stance remains conservative.

68945753B43731078897969.summary:
For a trans visitor, this province's standing is origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors: the model student human-rights ordinance — covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity — was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for this province, and the province stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances when the capital abolished its own in April 2024.

The protections credited to the province bear on enrolled students and school staff, not on visitors; no visitor-facing enforcement action, arrest, or incident is documented for this unit, and a teacher based in the province warned that wholesale abolition of such ordinances 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. sources.summary: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. 47653553B66835736668351.name: RegiÃ³n del BÃ­o-BÃ­o
47653553B66835736668351.summary:
Movilh-Biobío formally denounced (14 October 2016) what it called "brutal and illegal acts of discrimination" at the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where a trans woman was interned in men's beds even though public policy and the legal duty to treat trans people by their chosen name and social sex required the opposite — the complaint was lodged with the Seremi de Salud. (Law 21.120, the standard arguably breached, took effect only in December 2019, after the denunciation.) This remains the closest Chilean analogue to a facility-misassignment incident directly encountered by a visitor: an emergency-room or inpatient visit in Bío-Bío carries a documented risk of gender-mismatched placement. Separately, Concepción's municipality dismissed the staff of its Oficina de la Diversidad y No Discriminación during the January 2025 honourary-staff cuts (~100 workers), which LGBTIQA+ organisations called a "dismantling" leaving one person in post.

Bío-Bío held 5.89 % of the national case total in 2024 — third highest — reinforcing that the region's institutional failures occur against an elevated baseline of discrimination reports. Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.10 deviation driven by two concrete traveler-facing findings: the hospital bed placement (medical exposure) and the diversity-office dismantling (loss of local complaint infrastructure). Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), Bío-Bío is 0.06 higher: Valparaíso's problem is the volume of over half the national case load, while Bío-Bío has specific institutional incidents but a normalised share. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Bío-Bío is 0.02 lower: Tarapacá's finding is a judicial annulment that devalues trans life in theory, whereas Bío-Bío's hospital episode shows how that devaluation manifests in the care a visitor might actually receive.

Movilh XXIII annual report (Mar 2025, 2024 data): Bío-Bío held 5.89% of the national case total, the third-highest share of Chile's regions, with Concepción among the cities recording the most documented incidents (5).

47653553B84299910343297.name: RegiÃ³n de La AraucanÃ­a
47653553B84299910343297.summary:
Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: only 157 people used the Gender Identity Law (21.120) for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), La Araucanía is 0.01 higher: Tarapacá carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas Araucanía's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because Araucanía's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising region with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.

10402087B60477050509260.name: Bayern
10402087B60477050509260.summary:
Visitors in every Land stand under the national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove the federal floor.

Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German is prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration: the ban implements a December 2023 government declaration through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities, and its practical reach extends across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with, even though critics dismiss the measure as symbol politics.

The legal baseline a visitor stands under is the national Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024: adults over 18 may change first name and legal gender by self-declaration with three months' notice, same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and in goods and services. For a trans visitor the operative regional signal is therefore administrative-interface restriction on gender-inclusive language rather than any change to the national legal floor.

sources.summary: Tagesschau report on Bavaria's gender-language ban: from 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German is prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 and a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities; critics in the coverage dismiss it as symbol politics while noting its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom.

Antenne Bayern report on the Bundesrat initiative by several Länder — Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt, with Bavaria a partner — to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change, i.e. an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Germany
sources.summary: National framework applying to Bavaria. Adults have been able to change legal gender since 1980. The Self-Determination Act was approved by the cabinet in August 2023 and passed the Bundestag 374-251 on 12 April 2024; it lets adults over 18 change first name and gender by self-determination with three months' notice, in force since 1 November 2024. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods and services, with some protections varying by region. This is the federal baseline within which Bavaria's gender-language ban and the Länder push to tighten the SBGG operate.

sources.title: Selbstbestimmungsgesetz
sources.summary: German Wikipedia article on the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), the federal law the Bavarian Bundesrat initiative sought to tighten. It passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 (374-251, 11 abstentions) and the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, and was gazetted 21 June 2024; changes could be registered from 1 August 2024 and took effect 1 November 2024. Adults declare the change themselves before the registry office. Those aged 14-17 need a guardian's consent or the family court's; for under-14s only the guardian can declare. A three-month waiting period applies, with a one-year lockout after a change. The Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft let parents decide under-14 gender-entry changes 'without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare', the contested point behind the Bavarian-led tightening initiative.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales
sources.summary: The Welsh Government's February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales aims to make Wales 'the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe'. Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn announced it in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement. It was built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel (March 2021) and a 12-week public consultation with 1,328 responses, and it funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). The plan records the UK Government's blocking of the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023. Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, and parents of transgender children called for more help (BBC, March 2024). It is the official Welsh inclusion framework with its dates and numbers.

In Wales, trans adults were historically referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019 (BBC). This is the legal framework and local gender-identity clinic a trans visitor in Wales stands under.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 in force 27 July 2026) removed the civil provision making it unlawful to "offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate" a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, including gender identity. The NT is the only Australian jurisdiction that has actively reversed anti-discrimination protection rather than extended it; the government framed the rollback as "restoring freedom of speech and religion." For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is now deliberately outside NT law while other states have brought it inside.

Federal protections continue to apply uniformly: the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 covers gender identity in every state and territory, and NT hate-crime penalty enhancements for SO/GI-motivated offences (2022 amendment, effective 2023) remain in force. No criminal expression ban, no facility-access ban, and no conversion-practice-specific enforcement issue arises for a short-term visitor beyond the general federal framework.

Remote-area context amplifies practical risk: Alice Springs records approximately 2,600+ offences against a population of ~25,000, and trans community infrastructure in the NT is thin. A single domestic killing of a Tiwi Sistergirl (Darwin, October 2024) is recorded for completeness but is one non-patterned incident and does not support a regional violence finding on its own.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the NT sits 0.09 below: the deliberate legislative removal of the "offend, insult, humiliate" protection is the strongest negative sub-national signal in Australia, even though it is a civil-law rollback rather than a criminal prohibition. Vs Victoria (0.88), where the 2025 Anti-Vilification Act created the country's first criminal offence for public incitement against a trans person, the NT moved in the opposite direction in the same year.

ABC News, 17 Oct 2025: the NT government's anti-discrimination amendments passed parliament, framed as restoring free speech and religious freedom — narrowing the vilification provision and letting religious schools prefer staff sharing the same faith; the government had earlier backtracked from scrapping the vilification section. Marks reduced territorial vilification/discipline protections shaping discrimination exposure for visitors.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in the Northern Territory - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The NT timeline records male homosexual activity legal since 1 January 1984, with an equal age of consent since 2003; same-sex marriage nationwide from December 2017, the territory's postal-survey 'Yes' at 60.6%; full adoption rights since 2018; birth-certificate sex-marker change requiring clinical treatment since 2018; and territory discrimination protections since 2022, with a March 2025 government announcement and a July 2025 bill to repeal the vilification provision covering 'offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate'. The NT government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025 and issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors. The territory's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among its motives; federal coverage of those motives dates only from 2025. The territory is reversing rather than extending anti-discrimination protection.

sources.title: NT's CLP government confirms plans to scrap Labor's hate speech changes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News, 2 March 2025: the Country Liberal Party government confirmed it would repeal the vilification provision Labor added to NT anti-discrimination law three years earlier, which made it unlawful to 'offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate' a person because of a characteristic such as race or gender and could trigger action by the NT Anti-Discrimination Commission. Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby framed the change as restoring 'freedom of speech and religion', including letting religious schools again hire only co-religionists. NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the move, warning the government may be 'opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech'. The rollback was enacted as the Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025, assented 30 October 2025.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024, in force since 4 April 2025, makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person out of the state for the purpose or engaging a provider outside the state for it (taking a person out of the state for the purpose carries up to three years); a civil complaints scheme runs through the state anti-discrimination body. The state also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Violence context: a trans woman was killed in her apartment in January 2020, and the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and went to a murder trial — a positive institutional response. In a second case a trans woman who had arrived in the country roughly six weeks earlier was strangled, and her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that media reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in this state within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents.

No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this state is recorded in the dossier; the operative visitor-facing exposure is the violence pattern and the criminal conversion-practices ban rather than any state-specific document or travel rule.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

Western Australia's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute of 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex — a narrower, medically-inflected, binary formulation than the 'gender identity' language used in other Australian jurisdictions and in the federal Sex Discrimination Act. A non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may not meet the state-law definition and would rely solely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint; there is no state anti-vilification offence (civil or criminal) and no statutory charter binding public authorities.

Reform is underway: a registration amendment act received assent on 26 September 2024, removing medical and surgical prerequisites for registration of a sex or gender change, with substantive commencement still by proclamation; it is not yet fully in force as of the scoring date, so the narrower 'gender history' definition remains the operative complaints route a visitor stands under.

Complaints mechanics: a state complaint runs to the state equal-opportunity commission under the Equal Opportunity Act with a 12-month lodgement window, a one-week acknowledgement and a free conciliation conference; the alternative federal route runs to the national human-rights commission under the Sex Discrimination Act within 24 months (12 months for employment), and only one route may be chosen.

sources.summary: The consolidated PDF of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) could not be retrieved, as the state legislation portal blocks automated fetches. The official explainer quotes the operative definitions: the Act protects the attribute 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex, with complaint eligibility tied to recognition certificates or registry change under the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework.

WA Government guidance (first published 6 Aug 2020, last updated 12 Feb 2026): gender history is a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) — a person has gender history if they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such; direct discrimination (including treating a person as their former sex) and indirect discrimination are unlawful.

sources.title: Reforms to remove barriers for LGBTQIA+ community | Western Australian Government
sources.summary: On 16 April 2024, WA Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024 would be introduced to State Parliament that week. The Bill repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, which the ministers describe as the only remaining board of its kind in Australia, replacing it with a streamlined administrative process through the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Applicants would no longer need medical or surgical reassignment, providing instead a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling. A 'non-binary' sex descriptor would become available, stricter rules would apply to under-18s through parental consent or Family Court of WA permission, and the Bill contains a statutory review clause after three years. The announcement implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations and links the reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a conversion-practices ban in 2025. The 2024 Act removes medical and surgical prerequisites for registering a sex or gender change in Western Australia.

sources.title: Equal Opportunity Commission Fact Sheet - Gender Reassigned Person Discrimination | Western Australian Government
sources.summary: The WA Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet states that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (WA), passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a new definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The amendment will not operate retrospectively. Gender history discrimination complaints under the Equal Opportunity Act will need to be made in compliance with the new registration requirements once the Act commences. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001. The 2024 reform feeds back into the scope of WA's 'gender history' attribute for complaints purposes, and substantive commencement is by proclamation.

sources.title: How to deal with gender discrimination and transphobia (WA) | Justice Connect
sources.summary: Justice Connect's WA-specific resource, last updated 16 April 2026, states that in Western Australia a discrimination complaint can be made to the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA), with a 12-month lodgement window, an acknowledgment of receipt within one week, and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A federal route is also available: a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters. Only one route, state or federal, can be chosen. The resource names trans-specific local support in WA: TransFolk of WA and the Freedom Centre for under-26s. The state-level protective attribute in WA is 'gender history' rather than 'gender identity', and state complaints run through the Equal Opportunity Commission.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The territory's Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, giving a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or public facility a legal review mechanism that common-law states without a charter lack. The territory is also one of four jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for this territory; the absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and the self-identification custody rule, places it modestly above the national average.

A conversion-practices ban has been in force since early 2021, with offending practices attracting up to a 12-month custodial term or a fine, alongside civil penalties giving a tribunal power to issue orders and order redress; practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this territory is recorded in the dossier.

ACT-relevant: names the ACT's explicit self-ID prison policy.

The Human Rights Law Centre report 'Ending Strip Searching in Australian prisons' (2026), produced with the trans-community groups Flat Out and FIGJAM, documents strip-searching practice in Australian prisons and its disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners across jurisdictions. It bears on the custody screening a gender-nonconforming visitor faces when detained.

sources.title: Human Rights Act 2004 | Acts | ACT Legislation Register
sources.summary: The official ACT Legislation Register lists the Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) as In Force, with the current republished version and a full republication history back to 1 July 2004. Section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. The register also records uncommenced amendments by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025. The Act is the statutory rights framework that ACT public authorities must operate within.

sources.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. The study documents a shortfall of institutional capacity for transgender health care in the ACT.

sources.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. The statute is an ACT criminal and civil protection measure, and along with the Human Rights Act and the self-identification custody rule it forms part of the territory's protective legal framework.

25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Visitors in every autonomous community stand under the national framework: the 2023 trans-equality law grants self-declared gender marker change and national anti-discrimination protections, and the penal-code reform protects against hate crimes.

Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community that has never enacted a regional LGTBI or gender-identity law, and for a transgender visitor that vacuum has a practical administrative meaning: no dedicated regional equality office exists to receive a complaint, there is no institutional hate-crime observatory, and no region-specific administrative protocol governs responses to gender-motivated incidents. No criminal ban or facility restriction exists in the region, national criminal law fully applies, and the severity floor is therefore set by the state; the recorded deviation of approximately −0.07 from the national score (0.88) reflects sub-national administrative coldness and rural exposure rather than any region-specific criminal threat.

The pending regional LGTBI+ equality bill (registered December 2024, in processing since 11 June 2025) is framed around ending the sexilio — the documented exodus of LGBT people, especially the young, from the region's rural areas to larger cities — a resident-facing concern rather than a visitor protection; until it is enacted, a transgender traveller facing discrimination has no dedicated regional channel beyond the national institutions, and the protective infrastructure is thinnest in the rural areas where the exodus pattern is documented.

sources.summary: Europa Press (Valladolid, 11 Jun 2025): the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the PSOE-sponsored LGTBI+ bill into consideration (76 articles) after the PP abstained; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands.

Salamancahoy (20 Dec 2024): the PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León, aiming to end the "sexilio" (out-migration of LGBTI people from the region), one of three bills tabled that week; group leader Tudanca urged fastest possible processing.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 Jun 2025): the plenary approved taking the LGTBI equality bill into debate with opposition support except Vox and PP abstention; LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

25490228B48808997991554.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Visitors in every autonomous community stand under the national framework: the 2023 trans-equality law grants self-declared gender marker change and national anti-discrimination protections, and the penal-code reform protects against hate crimes.

Ceuta, an autonomous city rather than a comunidad autónoma, has no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute — a framework gap it shares with its neighbouring city Melilla and with Castilla y León, recorded in the national regional-law inventories as a gap case only. No incident evidence, no enforcement data and no hate-offence figure separating the city from the national aggregate was retrievable, so this is a statute-book gap, explicitly not an incident finding. National criminal law and the national police still operate here, so the enforcement floor for a transgender visitor is unchanged from the rest of the country; unlike some communities, the city has no regional equality office, LGTBI observatory or police force of its own.

The border-fence crossing environment and the city's religious-minority composition create a document-and-presentation context different from the rest of the country, adding modest friction for a visitor whose identity documents do not match presentation. The one LGTBI-specific episode the dossier records for the city concerns migrants remaining there after an irregular-entry wave, not visitor incidents.

sources.title: Radiografía de la educación en diversidad LGTBI+ 2025 - FELGTBI+ / Universidad de Salamanca
sources.summary: FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, states that Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta y Melilla are the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. A 2020 precedent study had placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings. The report notes legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and records no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla, leaving Ceuta in the inventory as a statutory-gap case with no regional LGTBI or gender-identity law.

sources.title: Arcópoli pide al Gobierno el traslado "urgente" a la Península de los migrantes LGTBI+ que permanecen en Ceuta - Europa Press
sources.summary: Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote by letter to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta. The episode shows how Ceuta's border-fence crossings shape the documents and self-presentation expected of LGTBI migrants and visitors there.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Spain - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute, so the national framework governs there. A registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in the autonomous city of Melilla in 2008, alongside Ceuta in 1998 and all 17 mainland communities, granting unmarried couples benefits regarded as mainly symbolic; this is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute. The national framework applying in Melilla provides same-sex marriage and adoption nationwide since July 2005, bans hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity since 1995 with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives, and has allowed legal-gender self-determination on documents without surgery or sterilisation since the trans law approved 16 February 2023 (vote 191-60 with 91 abstentions, applying to people over 16). National criminal and equality law and the state police govern in Melilla.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Every state and the federal territory stand under the national framework: Sharia law prohibits a man posing as a woman across all states (up to three years' jail), so the criminalisation baseline applies to every visitor in every region.

In August 2026 the Kelantan assembly passed a new Syariah Criminal Offences Bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state's syariah jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state's 2019 syariah criminal code that Malaysia's Federal Court had struck down as outside state power. The Bill also carries "protection of modesty" decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years.

The sequence — invalidation by the federal courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to syariah proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.

sources.summary: Kelantan passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 in Aug 2026, containing provisions on covering aurat, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts, replacing 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 struck down by the Federal Court. Clause 15 mandates Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. The state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

Kelantan passed strict new decency rules via the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 on 13 Aug 2026, legislating decency, aurat-covering, and gender-change provisions. The enactment replaces 16 provisions of the 2019 enactment struck down by the Federal Court. A related Feb 2026 case was the first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change. The new decency and gender-change legislation is in force and being applied by the Syariah courts.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
Every state and the federal territory stand under the national framework: Sharia law prohibits a man posing as a woman across all states (up to three years' jail), so the criminalisation baseline applies to every visitor in every region.

In May 2025 the city authority of the state capital erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a 'constant reminder' to steer people away from homosexuality. A transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.

The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences the state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary religious-law offences and the national criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What a transgender visitor meets here is open, ongoing official hostility, including state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.

sources.summary: A Terengganu state executive councillor (May 2025) openly confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations in the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, saying the state wants people to consider the acts 'dirty, wrong, and to be avoided'. For this record: official state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging — a direct indicator of the hostile official stance a transgender visitor faces in Terengganu.

Thirteen civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters (May 2025) urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove anti-LGBT signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law; they criticised the Terengganu state executive councillor's defence of the signboards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. For this record: corroborates the official anti-LGBT campaign in Terengganu and documents civil-society pushback with named actors.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
Every state and the federal territory stand under the national framework: Sharia law prohibits a man posing as a woman across all states (up to three years' jail), so the criminalisation baseline applies to every visitor in every region.

In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for 'encouraging vice'. The raid's design — isolating transgender women as a category from a mixed party — evidences enforcement capacity and willingness aimed at transgender people specifically. A coalition of national human-rights organisations publicly protested, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves.

The legal baseline for a visitor: the state's 2014 religious criminal enactment criminalises same-sex conduct (liable to fines, imprisonment or whipping) and criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, while female cross-dressing is not criminalised; a transgender visitor whose public presentation does not match her assigned sex is directly exposed under that provision, and same-sex conduct offences apply to a visiting couple as they do to residents.

sources.summary: The Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014) criminalises liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex) under sections 23 and 24, punishable by up to RM5,000 fine, up to 3 years' imprisonment, or up to 6 strokes of whipping, or any combination. A male posing as a woman in public is criminalised under section 26 (up to RM1,000 fine or up to 1 year imprisonment), while female cross-dressing is not. Women convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to 6 months under section 52. This is state criminal law covering same-sex conduct and trans male-to-female public presentation in Kedah.

65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by Pelangi Nusantara — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ('Bogor clean of LGBT'). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law — Amnesty demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to Perpres 111/2025, which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: 'people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence.' The pattern-plus-impunity combination is West Java-specific; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.

A trans woman quoted says those who previously appeared in public now live in fear. The attack shows street violence against trans women in West Java, enabled by that national regulatory backdrop.

Tempo (25-26 June 2025): Indonesian police detained 75 people at a villa in Puncak, Bogor Regency, West Java, at a gathering police called an LGBT 'family gathering' held 'to avoid detection'. West Java Regional Police confirmed the June 22, 2025 arrests, which followed a tip from local residents. Police in West Java investigate and detain LGBT gatherings inside the region.

Amnesty International (24 June 2025) condemned the arrest of 75 people in the raid on a privately rented villa in Puncak, Bogor, West Java, calling it a discriminatory raid and 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia. Amnesty said the gathering violated no law and demanded release and accountability. LGBTI gatherings in West Java face police action even where no law has been broken.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people recorded as swept up in LGBT sweeps/app findings jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed nagari regulations on social deviance). Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft (ranperda, articles 13-14) on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions of rupiah plus mandated "rehabilitation" (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation mapping of discriminatory regional regulations covers eight other provinces (not West Sumatra itself, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this province's bylaws instantiate.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most provinces; the documented apprehension counts show the bylaw environment is actively policed, though no caning (an Aceh-specific penalty) or prosecution under these provisions is recorded. It remains above West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.

For this record: documents a 2024 local anti-LGBT public-order regulation in a West Sumatra city, showing formal municipal-level restrictions.

Peer-reviewed study (2025) of LGBT cases in Bukittinggi City, West Sumatra: recorded cases rose from 56 individuals in 2023 to 272 in 2024; the Kurai Customary Law Community (Masyarakat Hukum Adat Kurai) acts as a non-state actor, initiating the customary sanction 'dibuang sepanjang adat' (expulsion under adat), proposing village regulations on social deviance, and implementing barcode monitoring in boarding houses to police LGBT presence. For this record: documents rising state-and-adat surveillance and customary sanctions against LGBT people within a West Sumatra city.

Mimbarsumbar.id (13 May 2026): the DPRD (regional legislature) of Limapuluh Kota regency, West Sumatra, finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation (Ranperda) within a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, including administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people; the drafting body chair stated the stages have reached finalisation. For this record: a 2026 draft regency-level regulation introducing fines and 'rehabilitation' targeting LGBT people in West Sumatra.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra, Yogyakarta) - the reference for Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism; West Sumatra's newer Bukittinggi regulation postdates the mapping.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.

sources.summary: Peer-reviewed article (Anthropology of the Middle East, 2025) on the 'precarious lives' of the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Indonesia based on four ethnographic case studies in Bali: documents how transpuan people navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition and discrimination, challenging the narrative of victimhood while showing real precarity. For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

Travel guide (Gayborhood/Traven) on Bali: ranks the destination '6.3/10' with a legal score of 2.0, warning same-sex relations are criminalised in Indonesia and that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risks; advises visitors to 'keep your love a little quieter' despite the island's tolerant reputation. For this record: practical traveller-facing warning that Bali's legal backdrop (Indonesian national law) carries criminalisation risk even where the local scene is accepting.

Travel guide (Mar 2026): Bali is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers on a 'live and let live' basis, and same-sex relationships are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, though the new Criminal Code (KUHP, in effect Jan 2026) adds complexity; same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia; Seminyak (Eat Street/Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, while public displays of affection warrant discretion. For this record: current, specific traveller guidance for trans/LGBTQ visitors to Bali including the 2026 KUHP law change.

65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.

Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report Q3 2025, dated 31 October 2025, covers West Papua and records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, arrests of protesters and the failure of accountability mechanisms as security forces expand across the territory, alongside a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. These findings describe a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in West Papua that bears on overall traveller safety. The report carries no trans or LGBTI findings.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP). Papua is among the provinces where trans residents have received them, alongside Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth gender is printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same national legal framework applies in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage, carrying up to one year in prison, takes effect on 2 January 2026; same-sex marriage is not recognised; and customary laws may apply. Trans people in Papua may therefore obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme while remaining subject to that framework.

No enacted local bylaw with specified penalties yet exists in the province, and no violence wave or mass police raid against trans people is documented in the dossier.

The small negative deviation from the national score reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway to eastern Indonesia, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement. It remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles specifying fines and rehabilitation is already on the books, and above Jakarta (0.12), where a 56-person raid without legal basis has already occurred: the law here is proposed, not enacted, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule the traveler-facing impact is prospective.

65028918B9551391119865.name: South Sumatra
65028918B9551391119865.summary:
On 19 July 2026 Palembang's city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation (Perpres) No. 111 of 2025 on the national defence policy 2025-2029, which lists the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats; Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. The regulation remains in preparation, not enacted, with no specified penalty; no enforcement event is documented for this province. South Sumatra is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight's discriminatory-regulation mapping, and its neighbour Lampung saw a documented Satpol PP raid on three transwomen (November 2018) - the Sumatran belt is where local enforcement is consolidating.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT measures from moral panic to national-defence doctrine - the August 2026 ABC reporting links the 'rule that deems them a threat' to a wave of street attacks on trans women, though it cautions the trend cannot yet be confirmed - but without an enacted local penalty the traveler-facing risk here remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions.

31927357B17004778023462.name: Aguascalientes
31927357B17004778023462.summary:
Aguascalientes stands under the national framework of Mexico. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009. The state's own record on trans-specific legal protection is thinner.

Legal gender recognition remains unfinished at national level and is administered state by state. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many Mexican states now operate administrative recognition procedures, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Its state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records specifically that Aguascalientes has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people, leaving the state without an administrative mechanism of its own. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The consequences of non-reform are documented in detail elsewhere. Human Rights Watch's 6 March 2024 report found that delays and refusals of name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

A court route now exists in Aguascalientes despite the absence of legislative reform. In Amparo en Revisión 430/2025, decided in April 2026 on a project by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, Mexico's Supreme Court ruled that the requirements in the state's Civil Code for changing the gender marker on birth certificates - judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations - are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the state's Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate reach is limited to the persons represented by the civil association that filed the amparo, so the administrative route exists on paper without yet applying to the wider public.

Conversion therapy persists in the state despite being prohibited by law. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem describe operations that continue under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes, and that a person who escaped one such space arrived at the group in the previous year. The same report states that trans women continue to suffer aggression motivated by prejudice. An ENDISEG survey shows that 7.3 percent of the state's population aged 15 and over self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexican states.

Transfemicide remains outside the state's criminal code. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City's Congress had approved the Paola Buenrostro law, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. Aguascalientes belongs to the states that have not adopted comparable reforms. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a national total second only to Brazil's 100. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, prompting LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, to investigate all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Formal rights and lived safety diverge. Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP, dated 22 November 2024, concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist on paper but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this is not evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Human Rights Watch report (March 2024) documents the human-rights cost of the absence of legal gender recognition in Tabasco, a reference case for how non-reforming states, Aguascalientes among them, leave trans people without any lawful marker procedure.

The Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024) covers Mexico City making transfemicide a criminal offence. Aguascalientes belongs to the non-reforming majority of states that have not adopted comparable reforms.

31927357B17004778023462.tangentialFactors:
Aguascalientes belongs to the majority of Mexican states that have not legislated for legal gender recognition, alongside Tabasco, where Human Rights Watch documented recognition failures in March 2024, while states that have reformed their legislation run administrative procedures with uneven implementation.

On the opposite side of the national record, Mexico City has moved furthest on trans-specific criminal law with its July 2024 transfemicide statute, while most states, including Aguascalientes, carry no equivalent offence, so a killing of a trans woman here is prosecuted under general homicide provisions rather than a dedicated transfemicide law.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction, which removes one category of uncertainty that trans and LGB visitors otherwise face.

The enforcement gap identified by Beer's LSE USAPP analysis applies to the state: a Supreme Court ruling and an administrative procedure can exist without being applied consistently to those who are not already part of litigation, so formal entitlement should not be read as guaranteed access.

National monitoring by Transgender Europe and reporting by AP and Agencia Presentes show sustained and rising lethal violence against trans people across Mexico, against which the state's lack of a dedicated transfemicide law and its undocumented conversion-therapy activity sit as local manifestations of a national pattern.
