31927357B35339934753022.name: Baja California
31927357B35339934753022.summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that divide.

The counterweight is lethal violence against women and the state's classification of it. The Baja California Attorney General's Office publicly identified Brayan Rivera as a serial perpetrator of feminicides; he was arrested in Downey, California in June 2023 and presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson for provisional extradition detention, with probable cause determined on 29 June 2023. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the attorney general linked him to at least three killings in Tijuana: Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed 24 January 2022 in room 404 of the Hotel Cascadas in the city's tolerance zone, Elizabeth on 14 February, and Karen, 28, on 30 August 2021 at the Motel Hacienda Soler; extradition was then estimated at between 15 days and two years.

Under-counting is the pattern rather than the exception. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in the state while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. Female economic participation in Baja California stands at roughly 46 to 47 per cent, ranking 14th of 32 states.

Mixed assessment: formal recognition law that now reaches adults, minors and non-binary people, alongside a border-city pattern of lethal violence against women that official statistics under-record.

31927357B75771156097737.name: Colima
31927357B75771156097737.summary: Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Colima, and no law targets trans presence. Legal gender recognition across the country remains an unresolved state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed state legislatures to complete, and the country overall is one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people, with high impunity - the operative backdrop a visitor stands under here.

sources.summary: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists: identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. The operative framework for Colima is this national picture, not any locally enacted certainty.

HRW and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 Mar 2024 from Tabasco, a Mexican state with no legal gender-recognition procedure: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. The account shows what an absent state procedure means for trans people on the ground in Colima.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years, the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it after Nayarit (up to 60 years). In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, with transfemicide impunity thought higher still. These figures set the national lethality level and the transfemicide-crime trend under which Colima sits.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
For a visitor, the state's position is no-recognition: as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists, so identity documents issued in Tamaulipas cannot be changed through any administrative route, and mismatched documents invite exactly the police checks and institutional mistreatment that a companion 2024 report documents in one such state - the daily-interaction risk that most endangers a visible trans visitor.

On protections, the congress of the state unanimously approved, on 18 June 2025, reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter covering crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression and explicitly banning 'conversion therapies', with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 times a local measurement unit; the penalties increase by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in family, medical or workplace settings. For practical safety, the documented armed-group targeting and extortion of trans women along the border is the trans-specific danger driver, against blanket border violence that affects every traveller regardless of gender expression.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Same-sex marriage in Yucatán was established first by the courts and then by statute. On 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners were able to marry, and on 8 August 2013 the first same-sex couple legally married in the state. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022. Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and other states. Federally, same-sex acts have been decriminalised since 1871, sexual diversity is documented as tolerated among Yucatán Maya groups, and the Chamber of Deputies passed a conversion-therapy ban in March 2023 by 267-104 after a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

For a trans visitor to Newfoundland and Labrador the local legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law, enforcement pattern or official statement was found; criminal law and the national human-rights framework apply uniformly, and the jurisdiction has no facility or expression rule differing from the national position. The documented risk signals are weak — police-reported hate crime is the lowest in the country (5.3 per 100,000 in 2024) — and risk is assessed at parity with the national picture.

Documents: the province's sex-designation change requires birth in the province or three months' residence, operates without any surgery requirement and without an application fee, and the province states it cannot guarantee that an 'X' gender marker on its documents will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the caveat that matters for a visitor carrying provincial records while travelling; the 2016 amendment also removed the surgery requirement for changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023, after a +34% jump in 2023); national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000 (with Manitoba), while Ontario recorded the highest (16.0); the province's +51% rise reflects only 19 incidents in 2023 to 29 in 2024 — very small absolute numbers, so the rate change is statistically fragile. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report examines national police-reported hate-crime data, including offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. Egale Canada is an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

sources.title: Changes to Vital Statistics Act Would Allow for Change of Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.summary: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 17 June 2021: proposed changes to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 would allow residents of the province who were not born there — but have lived there at least three months — to change their sex designation; the change certificate carries a $25 fee, counts as official provincial identification and 'could be leveraged by the applicant to update records in other jurisdictions,' serving as the identification document for people born outside the country. The release states the amendments align with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading that day and Royal Assent on 23 June 2021. Gives the province a resident-based legal gender-change route (three-month residency) relevant to document enrolment for trans people in Newfoundland and Labrador.

sources.title: Legislative Amendment Respects Rights of Transgender Individuals (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.summary: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 12 April 2016: an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 removes the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission (the December 2015 ruling on complaints from two trans women) and with LGBTQ advocates' requests. The province's gender-marker change on provincial records has therefore operated without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment (Royal Assent 13 April 2016).

sources.title: Changing Your Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador)
sources.summary: Current official Government of Newfoundland and Labrador page: applicants for a change of sex designation must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s (with consent of the other parent/guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15), and must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months; there is no fee for the change application, with charges applying only to official copies of updated documents (new birth certificate $35, or $30 online). The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate with an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the documented cross-border document caveat relevant to carrying provincial records elsewhere.

82249235B3191732862561.name: Prince Edward Island
82249235B3191732862561.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

For a trans visitor to Prince Edward Island the legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law, incident pattern, official statement or rate deviation was found; federal criminal law and human-rights protection apply uniformly, and the jurisdiction has no facility, expression or registration rule differing from the national position. Risk assessed at parity with the national picture; no systematic count of trans deaths exists to measure outcomes here specifically.

Documents: gender-marker change on provincial documents works through self-declared gender with a physician's letter and no surgery requirement (since the April 2016 amendment), and since December 2018 provincial photo ID — including driver's licences — can carry an 'X' or blank gender marker, the first such blank option offered anywhere in the country; adults need birth in the jurisdiction plus three months' residence, with physician attestation and signature formalities.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada, 30 March 2026 (police-reported hate crime, 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally, up 1% on 2023; national rate 12.1 per 100,000 population, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates. The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply in Prince Edward Island as across Canada.
Source: Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of national police hate-crime data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations.

sources.title: P.E.I. transgender community applauds ID changes (CBC News)
sources.summary: CBC News, 18 April 2016, reports that the MacLauchlan government tabled a bill to amend the Vital Statistics Act so Islanders can change their gender on official documents by declaring the gender they identify with plus a letter from a doctor, with sex-reassignment surgery no longer required; Pride P.E.I. board member Jesse Macmillan welcomed the move, noting surgery is expensive and the closest provider was in Montreal, and called for a future third gender category, adding that many of his friends in Charlottetown identify outside the binary; a linked item on the article page reports Health PEI would cover the costs of three surgeries for transgender patients. PEI's gender-marker change on provincial documents has worked without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment.

sources.title: Improving diversity and inclusion on driver's licences (Government of Prince Edward Island news release)
sources.summary: Government of Prince Edward Island news release, 30 November 2018: Islanders may now select 'gender not listed' (shown on the licence as X) or 'prefer not to say' (blank) alongside male and female when identifying gender on a driver's licence; the release states PEI is the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say'/blank option, quoting Transportation, Infrastructure and Energy Minister Paula Biggar and PEERS Alliance. The change took effect 4 December 2018 at Access PEI locations, meaning provincial photo ID can carry an X or blank gender marker.

sources.title: Change of Gender Designation (Government of Prince Edward Island)
sources.summary: Official Government of Prince Edward Island information page, as captured 1 July 2022: an adult may apply for a change of gender designation if born in PEI and resident in the province for at least three months and not in the lawful custody of another person; a legal custodian may apply for a minor under 18 who was born on PEI and has lived in the province at least three months, with written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if aged 12 or older. The application requires completed forms including a physician statement, a written statement by the applicant, and signature arranged before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics. The province operates a gender-marker regime without a surgery requirement and with physician attestation.

82249235B69645938038492.name: Nova Scotia
82249235B69645938038492.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

For a trans visitor to Nova Scotia the legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law or hostile official pattern was found; federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly. The capital hosts a large, organised 2SLGBTQ+ community with institutional support, while the documented national hostility pattern elsewhere concentrates in other provinces' school-board and library politics — not this jurisdiction. Outside the capital, expect the rural small-town profile national surveys find worse for trans and non-binary people. Risk broadly at parity with the national picture.

The one enforcement signal on record is a custodial case: a trans woman from the capital region is challenging the decision to hold her in a men's correctional facility while she serves a two-year sentence; a federal judge gave her more time to file for judicial review, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers that restricted her access to her lawyer (18 March 2025) — the documented case shows how a trans woman's correctional placement is being challenged and judicially reviewed in the jurisdiction's custodial system.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023), national rate 12.1 per 100,000 (−2% in 2024, +142% since 2018); eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates. No Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count appears in this release, so it supports the record's parity finding rather than a provincial deviation. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly.

The underlying source is Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of national police-reported hate-crime data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations. sources.title: N.S. transgender prisoner looking to challenge decision to hold her in men's prison - Saltwire / The Chronicle Herald
sources.summary: The Chronicle Herald reports (18 March 2025) that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence; the judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. This is the documented Nova Scotia case showing how a trans woman's correctional placement is being challenged and judicially reviewed in the province's custodial system.

sources.title: Grants to Support 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Groups, Provincial Conference - Government of Nova Scotia
sources.summary: The Government of Nova Scotia announced (10 June 2026) more than $176,000 through the first round of its new 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, with awards including $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth and $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, plus $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference; per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year. This is official, dated evidence of provincial funding and institutional support for 2SLGBTQIA+ communities across Nova Scotia.

sources.title: Province Releases First 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan - Government of Nova Scotia
sources.summary: The Government of Nova Scotia released (8 January 2026) the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022 - described as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people - and informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations; the plan maps actions to improve programs and policies and support full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people. This is official confirmation that Nova Scotia operates an explicit provincial inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation.

82249235B52639524229375.name: Quebec
82249235B52639524229375.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

For a trans visitor to Quebec the recorded risk profile rests on the national data series: the March 2026 release on police-reported hate crime (2024 data) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally for a fourth consecutive year — +8% to 139, nearly triple 2020 — and identifies no trans-specific provincial pattern for the jurisdiction.

Enforcement signals cut both ways: a June 2025 provincial directive places transgender inmates according to anatomical sex rather than gender identity, reversing prior practice and challenged by advocates as violating the provincial charter of rights; against that, a June 2024 human-rights tribunal ruling ordered damages against a bar that discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on gender-identity grounds — enforcement can favour trans complainants. No jurisdiction-specific anti-trans legislation, ordinance or incident series appears in the surviving sources; the national criminal law and human-rights framework apply, and the jurisdiction's largest city anchors one of the country's most established organised 2SLGBTQ+ communities.

No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in the release windows, so it supports the record's national-parity assessment. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly in Quebec.

sources.title: Quebec's new trans inmate policy goes against human rights, advocates say - CBC News
sources.summary: CBC News reports (19 June 2025) that Quebec's public security minister announced transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison; advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is dated, province-specific evidence of an official Quebec policy change reversing the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

sources.title: Gender Identity Protected by the Quebec Charter of Rights - Éducaloi
sources.summary: Éducaloi reports that on 10 June 2024 Quebec's Human Rights Tribunal found a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training; the page notes gender identity and expression were added as prohibited grounds of discrimination under Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms in 2016, and cites 2021 census data that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older (0.27% of those aged 15-34) identify as transgender. This is Quebec-specific enforcement evidence that trans people can win discrimination claims under provincial law.

sources.title: Center for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec - IMK
sources.summary: IMK's case note on Centre for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec records that after a two-month trial with 29 witnesses the Quebec Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people, that the Court of Appeal largely upheld the decision (2024 QCCA 348), and that the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. It is a dated, lawyer-verified account of the landmark Quebec court outcome that reshaped the province's rules on sex designation and identity documents.

82249235B66370767641120.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

For a trans visitor to Ontario the legal floor is neutral: no jurisdiction-specific anti-trans statute, policy or official hostility is on record; while two other provincial units have legislated restrictions on trans names, pronouns or care, Ontario's government has not. Criminal law and human-rights protection operate nationally and uniformly across the country, and the provincial human-rights code explicitly protects gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts and association membership — the formal protections a visiting trans person holds.

Risk signals are national, not local: the national police-reported hate-crime series (Statistics Canada, March 2026) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally — +8% to 139 in 2024, a fourth consecutive increase — without identifying a trans-specific pattern for the jurisdiction.

Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, above the national figure — the only province-specific number in this release pointing above the national average. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting is influenced by awareness and community trust.

The underlying source is Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of national police hate-crime data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations.

sources.title: 'Parents must be fully involved' in student's decision to change pronouns, Ontario education minister says - CTV News
sources.summary: CTV News reported on 28 August 2023 that Ontario education minister Stephen Lecce said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He spoke the same week Saskatchewan joined New Brunswick in legislating parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names and pronouns, and said teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child. Ontario did not adopt such legislation at that time.

sources.title: Policy on preventing discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression - Ontario Human Rights Commission
sources.summary: The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations; it defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

sources.title: Manitoba government eyes human rights protection for gender expression - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.summary: Global News Winnipeg (18 March 2025) reports that the Manitoba NDP government plans to expand the province's Human Rights Code to cover gender expression. The code already prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe says the change would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The amendment sits in a government bill before the legislature, to be debated later in 2025, and is welcomed by Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba.

sources.title: Bill to mark transgender and two-spirit day passed by Manitoba legislature - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.summary: Global News Winnipeg (30 May 2024) reports the Manitoba legislature passed a bill recognizing March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported. The Legislative Assembly's passage gives Manitoba a dated, legislatively enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level.

sources.title: Manitoba reaffirms support for trans community on Day of Remembrance - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.summary: Global News Winnipeg (20 Nov 2023) reports that Manitoba again raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance the province first marked eight years earlier. This time the flag was raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. In a statement, families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said the government 'supports and upholds the life-saving work' of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorializes people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing.

sources.title: Yukon MLAs pay tribute to transgender people Monday in the territorial legislature - Yukon News
sources.summary: Yukon News (31 March 2026) reports the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March, with MLAs rising to speak: Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praised 'the courage and resilience as well as the contributions and accomplishments of transgender, two-spirited, and gender-diverse Yukoners', acknowledged that 'too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment, and hate for far too long', and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of suicide attempt. The tribute is the territory's own cross-party, in-legislature acknowledgement of trans residents on record for Yukon.

sources.title: Yukon Government hears feedback on 2SLGBTQ plan - Yukon News
sources.summary: Yukon News (29 April 2025) reports the Yukon government published community feedback on its LGBTQ2S+ Action Plan, the first of two check-ins the government committed to when the plan was released in 2021. Of 302 survey respondents, 267 were eligible (165 self-identified 2SLGBTQ community members, 102 allies); 65 per cent agreed banning conversion therapy was beneficial - over 70 per cent of 2SLGBTQ respondents and 55.9 per cent of allies - while 11.7 per cent of allies and 9.7 per cent of 2SLGBTQ respondents judged the ban not beneficial. The article confirms conversion therapy was banned in Yukon in 2020, a year before it became illegal nationwide - a dated, quantitative record of a territorial official plan and an existing territorial law.

sources.title: Pride flag allegedly damaged, stolen from school prompts Yukon minister to double down - Yukon News
sources.summary: Yukon News (13 June 2024) reports a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend in June 2024, and that a replacement flag was promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123), saying Pride month celebrates 'the diversity that makes the Yukon vibrant and strong'. This is the concrete Yukon incident on record - vandalism of a Pride symbol at a Whitehorse school - paired with an explicit territorial-government response.

14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary:
Visitors across the whole country stand under the national framework: passport/documents, entry rules, national marriage and criminal law are uniform; the single-sex-services rollback applies under the national equality framework (with devolved divergences in the regions below).

England is where the national law applies without a devolved layer: no regional administration exists, and the national equality institutions and courts sit principally here. The decisive recent ruling for trans visitors is the decision of 16 April 2025 by the country's highest court (the national Supreme Court), which settled that 'sex' and 'woman' in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological or registered sex, and that an acquired gender certificate does not change legal sex for equality-law purposes. That definition is the ground on which services, searches and detention allocation operate for anyone detained here.

Operative enforcement guidance: after the ruling the national equality body updated its code of practice (May 2025) advising that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is 'genuine concern' about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport 'when necessary' for safety — the guidance a visitor meets at venues, transport and services day to day.

Practical-safety baseline: police-recorded hate crime in England and Wales (year ending March 2025) stood at 115,990 incidents, with the transgender strand down 11% year on year; recorded figures understate prevalence, and a February 2024 recording-system change means earlier years over-counted.

sources.summary: BBC News (19 June 2026): Lady Ross of the Court of Session ruled unlawful Scottish Prison Service guidance that allowed some trans prisoners to be housed according to gender identity, holding that sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, in line with the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment.

BBC News (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Australia - Wikipedia (South Australia-specific provisions)
sources.summary: South Australia was the first Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexual activity, the law commencing 2 October 1975, and it is the only jurisdiction whose scheme for historical gay convictions is 'spent' rather than expunged, under the Spent Convictions (Decriminalised Offences) Amendment Act 2013 in force 22 December 2013. Registered domestic relationships date from 1 August 2017 and same-sex marriage from December 2017 under the federal Act. The state was the last to abolish the gay-panic defence, in December 2020, effective 1 April 2021. The conversion-therapy ban passed in September 2024 and took effect as law in April 2025. With the ACT, South Australia was one of the first two jurisdictions to allow the sex recorded on a birth certificate to be changed without sex-reassignment surgery, under its 2016 Act. This is the state's own legal framework for documents, relationships and criminal-record history.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Australia - Wikipedia (dedicated article)
sources.summary: Since 23 May 2017, under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016 (royal assent 15 December 2016), a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery and no forced divorce if married. Non-binary and 'indeterminate' sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates. Hate-crime sentencing laws explicitly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021. The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and took effect 1 April 2021. The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 passed in October 2024 and is in legal effect from 1 April 2025. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation. Same-sex couples could adopt from 17 February 2017, and same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017, the 2017 postal survey returning 62.5% 'Yes' in South Australia.

sources.summary: The equality timeline for Tasmania is dated precisely. After the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania still refused to repeal its anti-gay Criminal Code provisions and, faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania, decriminalised male homosexuality with effect from 14 May 1997, the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. Equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018. As of 2019 Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. sources.title: Tasmania makes gender optional on birth certificates after Liberal crosses floor – ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 11 April 2019 that Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill the previous day, 10 April 2019, after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition; the legislation had already passed the Legislative Council. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal. This is enactment-level evidence of the equal-status finding for trans visitors in Tasmania, secured against government resistance rather than against any criminalisation or incident series.

14911670B45290909693812.name: Roraima
14911670B45290909693812.summary:
The national framework applies in Roraima with no documented state-level deviation for a visitor: protections are judicial rather than statutory - name and gender-marker change without surgery or court order under the national court's 2018 ruling, discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under the 2019 ruling, and marriage and adoption long settled by the national courts - with non-binary birth-certificate recognition handled case-by-case, varying state by state.

The country as a whole records the world's highest absolute toll of killings of trans people, concentrated away from the capitals, and observers stress that protections are uneven in practice, thinning in the interior; for a visitor the picture is the national one with an interior discount - rights on paper, thin services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility mechanism on record either way.

14911670B26412867168762.name: Amapa
14911670B26412867168762.summary:
Amapá stands under Brazil's national framework, and no state-level deviation affecting a visitor is documented in the sources. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14-1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015. Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018, and gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, docketed as ADO 26 and MI 4733, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. That ruling is the operative basis on which homophobia and transphobia are treated as criminal conduct anywhere in the country, including Amapá.

Documents remain the area where a visitor may see divergence. There is no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender as precedent. Non-binary birth-certificate practice varies from state to state, so the entry a person obtains in Amapá is not guaranteed to match what another state's registry will accept. Trans voters may also register under their lived name and identity before their documents are updated.

Enforcement does not track the statutory text evenly. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 records that enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. Major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. For Amapá this translates into the national position carried with a remote-interior discount on services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility on record. The national survey's per-state table carries a 2022-dated entry recording progress in Amapá on recognition documents.

14911670B46798344041190.name: Amazonas
14911670B46798344041190.summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis following the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 puts the term at one to five years and confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

No Amazonas-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement pattern is documented for a visitor. Registry practice in the state records non-binary or unspecified birth-certificate entries, and name changes are granted on documents there.

There is no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry non-binary or unspecified entries have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Enforcement is uneven: major cities are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

Detention carries a specific regime that applies to a visitor held in Amazonas. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, and documents housing in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units; it treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. National norms from 2014 and 2020 permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

14911670B96632893955983.name: Acre
14911670B96632893955983.summary:
Acre stands under Brazil's national framework, which applies in full in the state: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Justice Council resolution of 14 May 2013, joint adoption since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation.

Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018. There is no third-gender option on national identity documents, but civil registries have accepted "non-binary/unspecified" entries since 2020 and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. A trans visitor's documents and status are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity to be a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines; a Brazilian law firm's expatriate guide specifies terms of one to five years under ADO 26 and MI 4733. Acre carries protection at state level as well: a 2017 state anti-discrimination statute, with further state court rulings in 2025.

The statutory text does not describe what people meet. Brazil records one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and the highest absolute number of killings of trans people globally, weighted away from the capitals. A legal assessment updated in April 2026 finds major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Brasília broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. That distinction applies within Acre, between Rio Branco and the state's interior.

Arrest carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires a judge to consult a person about their preferred placement, with male, female and LGBTI-specific units set out, and LGBTI status established by self-declaration at the custody hearing.

Detention placement is governed by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. LGBTI status is established by self-declaration before a judge, including at the custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a change of placement can be requested later, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permitting people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

1811400B81659894240990.name: Puducherry
1811400B81659894240990.summary:
Puducherry is a union territory with a partial legislature: recognition and welfare policy for trans people is set principally by the federal government, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

The framework that governs it shifted sharply in March 2026: parliament passed an amendment removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinnar) and intersex people, and mandating medical certification for identity documents and for surgery; the medical-certification mandate is a direct documents consequence for a trans traveler whose papers now rest on that certification, and the change bears uniformly on every state and union territory, so it reaches visitors identically.

Practical safety: a nationally recurring policing practice treats trans appearance as a suspicion category in transit spaces, evidenced by an August 2024 railway-platform groping complaint — a formal complaint was filed and intrusive questioning reported — reaching visitors through federal transport policing rather than any local law.

sources.summary: The 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill amends the 2019 law: it removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted categories and intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition - HRW calls it a major reversal of the 2014 rights and urges the president not to sign it (articles dated 26 Mar 2026).

Amendment bill approved by both houses (article 2026, awaiting presidential assent): removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court 'third gender' ruling; narrows the 2019 definition of transgender person; government says the narrower definition improves welfare delivery, critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people; mandatory medical certification described as an attack on privacy and dignity.

1811400B84418948762846.name: Andhra Pradesh
1811400B84418948762846.summary:
Andhra Pradesh stands under India's national framework, and no Andhra Pradesh-specific recognition regime or deviation from that framework is sourced. The operative baseline is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026, which India's Parliament passed in both houses and which awaited presidential assent as of 26 March 2026. The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals, excludes self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. Human Rights Watch calls the change a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk; as national law it sets the recognition baseline a visitor faces in this state.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel, and it is where a visitor's exposure concentrates. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

The Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a Union Territory of India and stands under India's national framework for transgender recognition and protection. No territory-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, so a visitor to the islands is assessed against the national position, which changed materially in March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. The bill amends the 2019 law and removes the self-identification route to legal recognition that had been affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014. Protests were held in Mumbai on the day of passage.

Recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, with recognition in practice narrowed to male and female categories plus those traditional identities. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme entirely. Critics warn that the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist.

Medical certification becomes a condition of identity recognition. Gender-affirming surgery requires certification by a medical board and a district authority. For a trans traveller whose papers rest on that certification, this is a direct documents consequence: identity papers issued under the old route may not be reissued or amended on the same basis.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed and predates the amendment. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.

1811400B21325138943523.tangentialFactors:
The territory was scored at the national position because the country dossier identified no deviation material enough to score separately, within a tolerance of ±0.02, and no division-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file.

The March 2026 bill was passed against a visible protest backdrop, with demonstrations reported in Mumbai, and its passage was still unresolved as to presidential assent when the sources were compiled. Contested framing surrounds it: the government casts the amendment as broadening welfare access and protection from trafficking, while the People's Union for Civil Liberties, rights campaigners and critics characterise it as a rollback that excludes most self-identifying trans and non-binary people.

The scale of the affected population is national rather than local: about two million transgender people live in India, so the narrowed recognition scheme bears on a very large community and on the identity documents a visitor may be asked to present.

Comparatively, the 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, a protection lost while the recognition scheme was also being narrowed. Independent country reporting runs partly contrary to activist accounts: the UK Home Office note of December 2025 describes police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, whereas documented checkpoint incidents in 2024 and 2026 show targeted handling of trans individuals by transport and aviation security.

1811400B21325138943523.localsOnly:
For residents of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, identity recognition runs through the national scheme as amended in March 2026: application is confined to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and to intersex people, and requires medical certification, with gender-affirming surgery conditional on medical-board and district-authority certification. Residents who self-identify as trans men, trans women, non-binary or gender-fluid outside those categories have no recognition route under the amended scheme.

Residents continue to access welfare schemes through the same national channels the government says the amendment widens, and residents retain standing to challenge the amendment or its implementing rules in court. The People's Union for Civil Liberties and other organisations have publicly opposed the bill, and litigation or advocacy by them is part of the resident-facing environment.

Residents are also covered by the protection machinery that exists independently of the amendment: the Madras High Court guidelines of 7 June 2021 on police sensitisation and the ban on conversion therapy, and the constitutional protections arising from the 2018 decriminalisation judgment and the non-discrimination grounds that include sex as interpreted to cover gender identity.

Resident-facing criminal protection is weaker than it was before 2024, since the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita dropped the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences. Communities report fear of more assaults under the new code, and there is no territory-specific enforcement record documenting how that plays out locally. The national population context, an estimated two million transgender people, frames the domestic scale of these rules.

10402087B60055985875400.name: Baden-Württemberg
10402087B60055985875400.summary:
Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, identity documents and marriage law are uniform across the Länder, and no Land can remove that federal floor.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison.

Baden-Württemberg's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, and the Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 does not name the Land among those with updated provisions. A majority of the German Länder now operate revised rules: a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law has been in force since 1 March 2026, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg provisions have also recently entered into force. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the registered gender entry, while other Länder do so implicitly.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

Screening is a documented flashpoint. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity. She characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

sources.summary: July 2026 report on a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

Framework item for German Länder, incl. Baden-Württemberg: Verfassungsblog analysis (18 Mar 2026) of prison placement for trans prisoners. Placement rules in most Länder were unchanged since the 1970s and are being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, with Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules also recently entering into force — giving a majority of Länder revised rules. The piece argues there is no constitutional duty to anchor placement to the registered gender entry (a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination), and notes only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry while others do so implicitly. Baden-Württemberg is not named: its own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules.

10402087B44391416804171.name: Bremen
10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own on file. The city-state operates the national framework: the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, remains operative as of September 2026, and registry changes run through Bremen's own offices, so a trans visitor's documents rest on the national self-declaration regime; federal criminal law and the general equality act apply unchanged, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 October 2017 for partner travel.

No local hostile-offence series or event-security finding is on file, so practical risk tracks the national position; the only documented divergence is detention-time prison-placement machinery, which a visitor would meet only while arrested rather than on the street.

sources.summary: A 16 July 2026 France24/wire report covers the neo-Nazi prisoner in the 'Liebich' case, placed in a men's prison despite a legal gender change. The case drove Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The issue is framework-level for every Land, since prison administration and registry offices are Land competences.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

The article records that years of self-identification apply to adults without requiring the previous medical/court pathway, and that same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 October 2017. sources.title: Studie zu Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ* „Queer durch NRW“ (Ministerium für Kinder, Jugend, Familie, Gleichstellung, Flucht und Integration NRW / chancen.nrw)
sources.summary: The North Rhine-Westphalia state ministry records that on 25 April 2025 the Land government published the study „Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*“, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans*, inter*, queer and non-binary people (LSBTIQ*) in the Land. One Land-specific enforcement difference is documented and visitor-relevant: the Land constitution, amended in 2011, explicitly includes sexual orientation and gender identity in its anti-discrimination provisions, making transphobic hate speech prohibited in this Land unlike in most of the country — hate speech on those grounds is not banned nationwide, but it is prohibited in the states whose constitutions carry such clauses; the national equal-treatment law (in force since 18 August 2006) separately bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services, a clause a visitor also stands under when accessing services or facing hostile speech.

Cites Saarland's single-cell-with-en-suite-shower accommodation as a positive practice model for trans inmates; framework-relevant to Saarland, which has no separate placement statute.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. Gives the state-constitutional protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity that a trans visitor stands under within Saarland.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten
sources.summary: Zeit Online (10 April 2019) reports that, parallel to Federal Health Minister Jens Spahn's announced plan to ban so-called conversion therapies, Hesse, Berlin, Bremen, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein planned to present a joint Bundesrat motion (Entschließungsantrag) for a ban that same week. Saarland is one of the five tabling states in the run-up to the 12 April 2019 Bundesrat plenary presentation recorded on Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Germany page; the federal ban was subsequently approved by the Bundestag on 7 May 2020.

25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
This region is assessed at the national score: the dedicated country dossier identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02). A visitor stands under the national trans-equality law of 28 February 2023, which applies uniformly across the autonomous communities: adults rectify the registered sex marker by simple declaration with no medical diagnosis or treatment requirement and corresponding document adaptation, LGBTI non-discrimination protections extend to healthcare, employment and housing, and recognition from age 12 is available under conditions.

The regional base is permissive rather than restrictive: gender self-declaration has been possible since 2021, a gender-identity non-discrimination law has stood since 2014, and the region is listed among communities banning conversion therapies, so the national framework layers onto regional practice; parts of the region are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. For partner travel, the national law provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples; no region-specific marriage provision is recorded.

sources.summary: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), the 'Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons' (the 'Trans Law'), applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: Title II allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for corresponding document adaptation. The law further mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) reports the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. HRW places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Spain (Wikipedia): Canary Islands — same-sex registry 2003, gender-identity non-discrimination law 2014, gender self-declaration since 2021
sources.summary: The Canary Islands created their same-sex couple registry in 2003 and banned discrimination on gender-identity grounds through Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 (non-discrimination on gender-identity grounds and recognition of trans persons' rights, BOE-A-2014-11995). The community has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 communities to do so before the national Ley Trans of 28 February 2023. It is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. A trans traveler therefore stands under a regional anti-discrimination and self-identification regime alongside the 2023 national law.

sources.title: Historia LGBT en el País Vasco (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Spanish Wikipedia's article on LGBT history in the Basque Country records that the Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013 on the page, and for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system. Earlier institutional markers are the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex, and the page notes that Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation, reaffirming that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

sources.title: BOE-A-2016-6170 — Ley 8/2016, de 27 de mayo, de igualdad social de lesbianas, gais, bisexuales, transexuales, transgénero e intersexuales, y de políticas públicas contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género en la Comunidad Autónoma de la Región de Murcia (BOE)
sources.summary: The Region of Murcia's own LGTBI-equality statute sits beneath the national framework. Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170) prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics in public and private activity in the region, and within its scope bars any requirement to prove declared gender identity by psychological or medical report. Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation and consultation body in which LGTBI entities are represented. Title IV sets a sanctioning ladder: minor breaches draw a warning or a fine of up to €3,000; serious breaches run €3,001 to €20,000 and cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI persons or their families in the provision of services; very serious breaches run €20,001 to €45,000, with accessory penalties such as exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the infraction grade.

The operative regional instrument is Ley 8/2016 de la Región de Murcia.
