sources.summary: Official gazette text of Catalonia's own LGTBI-rights statute, Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014 (Generalitat de Catalunya; DOGC núm. 6730, 17 October 2014), the autonomous law after which the 2010s wave of Spanish regional LGTBI laws followed. It defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects gender identity. It extends protections across education, health, employment and sport (including broadening the Observatorio Catalán del Deporte to action against violence and discrimination in sport) and guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects. Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiencia de Catalunya (between seven days' and three months' worth); Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, with the Síndic de Greuges able to instigate proceedings.

25490228B61325010384209.name: Aragón
25490228B61325010384209.summary:
Aragón stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights applies uniformly across the country's autonomous communities, and no Aragón-specific deviation from that position has been identified. A visitor to Aragón is therefore governed by the national rules on recognition, discrimination and sentencing.

Under Article 43 of the law, any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. It replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment, and no prior surgical reassignment is required. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination: the gender marker recorded in the civil registry, not biological sex, is the operative basis for facility rules. A visitor whose documents have been rectified presents the marker obtained through that administrative route.

Discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned, discriminatory contract clauses are declared null and void, and LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing is addressed. Protections for unmarried same-sex couples are strengthened by the same statute.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so an attack motivated by gender expression has no free-standing offence and must be charged through the general offences, with the transphobia aggravation applied at sentencing.

Courts are applying that aggravation. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used it for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005.

25490228B88831207743232.name: Andalucía
25490228B88831207743232.summary:
Andalucía stands under the national framework of Spain: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities and governs the regional position. Any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious in the parliamentary passage of the law.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry, so a visitor's operative basis for facility rules is the entry obtained through self-declaration rather than any medical documentation.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence, although discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned under Ley 4/2023 itself.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Andalucía's own layer sits on top of that national floor and runs deeper than most Spanish regions. Ley 2/2014, an integral law for non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity, was among the first trans-specific regional laws in Europe. Ley 8/17 of 28 December, in force 4 February 2018, guarantees LGTBI rights and equal treatment for LGTBI people and their families. The regional government approved an equality strategy for 2024-2028 on 26 December 2024.

19177384B98145761763330.name: Catamarca
19177384B98145761763330.summary:
This division is assessed at the national score: the dedicated country dossier that covered it identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (within ±0.02), so a visitor stands under the national pattern. A 2025 national feature described the trans community facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation', with the national anti-discrimination agency closed, the national ministry responsible for gender and diversity portfolios eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed.

Practical safety for a traveler is set by the national profile: a 2026 report from a national hate-crime observatory counted at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — up 62% year on year, its highest count in ten years, one every 38 hours, with trans women and travestis 62.5% of victims — and tied the surge to institutional weakening and government legitimation of discriminatory discourse; this province sits under that pattern with no separate local record.

Violence, discrimination and poverty affecting the trans community are reported as worsened; this region carries no separate reporting, so the national picture stands as its baseline.

The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse; this province sits under that national pattern with no separate local record.

19177384B38635755405886.name: Chaco
19177384B38635755405886.summary:
No division-specific trans statute, quota-compliance finding or enforcement series survives in the record for Chaco, so visitor exposure in this province tracks the national position: no provincial criminalisation survives in the record, amid a documented national surge in anti-trans violence and a contested national law. An April 2025 national feature described the trans community facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation' after the decree roll-back of the gender-identity framework, and a national hate-crime observatory reported 227 SOGI-motivated hate crimes for 2025 — up 62% year on year, its highest decade count, one every 38 hours, with most attackers security-force personnel or unidentified — a baseline applying across the provinces including this one.

Practical-safety reading for a traveler: the national surge in anti-trans violence and the contested legal framework set the risk profile here, with the 2025 feature tying the worsening to institutional weakening and government legitimation of discriminatory discourse.

19177384B69455221212116.name: Chubut
19177384B69455221212116.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. Legal protections a visitor stands under are national: the 5 February 2025 national decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, trans people hired under the trans labor quota were dismissed, and the national anti-discrimination agency was abolished; the framework applies here as in every province.

Practical safety is set by the national picture: the national hate-crime observatory recorded 227 attacks based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — up 62% year on year, the highest count in its ten years of operation, roughly one every 38 hours — with perpetrators mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, beatings the main modality, institutional violence up from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32% of incidents in police stations or prisons. Activists report police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since the current national administration took office and is worst in the more conservative interior provinces; no division-specific incident series is documented, and the division has no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

19177384B51705615570562.name: Mendoza
19177384B51705615570562.summary:
No Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors. That silence is not reassuring: interior provinces without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real, and the country-wide security picture for trans and travesti people has sharply deteriorated.

What is documented is national. Per a March 2026 report by the LGBT news agency Agencia Presentes, drawing on the national hate-crime observatory's tally, at least 227 attacks motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were recorded in 2025 — up 62% year-on-year, the highest figure of the observatory's decade of operation, roughly one every 38 hours — with perpetrators predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, beatings the main modality, and the observatory attributing the surge to the national government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people. Attacks continued into early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of the president of an LGBTIQ+ organisation in a northern province. An April 2025 Blade feature described the transgender community as facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation' amid government policies; the underlying page is no longer retrievable.

17162690B9130125042960.name: Lower Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B9130125042960.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score, and the national framework is what a trans traveler stands under here. For a visitor the operative enforcement-relevant standards are detention-side: national law bars placing a person in a guarded centre wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence, and the framework was exercised in practice on 13 March 2024, when a court placed a transgender foreign woman (on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners, the border guard initially refused to move or release her despite the legal bar, and she was released only after a legal-aid association's application to the border-guard post commander.

On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that denying hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman in prison violated her right to private and family life and awarded damages, holding the refusal disproportionate with no reasonable legal grounds; the judgment binds the whole country and governs prison and detention healthcare in every voivodeship, including this one. No division-specific incident series, hostility mechanism or enforcement pattern is documented, so the visitor reads the national position without a local added risk factor.

sources.summary: Case report (Association for Legal Intervention, 13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreigners. The Border Guard refused to move or release her although Polish law bars placement where a stay would threaten life or health or where the person shows signs of having suffered violence. After the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander, she was released (page updated 28 Mar 2024). The case sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention and bears on any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship.

ECtHR ruling coverage (TGEU, 16 Jul 2024): on 11 Jul 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life (Article 8 ECHR) by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided but held that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland and governs trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including this one.

17162690B77437931625010.name: Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B77437931625010.summary: The anti-LGBT municipal-resolution wave (80+ municipalities and four voivodeship-level declarations as of March 2020) concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the country, so the absence of local findings here indicates thinner documentation rather than established safety. The national frame governs this division: no hate-crime protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (the March 2025 amendment bill referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, hearings held July and September 2025), court-based and medically gatekept legal gender recognition, and national sources documenting a trans foreign woman held in a male-only guarded detention centre and an ECtHR ruling that denying a prisoner hormone therapy violates private life.

sources.summary: Association for Legal Intervention (13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender woman (Vietnamese citizen, on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners; Border Guard refused to move/release her despite her identifying as a woman and warning that stopping medication would harm her. After an intervention by the legal-aid organisation citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, the Border Guard Commander released her because continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Useful to this record: in Poland, detained foreign trans women face placement in male-only facilities until formally challenged, and release can depend on legal intervention.

TGEU, 16 Jul 2024: on 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (right to private and family life) of the ECHR by denying a trans woman access to hormone replacement therapy while imprisoned, despite her having been prescribed hormones for almost two years; the Court awarded EUR 8,000 damages. Useful to this record: a trans visitor who is detained in Poland has a Europe-wide human-rights remedy against denial of HRT, though enforcement required litigation.

27671186B81745654473385.name: Cross River
27671186B81745654473385.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide with up to 14 years' imprisonment for all persons including tourists; additional Sharia criminal law applies in the northern states.

The national law applies here in full — the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (up to 14 years, extends to tourists, bans LGBTQ+ organisations and public expression of identity) plus the inherited criminal provisions; national monitoring recorded 89 extortions, 118 harassment incidents and more than 20 unlawful detentions of LGBTQ+ people by law-enforcement officials in 2024 alone, with detentions for "looking gay" and release on payment of a bribe reported. This division sits outside the twelve northern states that carry a separate religious-law death-penalty regime for same-sex conduct. Dating-app "kito" extortion gangs are a nationwide app-user risk, and foreign government travel advice warns LGBT travellers of arrest, violence and blackmail.

sources.summary: Report (August 2026) on the latest UK travel advice for this country: warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; up to 14 years for same-sex sexual activity; some northern states' religious law can prescribe the death penalty; the 2014 Act also punishes assisting, attending or promoting same-sex relationships and LGBTQ+ organisations; separately warns of short-notice curfews and vehicle-movement restrictions, mobile-network shutdowns with little notice, and political rallies and communal violence.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Cross River falls under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law carry up to a death-penalty maximum: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Cross River is not among them. The source documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023). No anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. Research was conducted in June and July 2010 in Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones. The report is national in scope and does not name Cross River. It substantiates the national baseline that police treat suspected same-sex conduct and perceived 'gayness' as an extortion opportunity, with release on payment of a bribe as the documented outcome.

The absence of state-specific records here reflects thin documentation rather than demonstrated safety.

sources.summary: Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). Twelve states apply Shari'a law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, where male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death. Police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito'), and mass arrests recur: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a Delta hotel raid in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023. No anti-discrimination protections exist. The 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations, and LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that applies in full to Oyo.

sources.title: The Nigerians lured into a trap and blackmailed for being gay (BBC News / BBC Africa Eye)
sources.summary: BBC Africa Eye, 15 May 2023, reported by Ian Wafula and Tamasin Ford: criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular dating apps, entrap men, film them, then extort, beat and kidnap them. The investigation interviewed 21 people about being 'kito'd'. Victims do not report to police for fear of being arrested or attacked. The piece shows enforcement against the gangs, including a commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of police catching a kito suspect. The underground scene described is Lagos-based, while the risk of dating-app 'kito' extortion applies to gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria.

27671186B25346211366833.name: Akwa Ibom
27671186B25346211366833.summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide under the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which passed the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and was signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The 2014 statute invalidates any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex and carries a maximum federal penalty of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Akwa Ibom stands under that secular national framework. The state lies outside the twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, so the death-penalty layer does not reach it and the ceiling for same-sex sexual activity in Akwa Ibom is 14 years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics (June 2025) records that the national criminal framework applies across all states, and documents countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. The same note confirms that the Shari'a penal codes of the twelve states remain in force, with penalties for same-sex conduct ranging from lashes or caning up to death by stoning.

Entry screening is a live risk. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, and notes that the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act reaches participants and guests at same-sex weddings, not only the couple.

Gender identity carries no legal recognition in Nigerian law, and the statute books contain no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. A visitor therefore has no protective instrument to invoke in Akwa Ibom, whether in a police encounter, an accommodation dispute or a medical setting.

No state-specific enforcement divergence from the national position is documented for Akwa Ibom in the sources on file.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia – Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national-framework overview, the position a visitor to Maluku stands under: private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised nationally, but the penal code as amended on 6 December 2022 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage effective 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within that outside-marriage restriction. Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with no third-gender or X marker; since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards (in nine provinces) as the document route. National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections and the Constitution is silent on sexual orientation and gender identity; on 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected 5-4 a petition to criminalise homosexuality, and the Sharia-based criminalisation outlier is Aceh, not Maluku. The page records that Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity and that a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.

65028918B10722647473585.name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
65028918B10722647473585.summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections exist for sexual orientation or gender identity anywhere in the national framework. Legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition.

Criminalisation operates at more than one level. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids: on 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands in either direction, and the province-specific source reviewed yielded no usable finding on trans safety. The national score therefore applies without adjustment.

Three further indicators of the surrounding climate are on record. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality "morally unacceptable".

65028918B10722647473585.localsOnly:
Residents of Bangka-Belitung Islands live under the same national code as visitors, with no provincial protection on sexual orientation or gender identity and no hate-crime provision to invoke after an assault. A complaint about a mob attack would proceed as an ordinary assault case.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery and a judicial approval, a route that requires both medical intervention and a court process. Until it is completed, identity documents continue to carry the sex assigned at birth, which affects banking, employment, travel documents and any interaction with officials that checks gender markers.

No form of same-sex relationship carries legal standing: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are all unrecognised nationally, so residents have no next-of-kin, inheritance, hospital-visitation or property claim through a same-sex partner. The extra-marital sex provision in force since 2 January 2026 exposes people in long-term same-sex relationships to the same exposure as anyone else, with prosecutions reported as selective rather than systematic.

Residents also face the national security framing introduced by the October 2025 presidential decree, which places LGBTQ+ people within defence policy as a category to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 links that framing to vigilante attacks on transgender women.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Indonesia sets out the national framework applied in North Kalimantan. Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery and judicial approval, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. Conversion therapy is widely practised and openly advertised.

15666254B97003483933575.name: Kuala Lumpur
15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Every state and the federal territory stand under the national framework: Sharia law prohibits a man posing as a woman across all states (up to three years' jail), so the criminalisation baseline applies to every visitor in every region.

National framework applies in full in the capital: same-sex "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" is criminalised under the 1936 penal code with up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, the "gross indecency" offence carries up to two years, and enforcement with arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment is documented since the 2018 election.

Local enforcement in the capital is documented on the ground: on 28 November the capital police, the city administration and the national religious department arrested over 200 people at an all-male health centre in the capital — a visible, high-volume enforcement signal a visitor could encounter. The national score of 0.16 is used, with the capital's concentrated scene and greater anonymity read as the model delta ().

It records a 28 November enforcement operation in Kuala Lumpur in which over 200 people were arrested at an all-male health centre by Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi), and notes enforcement with arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, with the Federal Court striking down some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia based on interviews with 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur; it states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground. It calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity.

28173009B80457268982215.name: Altai Krai
28173009B80457268982215.summary:
Altai Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources record no regional deviation: the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care, the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" statutes apply in full to a visitor in this region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the baseline a trans visitor here faces: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. A document presenting a gender marker that does not match the traveller's presentation therefore carries direct exposure at any check point where identity papers are examined.

Publicly "promoting" non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence punishable by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeat offences capable of becoming criminal and carrying up to four years' imprisonment. The 2023 extremist designation criminalises support of or activity within the designated movement, and at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory covering Altai Krai advises against all travel to Russia and states that foreigners found guilty of violating the "propaganda" law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, and that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Enforcement volume is documented by Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative. Since January 2024, 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag, and between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or of unknown outcome.

Charges have reached ordinary commercial activity as well. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an "extremist organisation" for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes; they face up to 12 years in prison. The enforcement regime described applies nationally and therefore equally in Altai Krai, and the sources report no Altai Krai-specific case.

28173009B80457268982215.tangentialFactors:
Risk in Russia is stratified by ground of identity. The UK Home Office note assesses that LGB people generally face no real risk of state persecution on sexual orientation alone, with the exception of the North Caucasus — a zone that does not include Altai Krai. The exposure identified for this region attaches principally to gender identity and to visible expression rather than to orientation alone, which places trans and gender-nonconforming visitors in a materially worse position than a cisgender LGB traveller.

The pattern of enforcement is symbolic and administrative rather than case-by-case: about 98 of the 101 recorded extremism-related convictions are administrative, and 81 people in 98 cases since January 2024 were convicted under article 20.3 for displaying symbols. The practical risk for a visitor therefore concentrates on visible markers, documents and public expression rather than on private conduct.

Comparison with the North Caucasus carve-out in the UK assessment is instructive for itinerary planning: the assessment of orientation-based risk differs by region of Russia, while the propaganda, document and extremist-designation regimes do not vary regionally in any of the sources reviewed.

28173009B80457268982215.localsOnly:
Residents of Altai Krai face the same prohibitions as visitors on paper, but with fewer options to leave. Gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited outright, so a resident cannot bring identity papers into conformity with lived gender; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023; and trans people cannot adopt or foster children.

No legislation in Russia prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment, so there is no statutory remedy for a resident refused service, housing or work on those grounds.

Administrative liability attaches to residents as well as foreigners: fines or detention of up to 15 days for a first "propaganda" offence, escalating to criminal liability of up to four years on repeat, and article 282.2 charges carrying up to 12 years for activity framed as running an extremist organisation. At least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

This division stands under the national position, which applies in full: the dedicated country dossier identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02), and the division is therefore assessed at the national score. For a trans traveller that position means: same-sex marriage is banned, gender transition is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Enforcement risk is active, not theoretical: same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised, but the 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years’ imprisonment on repeat offence; since the 2023 ‘extremist’ designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2-6 years and organising 6-10 years’ imprisonment. The policy assessment records at least 139 people (over a hundred) impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the authorities able but unwilling to protect.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges in connection with the designation, two of them sentenced to prison and seventeen pending or unknown. On 15 May 2025 three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Russia are not generally at real risk of persecution solely on the basis of sexual orientation, but that people in the North Caucasus, transgender people and those publicly active in LGBT+ advocacy are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. Adygea is not named as an exception to that assessment, so the note does not resolve whether the North Caucasus limb of the finding reaches this republic.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia covers general travel safety and includes the North Caucasus republics and interior-permission entry regimes among its stated concerns.

28173009B62882423633207.name: Arkhangelsk Oblast
28173009B62882423633207.summary:
Arkhangelsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, whose laws set the conditions in force across every region of the country. The sources assembled for this record contain no oblast-specific findings, so the assessment below describes the national climate a visitor to Arkhangelsk enters.

Same-sex activity is not criminalised. Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Public expression is itself an offence. 'Gay propaganda' charges carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, citing the risk of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024, at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, and the UK Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. 28173009B24080199016459.name: Amur Oblast
28173009B24080199016459.summary:
Amur Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the UK government's country policy and information note of June 2025 records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law signed by President Vladimir Putin banned gender reassignment surgery and the change of gender markers on official documents; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A trans visitor has no lawful route to have their documents recognised or amended in Russia, and must travel on documents as issued.

Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The expanded statute expressly reaches anything "justifying" gender transition, which places statements about transition and visible trans self-presentation within the scope of the offence.

The Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation opened criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences in 98 court cases since January 2024 for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. Charges are brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. It warns all travellers regardless of personal characteristic of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and notes that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

sources.summary: The UK Home Office country policy and information note on SOGI for Russia (June 2025) names Moscow and St Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open and where relocation may be a reasonable option. A 2023 Coming Out and Sphere Foundation survey found 57% of St Petersburg respondents out to most friends, 19% to most relatives and 24% to classmates or colleagues, against Moscow at 50%/15%/19%. The note records two St Petersburg policewomen fired for allegedly flirting on social media, and an August 2024 Citizens' Watch/Sphere Foundation study of enforcement of the 'propaganda' articles whose respondents included 13% living in St Petersburg. Nationally, same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, the LGBT+ movement was designated 'extremist' in November 2023, and at least 139 individuals were affected by enforcement in 2022-2024.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions connected to the 'International LGBT Movement' since its November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. A further 81 people in 98 cases have been found guilty since January 2024 of article 20.3 administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. St Petersburg appears in the article only in a photo caption for the 'X St.Petersburg Pride' rally of 3 August 2019.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. Ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. A July 2023 law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition. A 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fined Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits.

28173009B30008444211385.name: Altai Republic
28173009B30008444211385.summary:
The Altai Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, and no sub-national deviation from that framework has been identified in the sources; the territory is therefore assessed at the national score. For a visitor, Russia's laws apply in full within the republic: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, same-sex marriage is banned, and the expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition.

Penalties under that statute reach administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation in the designated movement carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising it 6 to 10 years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, do not travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, active war and arbitrary law enforcement. The advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated international LGBT movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Because any police, hotel or transport identity check can set a visitor's documents against their presentation, and because gender-marker changes remain prohibited, document screening is the principal everyday exposure point in the territory. Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity: cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Russia (June 2025) is the national framework this division is assessed under: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The note contains no division-specific information beyond that national framework.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison; HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences (article 20.3) for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 'gay propaganda' penalties imposed in 2023-24 versus 22 in 2021-22. This national enforcement baseline underlies this division's assessment at the national score; the article contains no division-specific detail.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. The national framework a visitor stands under is protective in form: the constitution bars sexual-orientation discrimination; after a 2005 judgment of the constitutional court, the elected national legislature legalised same-sex marriage in November 2006, so marriage-based partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse; and sex status can be changed in the population registry — and therefore on identity documents and passports — on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery (the 2003 alteration-of-sex-description law). The landmark ruling of 10 November 2025 in the trans-inmate case affirms gender-affirming healthcare as part of adequate medical care, although the case concerns a correctional facility in another division, so the national correctional policy is the correct frame for this division rather than any division-specific finding.

sources.summary: Court record (High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Medium B): the landmark ruling for a trans inmate against the Department of Correctional Services - refusal of gender expression (feminine attire, she/her pronouns), inadequate accommodation and denial of state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy held to be unfair discrimination; hormone therapy recognised as part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e).

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

sources.title: LGBT rights in South Africa - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The national dossier this Free State record is assessed under: the 1996 Constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination, the Constitutional Court's December 2005 judgment pushed Parliament to legalise same-sex marriage (Civil Union Act, National Assembly vote 229-41, November 2006), and the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act 2003 allows a person to change sex status in the population registry - and therefore on identity documents and passports - on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The page adds that gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like the Free State 'must travel long distances to major cities' to reach it, with private treatment costing hundreds of thousands of rands and long public waiting lists, and records the Justice Department's National Task Team (2011) and 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities aimed at hate crimes against LGBT people. This grounds the record's at-national-score assessment in the concrete national framework a Free State visitor stands under, since no Free State-specific trans source was surfaced.

Encyclopaedia overview of rights in the parent nation: the 1996 constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination; a December 2005 judgment of the constitutional court pushed the elected national legislature to legalise same-sex marriage, passed in November 2006; a 2003 law allows a person to change sex status in the population registry — and therefore on identity documents and passports — on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. Gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like this one must travel long distances to reach it, with private treatment costing hundreds of thousands of rands and long public waiting lists; this grounds this division's at-national-score assessment in the national framework a visitor stands under.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is custodial: prison placement follows the legal sex on identity documents (under the criminal-procedure code), so trans women whose legal gender is marked male — the vast majority — are placed in men's facilities. The national controller of places of deprivation of liberty reports that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers most in prison, and the national preventive mechanism documents persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights in adult prisons.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018) on transgender women in French prisons: under Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code men and women are held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, without sex-reassignment surgery) are placed in men's facilities; a detainee recalled inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' and threats of violence; Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, says transgender detainees — overwhelmingly women — are the group that suffers the most in prison, illustrated by American trans woman Kara B. held in 'worrying' conditions. National prison-placement framework; no division-specific detail for this region.

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (follow-up to its opinion of 30 June 2010): it records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres; the review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. National custodial-inspection framework; no division-specific finding for this region.

19338628B73800214047876.name: Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes
19338628B73800214047876.summary:
Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes stands under the French national framework. The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings, detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and no regional deviation from the national position was identified.

The legal baseline a trans visitor encounters is national. Same-sex marriage and full adoption have been legal since 2013, with France's first same-sex wedding performed on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect, and civil solidarity pacts available since 1999. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced the term sexual identity, itself protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

Legal gender recognition rests on a statute signed on 18 November 2016 and in force from 1 January 2017. It abolished the requirements of sex-reassignment surgery and forced sterilisation, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires an applicant to go before a court rather than undergo any medical intervention. Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees by the sex inscribed on their identity documents, and each establishment improvises around that provision, whether through special units or isolation restricting contact with other inmates. The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty has stated that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison. First-person accounts in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, the incarceration of an Argentinian trans woman, and heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements. The same feature covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. It was built on roughly forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The opinion finds persistent serious violations of fundamental rights, including placement by birth sex, isolation, exposure during strip searches and overcrowding risks, and it records no marked improvement since the authority's 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform. It recommends that the 2016 depathologising law be translated into prison regulations, and it explicitly extends its coverage to intersex and non-binary people.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

sources.summary: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. 68945753B85747362819570.name: Gangwon
68945753B85747362819570.summary:
No province-specific law, ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans people is documented for Gangwon; the framework a visitor meets here is the national one: being trans is not criminalised, and the courts are steadily tightening what legal gender recognition may demand. A May 2024 ruling ended any surgical requirement for changing registered sex, and in July 2024 a court held that police telling a trans person to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed their rights, awarding damages after both instances found for the claimant, with an appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

For a visitor the operational reality is documented social friction around public restrooms, reported nationally rather than locally: Gangwon's audited record offers legality, functioning courts, no documented local hostility machinery, and no local facility-restriction law; restroom friction is a national-pattern finding, not a Gangwon one.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom forms part of the national standard applied in Gangwon, where no specific incident is documented.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria. The court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the standard applied in Gangwon, where no province-specific case is documented.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
The Public Ministry's 2012–2021 study places La Libertad second in absolute LGTB-homicide count (10 of 88 — after Lima's 12, level with Lima Norte), centred on Trujillo. The region's population share (~3%) is far smaller than its death share (~11.4%), giving a per-capita lethality roughly 3.8× the national average — a materially concerning concentration not explained by population alone, and placing the unit below the national score (0.36).

Counterweight: Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (regional session 3 September 2024, approved 6 September 2024, published in El Peruano November 2024) promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people — their right to formal, dignified work in equitable conditions without discrimination on gender identity or expression, and recognition of the trans community as a vulnerable group. This is a resident-facing instrument (a visitor does not use it), but it evidences that this particular regional council legislated visibly for trans inclusion — the one such ordinance found in Peru's 26 departments. It also sits in the same department where rondas campesinas exercise recognised dispute-resolution authority, a structural caveat with no documented trans-specific case.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The per-capita violence concentration is the dominant factor; the ordinance prevents a larger deduction. vs Lima (now 0.38, above national): La Libertad's per-capita lethality remains worse, though Lima's higher absolute count and 2025 reporting case have lifted its score since the original comparison. vs Tacna (0.34): both are modestly below national, but La Libertad's multi-year dataset is more robust evidence than a single incident.

sources.summary: Public Prosecutor's Office (Ministerio Público) news note of 23 March 2022 on its Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru 2012-2021: 84 criminal complaints involving 88 victims and 72 identified suspects; 58% of deaths concentrated in six fiscal districts - Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6) - placing La Libertad second in absolute count (level with Lima Norte) behind Lima. The study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and monitoring systems.

Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR of the Regional Government of La Libertad, dated 6 September 2024, approves promoting labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region. It declares that every such person has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity and/or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad.

Official-gazette record (El Peruano, publication date 07/11/2024) of Ordenanza Regional N.° 000009-2024-GRLL-CR, presented in the regional council's ordinary session of 3 September 2024, debated, approved and signed in Trujillo on 6 September 2024: Its object is positive-action measures for the effective labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in La Libertad - the right to formal, dignified, productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code (discrimination as a crime), recalls a 2014 regional-council session framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, recommends local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabajo); it enters into force the day after publication in El Peruano.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.

Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. The body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired, and no suspect had been identified.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyer campaigns targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and threatened a further wave. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings of trans people continue in the country's ordinary, urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. A 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Atlántico sits inside that national pattern. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 annual report, "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", records 270 LGBTIQ+ victims nationally in 2025, a 63% increase over 2024, of which 165 were homicides, meaning one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours. The report describes the violence as a continuum running from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity, and documents its territorial expansion into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, criticising the state response as insufficient.

For the Atlántico department the same report documents 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases. It designates Barranquilla, the department's main hub, and the nearby municipality of Soledad as territories with a "high" threat level for this population. Publimetro Colombia reported the finding under the headline of increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Atlántico and Colombia.

Impunity is the operative condition. The report finds that threats show near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage, and names this failure of investigation and prosecution as the structural feature of the crisis rather than an incidental gap.

One institutional commitment is on record: the department's development plan, and Barranquilla's, commit coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.
