13589884B76063723503478.name: Amazonas
13589884B76063723503478.summary:
Amazonas stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America on legal gender recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe, and it is the national picture against which this department is assessed. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one count put hate-crime killings of trans people at 13 in the first quarter of 2025 alone. Sara Millerey, a 32-year trans woman, was beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, and died the following afternoon with no one arrested; her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia, and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.

Where armed groups operate, the threat is organised and announced. In Caquetá, armed groups gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulated "social cleansing" flyers against trans women, forcing her to relocate twice after death threats; in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". An activist quoted in the reporting states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases. Reported totals for that pattern include 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Protection machinery exists alongside that failure. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence against them as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; a Colombian court has also ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

No Amazonas-specific finding on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available for this entry. The assessment therefore rests on the national framework and the national pattern of violence and prosecution, which apply throughout the country including this department.

13589884B23733272568917.name: Cundinamarca
13589884B23733272568917.summary:
No finding specific to Cundinamarca on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources; the national framework these sources carry is what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country, and for this department the operative detail is documents. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a birth certificate — options include female, male and two further markers — and since August 2023 passports issued within the country offer three gender options; a 9 July 2026 decree obliges public notaries to complete a marker change within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free, and shields the change history from public disclosure, and a 4 February 2022 ruling by the national court ordered the further marker option to be offered to everyone. The process is a notarial one with no surgery or court ruling required, though a 2016 report documented some notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending psychiatric pathologisation.

The risk context reported elsewhere: an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in another part of the country circulating 'social cleansing' flyers naming trans women, giving them a week to leave, and killing more than forty trans women nationally in 2023; a further national report on the same pattern (August 2025) could not be retrieved in full at research time and is carried only as context; and a widely shared report of the killing of a trans woman in a metropolitan area elsewhere in the country prompted national alarm in April 2025 — that killing was reported in another department, not here.

Nothing in the record marks Cundinamarca as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and the absence of Cundinamarca-specific findings reflects where such violence gets reported, not proven safety.

sources.summary: EL PAÍS English, 14 April 2025, documents the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia. She was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025, the assault was filmed, and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. No Córdoba-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented. The national pattern is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested.

The Guardian, 30 July 2024, documented armed groups in Caquetá department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. No Córdoba-specific finding is documented. The pattern relied on here is territorial violence and displacement of trans people by armed actors.

13589884B25788978851461.name: Arauca
13589884B25788978851461.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

Colombian courts have also intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The source inventory establishes no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding for Arauca. What is documented for this department is the national pattern of lethal violence against trans people, episodic state response and armed-group activity elsewhere in the country, with no Arauca-specific aggravation or protection on the record.

Nationally the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025; 41 trans women were killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. The assault was filmed and the video went viral from 5 April 2025; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one was arrested. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was".

Armed groups continue to threaten trans people in territories under their control. In Caquetá, "social cleansing" flyers appeared on streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Colombia
sources.summary: Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, and in 2011 Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, with the first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016. Three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights, and a November 2015 ruling granted full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X. Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. Casanare adds no separate legal regime, so these national provisions define the formal legal exposure of a trans visitor to the department.

13589884B18807997781037.name: Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina
13589884B18807997781037.summary:
The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework. The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Targeted killings of trans people continue in ordinary urban settings. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia. The assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was", and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the same reporting records the stabbing death of a trans woman sleeping rough.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

The source inventory records no incident, law or enforcement finding specific to Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina. A trans visitor to the islands is therefore assessed against the national position: the recognition framework set out above, and a national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence in which no arrest was recorded even after an investigation was ordered at the highest level.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
For a trans visitor the mechanism is legal rather than customary: a national measure approved by the legislature in 2025 bars trans people from using public restrooms corresponding to their gender identity, with narrow carve-outs for medical care, custody and accompanying minors or disabled persons and a ban on "ambiguous" restroom signage; its own trigger was a complaint about toilet signage at the capital's airport, and enforcement is expected to rest on security staff checking identity documents to decide who may use a women's restroom, so restroom access is the flashpoint the law itself creates. Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation.

A national human-rights institute published a detailed critique calling the measure institutionalised discrimination, and a leading activist notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. No local variation is documented for Puno, and no department-level enforcement or incident appears in the audited sources.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025 and, as national law, binds Puno.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The analysis addresses the national framework that governs Puno and records no Puno-specific finding.

1875124B61751373376494.summary:

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

The piece recounts the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots (Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier), with two killers arrested in March 2023, and notes the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. 1875124B1797874831789.name: Amazonas
1875124B1797874831789.summary:
Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes and waived a second vote. Its Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement reaches private premises as well as public buildings. IDEHPUCP recalls SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, in which a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where bathroom assignment was grounded on the sex recorded in the DNI. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement of the national restriction would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

National monitoring is the only violence data available for this territory. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020-2023, the homicide victims comprising 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. The institute recalls a 2022 decision in which a national consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym chain, where bathroom assignment was grounded on the sex recorded in the national identity document. 1875124B63771233756824.name: Apurímac
1875124B63771233756824.summary:
Apurímac stands under the national framework of Peru. No Apurímac-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources attached to this record, and all three are national in scope; the operative rules for a visitor in the department are therefore the laws and enforcement patterns recorded at national level.

The most direct legal exposure concerns public restrooms. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were merged and approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025; the measure bars trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their sex at birth, with exceptions only for custody, situations requiring medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and it bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The congressional Plenary approved and exempted from a second vote on 2 April 2025 the bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', and it was enacted as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025. The package followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the Jorge Chávez airport.

The IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

In practice, access to restrooms now turns on the personal judgment of security staff, potentially including identity-document checks, a consequence flagged by LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho; she also notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private premises as well as public facilities: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome leaves Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023, of whom 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. Among the cases is the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Accountability has come once, after long litigation. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

1875124B76579830071892.name: Ayacucho
1875124B76579830071892.summary:
Ayacucho stands under Peru's national framework. No region-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for the department appears in the sources, and all three attached sources are national in scope, so the operative facts for a visitor are the national ones.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but public-facility access is now restricted by law. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025 and the merged dictamen was approved by the plenary and exempted from second vote on 2 April 2025. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their biological sex, with exceptions only for custody, where medical attention is required, or for accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the same package bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The legislative trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the Jorge Chávez airport.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same rule into force for trans people, including trans youth, and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Enforcement reaches private premises as well as state facilities: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied the policy. Whether the 2 April 2025 bill has formally entered into force is not documented in the attached sources, and if it is in force a trans traveller using public restrooms in Ayacucho faces a live national legal exposure.

Practical access depends on front-line discretion. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that restroom use would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, and violence against trans people is documented and rising: 54 TLGBI people were killed and 170 rights-violation cases recorded over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected.

One case defines the ceiling of protection. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was abducted by a gang in central Lima and killed in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.

Arequipa department has no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding on record. All three attached sources are national in scope, and as national measures they bind the department. The operative legal frame for a visitor to Arequipa is the national one.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

1875124B48847835594727.summary:
Moquegua has no recorded trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement finding, and the available sources are all national. The congressional committee on women and family unanimously approved the report backing bills 6506 and 8457, which would bar trans people from public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite their birth sex — exceptions only for custody, medical care and accompanying children under 12, the elderly or disabled — and require unambiguous signage; as of February 2025 the report still awaited full-chamber approval. 25984515B95172477822815.name: Adana
25984515B95172477822815.summary:
Adana Province stands under the Turkish national framework without any province-specific overlay: the source record contains no Adana provision on gender identity, documentation, policing or facilities, and no local enforcement data either. What a trans visitor meets in Adana is therefore the countrywide position, set at national level.

The baseline is permissive on its face. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the year gender reassignment surgery became lawful. A visitor whose passport marker has been changed abroad or at home can present that document without the change itself constituting an offence.

The direction of travel runs the other way. A leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people across Türkiye; Human Rights Watch described it as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. The measure is national, contains no province-specific provisions, and would apply in Adana if adopted. Istanbul activists held a press conference against the draft on 28 October 2025.

Two further gaps bear directly on a visitor. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so there is no statutory complaint to make against a hotel, clinic or officer who treats a trans guest differently. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition at all: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. A partner travelling alongside a trans visitor has no recognised standing in any Turkish proceeding.

LGBT people are also barred from serving openly in the military, a restriction that falls on residents rather than tourists but that shapes the official attitude a visitor encounters at any checkpoint where identity is examined.

25984515B26209284550223.name: Afyonkarahisar
25984515B26209284550223.summary:
Afyonkarahisar stands entirely under Turkey's national legal and policing framework on LGBTI+ matters. The draft omnibus justice package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision, and no provincial record exists that would make this province either more protective or more hostile than the country-wide picture. A visitor to Afyonkarahisar is subject to the same national rules, the same document regime and the same street-level policing practice documented elsewhere in Turkey.

The leaked '11th Judicial Package' would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison; participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would carry up to four years, and because same-sex marriage is not legal in Turkey such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. The measure had not been enacted when reported, but authorities have already been documented acting against trans people as though comparable prohibitions were in force.

The same draft would restrict gender-affirming care: the minimum surgery age raised from 18 to 25, permanent infertility imposed as a condition, medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years, and transgender patients facing up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Rights groups assess that these limits would push transition care into underground settings.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records 313 violations of the right to liberty, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total and consisting mostly of detentions, alongside 336 violations of the right to assembly and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51. The torture figure is linked mainly to peaceful assembly, and the report documents event-specific bans together with violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. These are national figures; no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding appears in the source.

The same report records six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them counted as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. These totals are compiled from media and civil-society reporting because the Turkish state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the true figure cannot be verified from official records.

Hostility has been institutionalised under a 'Year of the Family' banner: instructions issued to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The source presents this as national practice rather than a choice available to any province, which means it applies in Afyonkarahisar as it does in Istanbul or Ankara.

Two national rules bear directly on a trans visitor's exposure at any checkpoint. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, and police conducting 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) stops have required trans women to produce documents. Any such interaction is an occasion on which passport details can be compared against presentation. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT checks before release; that city-level pattern is one illustration of a national practice, not a separate local regime.

Two further national measures shape what a trans person faces if detained. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex rather than gender identity, confirmed by the death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 and by the parliamentary question filed by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option on gender-related medical-board reports and required electronic reports, a change assessed as risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

25984515B26209284550223.tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch describes the draft package as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades, a framing that places the current Turkish position at the severe end of European practice rather than within ordinary regional variation.

The pattern has depth rather than being a single legislative moment. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's continuity, not as a statement of current law.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Istanbul Pride is the country's most visible single flashpoint and should be read as an indicator of national direction, not as a distinct local rule.

The asymmetry of state response is documented at case level. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

25984515B26209284550223.localsOnly:
Kaos GL compiles its violation counts from media and civil-society reports because the state maintains no official hate-crime statistics. Residents therefore have no official channel through which to establish the scale of anti-trans violence, and the association's annual totals are the working reference for advocacy.

The 'Year of the Family' designation operates as an instruction to public institutions, and the resulting hostility is expressed through hate speech from senior officials, censorship of broadcasts and cancellation of artistic events. For residents this reaches employment, public service delivery and cultural participation, not only policing.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The Sincan Women's Prison case drew a coordinated response from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanding an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before Poyraz's death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 followed a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports. For residents already in the system, the change alters how transition care is recorded and authorised, and online framing of it as an 'LGBT opening' is contested.

Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison; participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would carry up to four years, and since same-sex marriage is not legal such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. The draft would also restrict gender-affirming care, raising the surgery age from 18 to 25 and requiring permanent infertility as a condition, with medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years and transgender patients facing up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Human Rights Watch assessed that the restrictions would push transition care into underground settings.

The draft had not been enacted when reported, but its pending status has not stopped authorities from behaving as though equivalent prohibitions already bind them. The national LGBTI+ association's 2025 report documents hostility institutionalised under a 'Year of the Family' banner, with instructions issued to public institutions and hate speech from senior officials, alongside censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report presents this as national practice, not as a choice made by any one province.

The same report counted six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them recorded as hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected. These figures were compiled from media and civil-society reporting because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the true total cannot be verified from official sources.

It also records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly; 336 violations of assembly rights; and 313 violations of liberty, a roughly 2.5-fold increase made up largely of detentions, alongside event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings.

Checkpoint contact is the principal routine risk for a foreign visitor. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 local currency units for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Police stops of trans women for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks have been recorded in 2025, with those stopped required to produce original documents; any such interaction is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk where the two do not match.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. a transgender prisoner was found dead in a women's prison cell on 1 December 2025, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. a health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required electronic reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

25984515B97476213604692.name: Antalya
25984515B97476213604692.summary:
Antalya stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality". It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on condition of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it.

The Kaos GL report "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy", presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, documents senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner, creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

The draft package contains no province-specific provisions, and the surviving record carries no Antalya-level breakdown. Neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established for this province; the documented national picture applies here unchanged.

For a visitor, the practical exposure point is the identity-document checkpoint. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any such stop is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, and foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original documents.

Street-level enforcement elsewhere in Turkey shows how these stops are used. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police issued no fines but documented them anyway, and that enforcement was being applied before the new law had been passed.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Street-level enforcement in the largest city shows that gap in practice. During 2025 police there stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in a central district and held them at a police station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate protections against degrading treatment under the international human-rights convention. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule compounds this. Foreign nationals must carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 units of the national currency and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in a major city by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring of the 2025 trans and LGBTI+ pride week in that city found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

The national prison profile, prepared with a civil society penal-system association using international LGBT national data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. a health ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a provincial health directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the report launch.

25984515B40051660631000.summary:
Aksaray stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy under a Year of the Family banner, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between pending legislation and practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk for a visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

The surviving record for this province is entirely national-level and carries no Aksaray-specific breakdown. Neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established from the inventory, and the documented national picture applies here unchanged.

25984515B40051660631000.tangentialFactors:
Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting the family and public morals, language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. The pending status of the draft package has not prevented enforcement from preceding legislation, a pattern the detained woman in Istanbul described directly.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

25984515B40051660631000.localsOnly:
Transition-related care is tightening for residents. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison, with custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.
25984515B40051660631000.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses Aksaray directly. The absence of provincial material is a gap in sourcing, not a finding that conditions in Aksaray differ from the national record; local police practice, municipal services and any provincial health-directorate circulars specific to Aksaray remain unresolved.

The 11th Judicial Package was reported as a leaked draft and had not been passed as of October 2025. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not sourced here and should be rechecked against current legislation before travel.

The claim that street-level GBT checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights rests on legal experts cited in reporting rather than on a court ruling; no judgment establishing that position is sourced in the inventory.

Figures on detentions and violations come from Kaos GL's own monitoring and may undercount incidents that never reached formal channels, as the 43 off-record detention decisions suggest.

25984515B60965754972902.name: Ardahan
25984515B60965754972902.summary:
Ardahan province stands under the national framework of Turkey. The documentation available for this jurisdiction is national in scope, and the draft instrument described below contains no Ardahan-specific provisions; without any provincial breakdown in the record, the national picture governs what a trans visitor to Ardahan should expect to face.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus justice package, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality". Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades.

The draft reaches ceremonies and medical care as well as public conduct. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, with penalties of up to four years in prison. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility to that care, and punish the health professionals who perform it. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft.

The package had not been enacted at the time of reporting. Kaos GL's 2025 report, whose findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, documents that hostility toward LGBTI+ people had already hardened into explicit state policy during the year, carried under a "Year of the Family" banner by senior officials whose hate speech and instructions to public institutions created a climate encouraging human-rights violations.

For a visitor, the practical point of contact with that policy is the identity check. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, and any police stop becomes an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, with an outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match the gender marker recorded in the document.

25984515B60965754972902.tangentialFactors:
Kaos GL records that the 2025 campaign extended well beyond policing into the regulatory sphere, with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The breadth of that instruction set, issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner, indicates a coordinated administrative posture rather than isolated incidents of official prejudice.

The gap between a leaked draft and enacted law is real, but the Kaos GL findings describe institutions behaving as though the direction of travel were settled.

25984515B60965754972902.localsOnly:
Residents of Ardahan live under the national framework's provisions directly. The draft would expose people to prison for participating in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, would place the age floor for gender-affirming health care at 25 with mandatory permanent infertility, and would make clinicians liable for providing that care. Each of those provisions would fall on residents' family life and long-term access to treatment rather than on visitors.

Kaos GL's report describes senior officials issuing instructions to public institutions during a "Year of the Family" year, accompanied by hate speech from senior officials. For residents, that means the administrative bodies handling permits, schooling, health and documentation operate under an explicit directive, which shapes how ordinary applications and complaints are received.

Regulatory and supervisory bodies were found to be systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom across the year. Residents working in the arts, publishing, academia or advocacy face that supervision as a matter of working life. Findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the report launch.
25984515B60965754972902.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved. The inventory supports the draft's contents and its status as reported on 29 October 2025, and carries nothing later.

No Ardahan-specific material appears in the inventory. There are no documented stops, detentions, prosecutions or facility conditions for this province, and no evidence in the record showing whether local practice is stricter or more permissive than the national picture; that question is not sourced either way.

The inventory also does not resolve how existing criminal provisions were applied in Ardahan before or alongside the draft, nor does it identify any court, prison, hospital or police unit in the province for verification purposes.

25984515B19802935753104.name: Bitlis
25984515B19802935753104.summary:
Every province in Türkiye sits under the same intensifying national framework. A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package (October 2025) would criminalise LGBT conduct and advocacy — up to 3 years for behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and 4 years for same-sex ceremonies — and would raise gender-affirming-care eligibility from 18 to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate, exposing providers to fines and up to 7 years and patients to up to 3 years; 15 LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. The Kaos GL 2025 human-rights report ('A Major Siege', published February 2026) finds hostility became explicit state policy in 2025 — presidency-centred, implemented through the family ministry — documenting 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment cases (up from 51) and 313 liberty violations (about 2.5-fold), counted from media coverage because the state keeps no hate-crime statistics.

The absence of recorded provincial enforcement is not evidence of local tolerance, and equally not evidence of a local ban.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's Turkey country overview records the national framework a visitor to an interior province like Düzce stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been decriminalised since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkish marriage law gives same-sex relationships no legal recognition and offers no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption, while no comprehensive law bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service. It also tracks the criminalisation push described in the HRW source: in early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants, per Amnesty International.

sources.summary: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW news release, Oct 29, 2025, reports a leaked omnibus draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years. 25984515B11362042972294.name: Kırıkkale
25984515B11362042972294.summary: central; military-industrial conservative; Assessed relative to the national picture in Turkey. Kırıkkale has no province-specific law, ordinance or incident series in the record; a trans visitor here stands under the same national framework that binds every province. A leaked draft omnibus justice package (the '11th Judicial Package', October 2025) would enable criminal charges against LGBT people nationwide: conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' — including its so-called promotion — would carry up to three years in prison (an amendment to the article on 'indecent acts'), participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years (same-sex marriage is not recognised, so such ceremonies are symbolic, which bears on travelling with a partner), and gender-affirming healthcare would be restricted to people 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules, allowing charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them, with the package justified as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. Enforcement context: authorities have banned Pride events in most years, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans, and in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, arbitrarily detaining more than 90 people. A February 2026 newspaper report says the government is considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with one to three years in prison.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch news release (29 October 2025): a leaked draft omnibus reform (the '11th Judicial Package') would amend the penal code so that acting 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' — or its promotion — carries up to three years in prison (an amendment to article 225 on 'indecent acts'), restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules, and allow criminal charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them; justified as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. HRW called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade and urged withdrawal.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Kırıkkale included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. central Anatolia. Assessed relative to the national picture in Turkey. What a trans visitor faces here is set by the national framework, and the record documents no province-specific law, ordinance or incident for Kırşehir.

Legal protections and enforcement: there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition — no marriage, union or adoption — so partner-travel status rests on nothing. A leaked draft omnibus justice package (October 2025) would criminalise conduct and its promotion deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to three years in prison, would restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under mandatory infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and would expose medical professionals and the trans people they treat to criminal charges, forcing treatment underground.

Practical safety: Pride events have been banned in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions; the 2025 monitoring report describes hostility turned into explicit state policy, and national monitoring logged an identity-check round-up of about twenty trans women.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch news release (29 October 2025): a leaked draft omnibus reform (the '11th Judicial Package') would amend the penal code so that acting 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' — or its promotion — carries up to three years in prison (an amendment to article 225 on 'indecent acts'), restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people 25 and over under onerous eligibility rules, and allow criminal charges against trans people and the professionals who treat them; justified as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals'. HRW called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks of the decade and urged withdrawal.

Kaos GL (24 February 2026): presentation of its 'LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025', titled 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People'. Findings: anti-LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy in 2025 — targeting of LGBTI+ people as 'deviant' or 'a threat' by the president and senior officials raised officials' motivation and third-party impunity; the new Family Ministry became the implementing ministry; one LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed; platforms and broadcasters were penalised or withdrew; artistic events were cancelled. The report documents six violations of the right to life (three hate-motivated killings; trans people most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (51 the previous year, largely during assemblies) and 313 liberty violations in 2025 (about 2.5 times the previous year, mostly detentions). No official hate-crime statistics exist; cases rely on media.

sources.summary: Muş province stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; no Muş-specific ordinance, incident or court decision is documented for the province. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' being leaked publicly. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches; police used water cannon and tear gas on the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. Press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.summary: Under Türkiye's national framework, which applies in Niğde: homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, and Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions, and ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible. No Niğde-specific source covers these points.

sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26), which covers the national situation applying to every province including Niğde: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end, and in December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Amnesty records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.
