sources.title: Human rights in Türkiye - Amnesty International (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records the national framework governing a visitor to Siirt: in June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. No Siirt-specific incident is documented; this is the province-level applicable national framework.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia

No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence — not as evidence of local permissiveness: the nationwide framework below governs here as in every province.

As documented nationally: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would make conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality punishable by up to three years, criminalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and bar gender-affirming care under age 25 behind a permanent-infertility assessment, with patients and providers exposed to prosecution; civil-society groups and the country's medical association protested, and an established human-rights court precedent is invoked against it. sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) on Türkiye's leaked draft 11th Judicial Package: amendments would criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' under penal-code article 225 (up to 3 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care to 25, expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges, and penalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to 4 years); the package rides the 'Year of the Family' framing.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Turkey permits transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery and court approval) but has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable, and because marriage eligibility is determined by the gender recorded in the civil registry rather than by trans status, a person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. 19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law alongside the national femicide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. For a trans visitor, the operative risk is police identification and detention: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident.

sources.summary: The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on April 10, 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. According to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026, 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases). Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty, inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. The latter decree prohibits those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Direction: worse than national — the only Brazilian state in the country to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and the venue of a nationally decisive refusal. A trans woman was refused entry to the women's bathroom by staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre, urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to take public transport home; on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving these refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules — the legal exposure a visibly trans visitor faces using bathrooms in shops, restaurants and transport hubs.

In the other direction, the state has a visible LGBTQ tourism scene with pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages and marker changes, and nationwide legal rights are identical, so visitors see the same national protections as elsewhere.

sources.summary: Santa Catarina's constitution contains an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among non-discrimination grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions adopted after the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity. A deeply conservative Congress has nonetheless generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. These guarantees apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy. The Superior Court of Justice ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes. Joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed by STF RE 846.102 (2015). Gender-marker changes proceed without surgery. ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

82249235B24619009834807.summary:
Visitors in every province stand under the national framework: gender identity and expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions, and marriage and identity documents are national.

BC: consistently Canada's most progressive province on LGBT issues (first human-rights code inclusion 1992); Vancouver Davie Village scene. Regional evidence: no hostile provincial legislation, but a documented 2023 wave of coordinated disruptions against public drag-storytime events at libraries — Coquitlam Public Library postponed/cancelled repeatedly (Jan 14 2023 protest at the Town Centre branch; Oct 13 2023 postponement) under "public safety risk" claims, with a counter-gathering becoming the largest queer gathering the Tri-Cities had seen; at a Richmond library event with no police on scene a man pushed through to photograph the performer; a Granville Island children's drag camp was threatened and required a public rally of support. Assessed relative to the national picture in Canada.

Incidents targeting sexual orientation declined 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. The figures are national and contain no British Columbia breakdown.

sources.summary: Outright International country page (12 March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since March 2022; since 2012 Chile's hate-crime law has included sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances; same-sex civil unions have been recognised since 2015. 13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry trans and non-binary markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans violence. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a city in Antioquia near Medellín, the 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed her. The video went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured limbs flailing in a creek unable to swim. She died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events were held in several cities, and protests followed. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025; the first two victims were gay men. Her mother Sandra Borja stated that they killed her for being who she was.

Care access in the same episode is documented: a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency because she had not been shot. One report counted 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone, alongside 41 transgender women killed in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024.

Where armed groups operate, the risk is structured rather than incidental. In the department of Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, armed groups distributed flyers on streets and on WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave; trans women there fled after death threats. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording 'All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'. In Caquetá, trans women reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Céspedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

13589884B40908771570386.name: Bogota Capital District
13589884B40908771570386.summary:
Bogotá Capital District: the best-documented trans community and services in the country, alongside a documented police-violence pattern in its tolerance zone. Red Comunitaria Trans, a trans community organisation, reported police shouting at, baton-beating and shooting at trans sex workers in the early hours on a central street (the district mayor's office took up the case); two trans women were killed within hours of each other on the night of 2 January 2026; and a 32-year-old trans activist was found dead in the eastern hills in December 2023.

For a visitor, the operative screening reality is mass identity-check operations: 200+ officers in one district, San Bernardo (April 2025), and over 1,200 uniformed officers with background and migrant control in another, Santa Fe (January 2026) — a visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá is therefore statistically likely to be in the path of a sweep. Assessed relative to the national picture in Colombia; nationwide legal rights — same-sex marriage since April 2016, adoption from 2015, an anti-discrimination law since 2011, gender-marker change without court proceedings since a 2012 ruling, and nonbinary and transgender markers on the national identity card from 2026 — are what a visitor's documents stand under.

sources.summary: El País in English (April 14, 2025): the transphobic murder that shocked the country - Sara Millerey, 32, a trans woman, beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello (Antioquia) on 4 April 2025; national context: 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025, presidential call to investigate, vigils in several cities. Cited in this record as national lethal-violence context.
CNN (August 6, 2025): the article covers attacks against LGBTQ people in Colombia in the context of the Millerey case.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's Colombia overview is the national framework every visitor to Bogotá Capital District stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016 (making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so); adoption equality came in 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; and transgender people have had a right to change legal gender recognised since 1993, reinforced by a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling allowing civil-registry change without a family court. It also records Bogotá-specific facts: a 2012 ruling let a transgender woman choose her own hairstyle and makeup in prison, Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá, pride parades in Bogotá number among the country's large LGBTQ events, and a Washington Post report describes thriving gay neighbourhoods in Bogotá. Beginning in 2026, nonbinary and transgender options are offered on the national identity card.

25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid (Chueca) ranks among the most visible LGBT urban scenes in Europe, with total anonymity in daily life; its Pride is among the largest in Europe. The national framework a visitor's documents stand under is the self-ID law of 28 February 2023: legal gender recognition from age 16 with no diagnosis required, with broad anti-discrimination guarantees and employment and health measures.

This community's own legislative divergence is statutory but narrow: on 27 December 2023 two community laws — Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023 — amended its 2016 gender-identity law and its anti-LGBTBI law on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, stripping the provisions that obliged educational institutions; the resulting restrictions sit in the school environment and do not touch a visitor's public conduct, documents or entry.

sources.summary: Official text (BOE) of Ley 4/2023 (28 February 2023), "for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGTBI people": establishes self-ID legal gender recognition (16+, no diagnosis), broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy. National framework that Madrid's 2023 amendments sit beside.

Human Rights Watch (Feb 2023): "Victory in Fight for Gender Recognition in Spain" - hails Spain's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory after years of activism. National framework context.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles three statutes - what Law 4/2023 does and does not do; the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 of the Penal Code (gender identity/expression motives); and the hate offences of Article 510 CP extended to trans/LGBTI people. National framework context.

sources.title: Diversidad sexual en Madrid - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
sources.summary: Spanish Wikipedia's Madrid LGBT article describes Madrid as one of Europe's main LGBT hubs and records the city's scene: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2005; Madrid Pride (MADO), held annually in late June or early July, is described as one of the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees; the Chueca district is the epicentre of the community. It records local institutions: COGAM, founded 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation; the city government runs an Oficina de Atencion a la Diversidad Sexual y de Genero; Arcopoli focuses on fighting discrimination and violence. For a traveler's assessment, the article states that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in Madrid, and that marginalised LGBT groups, such as migrants and trans people, face additional barriers.

sources.title: Ley trans (España) - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
sources.summary: The Spanish Wikipedia article on trans law records that the Comunidad de Madrid was among the first Spanish regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and Region de Murcia, following Extremadura in 2015. That 2016 regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023. The article also covers the state-level Ley 4/2023 (Organic Law of 28 February 2023) on gender self-determination and the framework with which regional statutes such as Madrid's must comply, which sets the statutory floor a trans traveler in the region stands under.

19338628B30439183828151.name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
19338628B30439183828151.summary:
Visitors in every region stand under the national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions.

Dijon / Cote-d'Or: rural traditional department. Regional evidence: the only prefecture in the country found to have twice banned a Pride march from its city centre with the ban upheld - on 12 June 2025 the prefecture prohibited the Pride 2025 march in central Dijon citing "risk of trouble to public order", the second consecutive year of the same restriction; the organisers' withdrawal citing LGBT visibility was itself called significant by the city. On 14 June 2025 the administrative court rejected the legal challenge, and the march (about 1,500 people per police) proceeded on a diverted route around the historic centre; the prefecture justified the ban by estimated organiser numbers (200 vs previous 2,500 and 1,500 turnouts) and a stated risk of violent individuals attaching themselves. The march itself passed peacefully ("joyful and festive, without a hitch") - the harm documented here is the restriction and its chilling effect, not violence. Assessed relative to the national picture in France.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): trans women incarcerated in the country on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal grey area and are punished beyond their alleged crimes - placement problems in the prison system. National prison-system context (not prefecture-specific).

The national detention ombuds's opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: based on about 40 referrals since 2010, finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across all places of detention; recommendations also apply to intersex and non-binary persons. National prison-system context.

Its transidentité section covers the legal framework for gender recognition in France. This supplies the national legal baseline (marriage, anti-discrimination law, gender recognition) that applies identically in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, against which the region's own documented restriction (the Dijon Pride march ban) is an exception rather than the rule.

The page also records the nationwide growth of marches since the mid-1990s (with marches spreading to provincial cities from 1994-1995 onward), providing the French regional context in which the Dijon restriction occurred.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
Visitors in every region stand under the national framework: national law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions.

The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: Paola, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — Kara B., held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.

The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the state and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the state, including here.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

65028918B14696209246677.summary: Region research direction: mixed — the country's largest LGBTQ+ community and its biggest police raids coexist, with police acting without legal basis. sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Indonesia' page supplies the national framework the capital stands under and documents Jakarta's raid pattern in detail: police arrested 141 people over a 'gay sex party' in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 (ten charged), and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 (six charged), all pursued under the pornography law. More recently it records 56 people detained at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine detained at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 arrested at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025 — offences there can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'. Transgender people may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval, and there is no general anti-discrimination law, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific statute.

1811400B15614733245507.name: Mahārāshtra
1811400B15614733245507.summary: Region research direction: worse than national on public-festival access screening — religion-based identity verification doubles as an outing mechanism for gender-nonconforming visitors. After the VHP publicly urged garba (autumn dance festival) organisers not to allow non-Hindus and to check Aadhaar cards for entry, a political row erupted; in Nagpur organisers imposed Aadhaar verification, security checks with "male and female" boundaries and a ritual bow before a Varaha avatar as entry conditions. An identity-checked, religion-screened entry gate at a public festival is precisely the mechanism by which a gender-nonconforming visitor is examined and outed by authorities who are not supposed to be involved — and it is happening in named cities, not nationwide. National backdrop from this record's sources: parliament passed a 2026 amendment bill removing the right to self-identify, limiting recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification for gender-affirming procedures, and creating offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender punishable with up to life in prison — prompting nationwide protests from trans communities, with a Supreme Court-appointed panel asking the government to withdraw it; the national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards needed for social security.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch news release, 26 March 2026, on the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill. The bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender, provisions HRW calls reminiscent of colonial-era laws criminalising transgender persons for appearing dressed as women. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, while only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security. The national framework applies in every state, including Maharashtra.

BBC News article on the 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now needing presidential assent. It removes the right to self-identification and narrows recognition, reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling on third gender and self-determination. Critics warn it could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits. Lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar called the medical-certification requirement an "attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual", while the government argues the narrower definition targets those facing "extreme and oppressive" discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. The framework applies in every state, including Maharashtra.

1811400B23625213884851.name: Delhi
1811400B23625213884851.summary:
Delhi sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a supreme-court-appointed advisory panel urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.

The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems. HRW calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security. This national documentation gap bears directly on Delhi as the capital, and the source records no Delhi-specific event.

BBC News reported that the 2026 amendment bill has been approved by both houses and now awaits presidential assent, removing the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court ruling. In Delhi, activist Grace Banu told a press conference that the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation". A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider amid privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary:
The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 national human-rights-commission survey (591 trans respondents) quantified the underlying fear: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, 36% went without; a 2021 district-court judgment awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Recognition has also liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved gender-marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.

sources.summary: Seoul-specific ruling coverage (Korea Times, 22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court, presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for plaintiff A in a damages lawsuit against the state, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed. The decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed. The court held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights, stating that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found that 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. A 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling awarded 7 million won in damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The court sits outside Seoul, and the ruling bears on this jurisdiction as evidence of the national judicial trend cited for it.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Worse than national for what a visitor actually meets: this is the main tourist corridor, a large international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but police forces at both municipal and state level have repeatedly been documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people. Multiple recorded assaults during detention are concentrated in the two most visited resort towns; officers are described as untrained in human-rights standards; the municipal diversity office recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman; and two tourist-police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals.

Documents and screening: the airport city's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — directly relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Useful legal counterweights are resident-facing, and the record is scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch feature (31 March 2025), 'Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges'. Country-wide survey of legal gender recognition: 22 of 32 states had legislated an LGR procedure by March 2025, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco, Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans people's documents permanently mismatched; also documents coercive detention and border scrutiny risks for document-mismatched travellers.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Mexico' page gives the state-level legal picture a Quintana Roo visitor stands under: same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012 (two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded its Civil Code sets no gender requirement), and the state congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. The page records Quintana Roo among the states that enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and that banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, and lists the Quintana Roo penal code among hate-crime laws punishing crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender. It also notes the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination and that Cancún is among Mexico's principal gay-tourism destinations.

sources.title: Quintana Roo y Morelos prohíben las terapias de conversión - Tribuna de la Bahía
sources.summary: Local reporting (Tribuna de la Bahía, 15 December 2023) states that the Quintana Roo congress, following Morelos, banned conversion practices. Both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies. Penalties are two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA (measurement and updating unit) value for those who carry out such practices. The reform dated 15 December 2023 applies across the state, including tourist corridors such as Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

27671186B76269877687363.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework with no territorial carve-out. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforces colonial-era offences of "carnal knowledge against the order of nature" punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, and its own provisions carry 10 to 14 years for same-sex cohabitation, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advisory, as reported by Sahara Reporters, adds that the law reaches people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations.

The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and states that some states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that police have used the 2014 Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest, and that the statute reaches far beyond marriage.

A trans visitor should treat the territory as a place where a documented killing has gone unpunished. On 8 August 2024 the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker "Abuja Area Mama" was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja, hours after she posted a final video and having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". The Abuja police chief, Benneth Igweh, ordered a thorough and discreet investigation; six months later no suspects had been charged. A petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demands investigation of the killing as a hate crime, and a human-rights group has sued the national government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order compelling investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored.

Everyday enforcement is extortionate and violent. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, which makes dating apps an active entrapment vector rather than a social convenience.

Gender presentation carries exposure independent of identity documents. There is no legal route in Nigeria to change gender. Cross-dressing is banned under Sharia law in twelve states and in the Nigerian military, and Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available. Police in the Area Mama case recorded her as a man in female clothing, indicating how an officer's report can fix a trans person's legal status at the scene.

Detention carries a further uncertainty: placement between male and female sections is left to official discretion. Press coverage at the sentencing of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in.

An LGBTI human-rights observatory at a national university counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected, amid rising hate crimes. In 2025 the national congress — sitting and operating out of the capital — approved a norm against trans people's use of public bathrooms (committee vote February 2025; floor vote April 2025), which a national human-rights institute published an analysis calling legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space.

For a trans visitor, the capital is therefore where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence risk when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.

sources.summary: National-framework source (binds Lima as national policy): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the Muñante initiative barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth, stating the text also bars “ambiguous” bathroom signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”) and that the norm still required plenary backing. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and describing how enforcement would reduce to security staff demanding ID (DNI) based on their own judgment of whether a woman entering is trans.

National-framework source (the norm is national policy, enacted by the congress that sits and operates in Lima): IDEHPUCP analysis (15 Apr 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte) reports the Congress plenary on Wednesday 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR; article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The authors call the rule direct legislation that conditions basic rights on a “biological sex”, a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note trans people, though framed as aggressors, are more often victims of violence and discrimination.

National-framework source (observatory counts include Lima): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023, more than half of the dead being trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; 2023 saw the most homicides (19) and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. It recounts the 12 Feb 2023 kidnapping of transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the “Los Gallegos” extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots, and flags state inaction: no official system records victims’ sexual orientation and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara stands within Turkey's national framework, where hostility toward LGBTI people has hardened into explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice. Kaos GL's annual report "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", launched in 2025, places the hostility at the presidency, identifies the Ministry of Family as the implementing ministry, and records censorship of broadcasts, cancellation or banning of artistic events, and the closure of an LGBTI+ association for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The same report documents six violations of the right to life during the year, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with transgender people the most affected. It records a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year, and states that the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

The leaked draft "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. The package had not been enacted when reported, and its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

The capital houses the institutions that draft, contest and enforce those measures. Nothing on record shows local countervailing protection in Ankara, and the same courts and ministries implicated in the reporting operate here.

Prison conditions reach the capital directly. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Rights groups coordinated through Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison.

Document checks are the standing everyday exposure for a visitor. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation, which is a direct outing risk for a trans visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

25984515B47806653651907.tangentialFactors:
Street-level enforcement outside the capital shows how the framework operates before it is enacted. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. One of the women stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The depth of the regime is not new. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the pattern's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
25984515B47806653651907.localsOnly:
Residents face an administrative apparatus aimed squarely at them. Kaos GL records that the Ministry of Family operates as the implementing ministry for the hostility campaign, that broadcasts have been censored and artistic events cancelled or banned, and that an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so residents have no official measure of the violence they face.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

25984515B12971548112787.name: Eskişehir
25984515B12971548112787.summary: Eskişehir — university city, the most youthful-anonymous interior city; Amnesty's 2024 provincial monitoring records that authorities unlawfully prevented its Pride march, in a city that had previously hosted one of the country's few functioning pride events. National frame: the leaked October 2025 draft would criminalise 'conduct contrary to biological sex' and its promotion (up to 3 years) and restrict gender-affirming care (minimum age 25); a 2025 rights report records hostility as explicit state policy, six violations of the right to life, trans people most affected. Assessed relative to the national picture in Turkey.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a leaked '11th Judicial Package' would amend the penal and civil codes with articles threatening LGBT people — behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion' (up to three years' prison, amending the indecent-acts provision); sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility); potential charges against trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists; justified as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Eskişehir stands, and it names the province directly: in June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. It also records that Kadir Has University surveys saw public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rise from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

sources.title: Turkish police attack Eskişehir's first planned Pride march, detain 20 - Duvar English
sources.summary: Duvar English reports that Turkish police attacked Eskişehir's first planned Pride march days after police interventions in Istanbul and Ankara. Officers reached the area hours before the scheduled meeting time and carried out identity checks. Organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of 'violating the ban on the march'. Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years, citing security concerns and public order.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Gaziantep sits fully under Turkey's national baseline on LGBT rights, and the province shows no divergence from it. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. A visibly trans visitor's exposure in the province is the national one, locally enforced.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. For Gaziantep this evidences the state-level hostility and case-by-case prosecutions under the same meeting-and-demonstrations law that a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in Turkey, including this province.

66186276B86072070009793.name: Puerto Rico
66186276B86072070009793.summary:
Puerto Rico stands under the full the United States federal regime: the United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker has been eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor arriving on the United States documents faces that mismatch at entry; airport screening follows federal procedure; the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions here, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed; and in February 2025 the the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sports.

A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.

sources.summary: NCTE airport-security guide for trans travelers: all luggage is screened and may be hand-searched; prosthetics (incl. breast forms) are treated as medically necessary and not subject to the 3-liquid rule; medical equipment/prosthetics allowed through checkpoint after screening; advises packing strategies to reduce invasive searches. Applies at PR airports as federal TSA procedure - the framework a trans visitor actually stands under.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report.

sources.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory; the search found no separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling.

SYN-ASM.name: American Samoa
SYN-ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies, including the orders on sex classification in documents and federal facilities (EO 14168), gender-affirming care funding (EO 14187) and athletic participation (EO 14201), the last of which is paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all US identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth, new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; Lambda Legal and the Human Rights Campaign document how name and gender changes now interact with federal records. A trans visitor holding US documents faces that mismatch at Pago Pago, where screening follows US federal procedure.

The same January 2025 order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities used in accordance with their gender identity. The territory's hospital is federally funded, and the orders halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reach it, so a trans visitor who needs emergency or inpatient care may be placed in a ward or room corresponding to sex assigned at birth, or be separated from care that was previously funded.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in territory employment has produced federal enforcement. In September 2023 the US Department of Justice secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen, one of the documented trans-specific violence records for the territory.

Marriage recognition remains contested on the ground. The Fono Senate voted down a bill in March 2003 that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling, and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws changed. As of July 2024 an on-island constitutional survey by Professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the territory's same-sex marriage ban would survive a Fourteenth Amendment challenge, indicating the local ban is treated as operative. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; no same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date, and the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar and then the US Department of the Interior.

Social climate differs from the legal posture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, is described in university research as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association on an explicitly cultural-pride footing. Contemporary commentary reports homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, so visible nonconformity attracts comment more readily than official sanction.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

SYN-ASM.tangentialFactors:
Other US territories moved to apply the 2015 federal marriage ruling while American Samoa's attorney general said in 2015 that applicability was still under review; Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands had resolved the question, and no licence applications had been made in American Samoa at that point.

A 2009 travel column contrasts the territory with what it calls homophobia in Fiji, and records that fa'afafine locals openly courted Western visitors; the same source notes the fa'amatai chiefly system structures social life in both Samoan nations, and that Pago Pago hotels skew business rather than leisure travel. Local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin has called the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture.

At the 2003 committee hearing on the marriage ban bill, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine did not seek marriages with other men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. The bill's sponsor, Representative Sua Carl Schuster, introduced it to preempt the marriage litigation then unfolding in US states.

The 2024 survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tests not only constitutional durability but also whether the territory's collectivistic orientation and polychronic relationship to time bear on how such a challenge would be argued locally.
SYN-ASM.localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the terms of the September 2023 Department of Justice settlement with the American Samoa Government on harassment of a transgender employee, and by the litigation that produced the June 2023 hostile-work-environment finding against the territorial government; these are resident-facing employment protections and complaint routes rather than visitor entitlements.

Local gender-nonconforming residents organise through the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, founded in 2010 from the merger of the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, with fa'afafine identity framed as cultural reclamation rather than a Western import.

The fa'amatai chiefly system and church affiliation shape everyday expectations of dress and conduct for residents of all orientations, and reserved public behaviour is the local norm.

Resident couples seeking a marriage licence apply through the Territorial Registrar; a 2026 analysis by attorneys practising locally holds that the registrar must issue a certificate to a same-sex couple, and maps the challenge route through the High Court of American Samoa and then the US Department of Interior, though no couple has applied.

Fiti Alexander Sunia, confirmed unanimously as District Court judge in January 2016, remains the named judicial officer on record regarding performance of same-sex weddings absent a change in local law.
SYN-ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Obergefell is operative in American Samoa in practice is asserted in both directions by sourced material, a 2016 judicial statement and a 2026 law review conclusion, and no case has tested it; the territory's own marriage statute and its constitutional durability after the July 2024 survey are not settled in the sources.

Not sourced: whether the territory's hospital has actually altered ward assignment or care-funding practice since the January 2025 orders, and whether any trans visitor has been refused entry, detained or referred at Pago Pago on document grounds.

Unverified in the inventory: the current status of the ACLU suit against the State Department, the outcome of the Lambda Legal guidance as litigation proceeds, and the precise scope of the SWS25 visa restriction as applied to arrivals in this territory.

Open: whether the September 2023 DOJ settlement terms have been implemented, and whether any hate-crime or employment complaint by a trans person has been filed since February 2023.

SYN-GUM.name: Guam
SYN-GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the full the United States federal regime: the United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker has been eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor arriving on the United States documents faces that mismatch at entry; airport screening follows federal procedure; the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions here, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed; and in February 2025 the the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sports.

An unincorporated US territory, so the 2025–26 federal turn — marker/document policy, TSA screening, the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard on an island whose economy and society carry a large permanent US military presence. Local law partly cuts the other way: Guam was the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, after a local lesbian couple sued over a denied licence), its statute book bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009.

Academic Pacific-identity surveys record indigenous Chamorro understandings of gender diversity, and a local advocacy scene maintains ID-documents guidance for residents. The synthesis for a visitor: real written protections and a quiet, integrated public record, against military-community conservatism, federal volatility amplified by the base, and small-island visibility where an outed stranger is noticed.

Federal rollback above, a thin but genuinely welcoming local posture beneath.

A US commonwealth in political union: federal document, immigration and screening policy applies (including 2025–26 marker restrictions), while marriage recognition reached Saipan in 2015 by operation of the federal constitution — recognition exists, and nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression. In 2023 the legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute whose sentencing criteria expressly cover sexual orientation and gender identity — a formal, if recent, protection.

The policy accounting is nonetheless near-bottom: a comprehensive US equality index scores the commonwealth's gender-identity law in negative territory (sexual-orientation law 'low'), citing family-law gaps — no second-parent adoption, no assisted-reproduction recognition, no family-services protection. Visitor reality: no documented legal danger, a fresh hate-crime shield, minimal other institutional support, and high social visibility in small, church-influenced islands.
